108679.q: Roughly how much primary urine do an adult's kidneys filter each day?
108679.e: Every day the kidneys filter around 180 litres of primary urine from the blood. They take back over 99 per cent of it, so only a small remainder is passed out.
108679.m: The kidneys filter around 180 litres of primary urine every day.

108680.q: Why is urine often darker in the morning than during the day?
a: The kidney saves water at night, so the urine is more concentrated
You drank too much at night
The light in the bedroom colours it
The kidney rests completely at night
108680.e: At night you drink nothing. So the nephrons take more water back into the blood, and the urine becomes more concentrated and darker.
108680.m: Little water in the body makes urine darker.

108681.q: Which valuable substances do the tubules of the nephron take back from the primary urine into the blood?
108681.e: In the kidney tubules, water, glucose and many salts are taken back into the blood. Waste substances such as urea mostly stay in the urine.
108681.m: The nephron takes water, sugar and salts back into the blood.

108682.q: What does the kidney do if you have drunk too little on a hot day?
a: It saves water and makes less urine
It makes a lot of pale urine
It gives water to the stomach
108682.e: When water is short, a hormone makes the kidney take more water back into the blood. A small amount of dark urine is made.
108682.m: When water is short, the kidney saves water.

108683.q: What job does the renal pelvis do?
108683.e: In the renal pelvis, the finished urine from all parts of the kidney flows together. From there it flows on towards the bladder.
108683.m: The renal pelvis collects urine before it flows on.

108684.q: Where does urine flow from the renal pelvis?
108684.e: The renal pelvis narrows like a funnel and leads into the ureter. This carries the urine to the bladder.
108684.m: From the renal pelvis, urine flows into the ureter.

108685.q: Where does the ureter carry urine from the renal pelvis to?
108685.e: The ureter is a thin tube. It carries urine from the renal pelvis into the bladder, where it is collected.
108685.m: The ureter carries urine to the bladder.

108686.q: What are typical signs of a kidney infection?
a: Fever and pain in the side
108686.e: In a kidney infection, bacteria usually travel up from the bladder. Fever and pain at the side of the back are typical; it is treated with antibiotics.
108686.m: A kidney infection must be treated by a doctor.

108687.q: On which side of the bean-shaped kidney is the renal pelvis?
a: At the dent facing the spine
On the outside facing the back
108687.e: The kidney has a dent on its inner side, the hilum. Blood vessels go in and out there, and the renal pelvis is there too.
108687.m: The renal pelvis lies at the dent of the kidney.

108688.q: What shape is a human kidney?
108688.e: The kidney is bean-shaped and about as big as a fist. The kidneys lie to the left and right of the spine in the back.
108688.m: The kidney is shaped like a bean.

108689.q: What happens if the outflow from the renal pelvis is permanently blocked?
a: Urine backs up in the kidney.
The liver takes over the urine.
108689.e: If the outflow is blocked, for example by a stone, urine backs up and the renal pelvis widens. Without treatment, the kidney can be damaged.
108689.m: A blocked outflow makes urine back up into the kidney.

108690.q: The kidney has an outer and an inner layer. What is the outer one called?
108690.e: The renal cortex is on the outside, the renal medulla on the inside. Right in the middle, the renal pelvis collects the urine.
108690.m: The outer layer of the kidney is the renal cortex.

108691.q: Which formula is used to calculate mechanical work when force and distance point in the same direction?
108691.e: Work W is the product of the force F and the distance s, so W = F · s. The greater the force and distance, the more work is done.

108692.q: In which unit is work measured?
108692.e: The unit of work is the joule (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton acts over 1 metre.

108693.q: You push a trolley with a force of 50 N over 20 m. How much work is done?
108693.e: W = F · s = 50 N · 20 m = 1000 J. Force and distance point in the same direction.
108693.m: For work, you multiply force and distance.

108694.q: A force does 1500 J of work and acts over 300 m. How great is the force?
108694.e: From W = F · s, it follows that F = W : s. So F = 1500 J : 300 m = 5 N.
108694.m: Force is work divided by distance.

108695.q: You hold a heavy bag still in the air. How much work in the physics sense are you doing on the bag?
a: as much as when lifting it
twice as much as when lifting it
108695.e: In physics, work is only done when the object moves along the force. The bag does not move, so the distance is zero and the work is zero, even if your arms get tired.
108695.m: Without distance, no work in the physics sense is done.

108696.q: A force of 8 N does 400 J of work. Over what distance did the force act?
108696.e: From W = F · s, it follows that s = W : F. So s = 400 J : 8 N = 50 m.
108696.m: You get the distance by dividing the work by the force.

108697.q: A bike pulls a trailer with a force of 40 N over 2 km. How much work is done?
108697.m: Kilometres must be converted into metres before calculating.

108698.q: Which unit is equivalent to one joule?
108698.e: Because W = F · s, 1 J = 1 N · 1 m. So one joule is equal to one newton-metre.
108698.m: One joule is equal to one newton-metre.

108699.q: A crane pulls a load 0.4 m with a force of 2.5 kN. How much work is that?
108699.m: Kilonewtons must be converted into newtons before calculating.

108700.q: What does power in physics tell you?
a: how much work is done per unit of time
108700.e: Power P is the work done divided by the time taken, so P = W : t. Anyone who does the same work faster has more power.
108700.m: Power is work per unit of time.

108701.q: A machine does 3000 J of work in 60 s. What is its power?
108701.m: Power is work divided by time.

108702.q: A motor delivers 200 W for 30 s. How much work does it do?
108702.e: From P = W : t, it follows that W = P · t. So W = 200 W · 30 s = 6000 J.

108703.q: A pump with a power of 400 W is to do 12,000 J of work. How long does it take?
108703.e: From P = W : t, it follows that t = W : P. So t = 12,000 J : 400 W = 30 s.
108703.m: Time is work divided by power.

108704.q: Anna and Ben carry equally heavy boxes up to the same height. Anna takes 20 s, Ben 40 s. What is true?
a: Anna’s power is twice as great.
Ben’s power is twice as great.
Anna does twice as much work.
108704.e: Both do the same work. But Anna takes only half as long, so her power is twice as great.
108704.m: Anyone who does the same work faster has more power.

108705.q: Which letter is usually used for power in formulas?
108705.e: Power is written as P, from the English word “power”. W stands for work.
108705.m: In formulas, power has the symbol P.

108706.q: A force of 50 N moves a box 4 m in 10 s. What is the power?
108706.e: First the work: W = 50 N · 4 m = 200 J. Then P = 200 J : 10 s = 20 W.
108706.m: For power, you first work out the work and then divide by the time.

108707.q: How does the power change if the same work is done in half the time?
108707.e: In P = W : t, time is in the denominator. If you halve the time with the same work, the power becomes twice as great.
108707.m: Less time for the same work means more power.

108708.q: Which physical quantity is given in watts?
108708.e: The watt is the unit of power. Work is measured in joules, force in newtons and pressure in pascals.

108709.q: What is one watt equal to?
108709.e: One watt means that one joule is converted every second. So 1 W = 1 J/s.
108709.m: One watt is one joule per second.

108710.q: Who is the unit watt named after?
108710.e: The Scottish inventor James Watt greatly improved the steam engine in the 18th century. The unit of power is called the watt in his honour.
108710.m: The unit watt honours the inventor James Watt.

108711.q: How many watts are one kilowatt?
108711.e: The prefix “kilo” means thousand. So one kilowatt is 1000 watts.
108711.m: One kilowatt is a thousand watts.

108712.q: How many watts are one megawatt?
108712.e: “Mega” means one million. So one megawatt is 1000 kilowatts or 1,000,000 watts.
108712.m: One megawatt is a million watts.

108713.q: A hair dryer has 2.4 kW. How much is that in watts?
108713.e: You multiply the kilowatts by 1000: 2.4 · 1000 = 2400 W.
108713.m: To convert kilowatts into watts, multiply by a thousand.

108714.q: What does “2000 W” on a kettle mean?
108714.e: The number of watts on a device gives its power. A 2000 W kettle takes in 2000 J of electrical energy every second.
108714.m: The number of watts on a device gives its power.

108715.q: Which of these devices typically has the lowest power?
108715.e: An LED lamp often needs only about 5 to 10 W. Kettles, ovens and hair dryers, on the other hand, usually have well over 1000 W.
108715.m: LED lamps need only a few watts.

108716.m: Three quarters of a kilowatt is seven hundred and fifty watts.

108717.q: Roughly how many watts is one metric horsepower (PS)?
108717.e: One metric horsepower equals about 735.5 watts. That is just under three quarters of a kilowatt.
108717.m: One metric horsepower is about 735 watts.

108718.q: Who introduced the unit of power called horsepower?
108718.e: James Watt wanted to show customers how many horses his steam engine could replace. For this, he created the unit horsepower in the 18th century, from which the metric horsepower developed.
108718.m: Horsepower was used to compare steam engines with horses.

108719.q: Which unit is officially used today instead of horsepower for the power of car engines?
108719.e: Horsepower is not an SI unit. In vehicle registration documents and technical data, power is officially given in kilowatts, and horsepower is often only mentioned as well.
108719.m: Engine power is officially given in kilowatts.

108720.q: A car has 100 metric horsepower. Roughly how much is that in kilowatts?
108720.m: For kilowatts, multiply metric horsepower by about 0.74.

108721.q: An engine delivers 110 kW. Roughly how much is that in metric horsepower?
108721.e: You divide by 0.7355: 110 : 0.7355 ≈ 149.6, so about 150 horsepower.
108721.m: For horsepower, divide the kilowatts by about 0.74.

108722.q: What is the German abbreviation for metric horsepower (Pferdestärke)?
108722.e: In German, Pferdestärke is abbreviated to PS. In English, the unit is called “horsepower” and is abbreviated to hp.

108723.q: A cyclist delivers 250 W. Roughly how much horsepower is that?
108723.e: 250 W : 735.5 W ≈ 0.34 hp. So even a sporty cyclist only reaches about a third of a horsepower.
108723.m: Human muscle power reaches only a fraction of a horsepower.

108724.q: Can a real horse briefly deliver more than 1 horsepower?
108724.e: The unit horsepower roughly describes the steady power of a working horse. In short bursts of effort, a horse can deliver several times that.
108724.m: A horse can briefly deliver far more than one horsepower.

108725.e: A kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy: power times time. It is used, for example, to bill electricity use.
108725.m: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.

108726.q: How many joules are one kilowatt-hour?
108726.e: 1 kWh = 1000 W · 3600 s = 3,600,000 J, which is 3.6 megajoules.

108727.q: A 2 kW fan heater runs for 3 hours. How much energy does it use?
108727.e: Energy = power · time = 2 kW · 3 h = 6 kWh.
108727.m: Energy in kWh is kilowatts times hours.

108728.q: How long can a 100 W lamp shine with 1 kWh?
108728.e: 100 W is 0.1 kW. Time = 1 kWh : 0.1 kW = 10 h.
108728.m: The lower the power, the longer a kilowatt-hour lasts.

108729.q: A 1.5 kW oven runs for half an hour. How many kilowatt-hours does it use?
108729.m: Power times running time gives the energy used.

108730.q: A 1200 W coffee machine runs for 10 minutes. How much energy is that?
108730.e: 1200 W is 1.2 kW and 10 min is 1/6 h. E = 1.2 kW · 1/6 h = 0.2 kWh.
108730.m: Minutes must be converted into hours before calculating.

108731.q: Which device in the house counts the kilowatt-hours used?
108731.e: The electricity meter measures how much electrical energy the household has used. The electricity bill is based on its reading.
108731.m: The electricity meter measures use in kilowatt-hours.

108732.q: Electricity costs 30 centimes per kWh. How much do 4 kWh cost?
108732.m: The cost of electricity is kilowatt-hours times the price per kilowatt-hour.

108733.q: What is the correct way to write the abbreviation for kilowatt-hour?
108733.e: Kilo is written with a small k, watt with a capital W and hour with h. Writing “kW/h” is wrong, because power is multiplied by time, not divided.

108734.q: How do you calculate the work done in lifting?
a: Mass times gravitational field strength times height
108734.e: When lifting, you have to overcome the weight m · g. The work done in lifting is therefore W = m · g · h.
108734.m: Work done in lifting is weight times the height lifted.

108735.q: How much work is done in lifting if you raise 5 kg by 2 m (g = 10 N/kg)?
108735.e: W = m · g · h = 5 kg · 10 N/kg · 2 m = 100 J.
108735.m: For work done in lifting, multiply mass, gravitational field strength and height.

108736.q: How much work does it take to lift a 1 kg bag of flour 1 m (g = 10 N/kg)?
108736.e: The weight is 1 kg · 10 N/kg = 10 N. W = 10 N · 1 m = 10 J.
108736.m: Lifting one kilogram one metre takes about ten joules.

108737.q: A 20 kg box is lifted with 600 J of work (g = 10 N/kg). How high was it lifted?
108737.m: The height lifted is the work divided by the weight.

108738.q: Does the work done in lifting depend on whether you lift a box quickly or slowly?
a: No, only mass and height count.
108738.e: The work done in lifting depends only on mass, gravitational field strength and height. The speed changes the power, not the work.
108738.m: The work done in lifting does not depend on the speed.

108739.q: A crane lifts a 1000 kg concrete beam 15 m (g = 10 N/kg). How much work is done in lifting?
108739.m: Large loads also need a lot of lifting work.

108740.q: Which form of energy does an object have in addition after it has been lifted?
108740.e: The work done in lifting is stored in the object as potential energy. If it falls back down, this is turned into kinetic energy.
108740.m: Work done in lifting is stored as potential energy.

108741.q: You lift a 2 kg dumbbell 1.5 m ten times (g = 10 N/kg). How much lifting work is that altogether?
108741.e: Once: 2 kg · 10 N/kg · 1.5 m = 30 J. Ten times: 10 · 30 J = 300 J.
108741.m: Repeated lifting adds up the work done.

108742.q: Does a ramp save lifting work when pushing a load up?
a: Yes, it saves all the work.
No, it saves time and distance.
108742.e: With a ramp you need less force, but a longer distance. Without friction, the product of force times distance stays the same; this is called the golden rule of mechanics.
108742.m: What you save in force, you must add in distance.

108743.q: A 50 kg person climbs a staircase 3 m high (g = 10 N/kg). How much lifting work does she do?
108743.m: When climbing stairs, you lift your own body weight.

108744.q: The person doing 1500 J of lifting work takes 5 s for the stairs. What is her power?
108744.m: Anyone who climbs the stairs faster has more power.

108745.q: Leo (60 kg) runs up a staircase 4 m high in 8 s (g = 10 N/kg). What power does he deliver?
108745.m: For power on the stairs, you need mass, height and time.

108746.q: Which three quantities do you need to work out your own power when climbing stairs?
a: Body height, number of steps and pulse
108746.e: With mass and height, you calculate the lifting work m · g · h. If you divide it by the measured time, you get the power.
108746.m: Mass, height and time reveal your power on the stairs.

108747.q: Mia (40 kg) takes 6 s, her father (80 kg) 12 s for the same staircase 3 m high. Who has more power (g = 10 N/kg)?
108747.e: Mia: 40 · 10 · 3 : 6 = 200 W. Father: 80 · 10 · 3 : 12 = 200 W. The powers are the same.
108747.m: Twice the mass in twice the time gives the same power.

108748.q: Why does only the height of the stairs count for the lifting work, not their length?
108748.e: The weight points vertically downwards. Lifting work is only done along the vertical distance, which is why only the difference in height counts.
108748.m: For lifting work, only the difference in height counts.

108749.q: A 50 kg pupil climbs four floors of 3 m each in 30 s (g = 10 N/kg). What power does she deliver?
108749.m: For several floors, first add up the heights.

108750.q: A 70 kg man delivers 420 W when climbing stairs. How long does he take for a height of 3 m (g = 10 N/kg)?
108750.m: Time is the lifting work divided by the power.

108751.q: A 2000 W kettle runs for 3 minutes. How much energy does it use?
108751.e: 2000 W is 2 kW, 3 min is 0.05 h. E = 2 kW · 0.05 h = 0.1 kWh.
108751.m: Powerful devices that run briefly often use little energy.

108752.q: A 10 W LED lamp is on for 5 hours every day. How much energy does it use in 365 days?
108752.e: Per day: 0.01 kW · 5 h = 0.05 kWh. Per year: 0.05 kWh · 365 = 18.25 kWh.
108752.m: Even small users add up over the year.

108753.q: A 60 W filament bulb is replaced by an 8 W LED. How much energy do you save in 4 hours?
108753.e: The power drops by 52 W, which is 0.052 kW. Saving: 0.052 kW · 4 h = 0.208 kWh.
108753.m: LED lamps save a lot of electricity.

108754.q: An old device constantly draws 150 W. How many kWh does it use in a year (365 days)?
108754.m: Devices that are always on use a lot of energy in a year.

108755.q: A 1500 W hair dryer runs for 15 minutes every day. How many kWh does it use in 30 days?
108755.m: Daily use multiplies over the month.

108756.q: A washing machine uses 0.5 kWh per wash. Electricity costs 25 centimes per kWh. How much do two washes cost?
108756.e: Two washes use 1 kWh. Cost: 1 kWh · 25 centimes = 25 centimes.
108756.m: The cost comes from consumption times price.

108757.q: Which habit saves electricity when cooking?
a: Using a pan with a lid
Using a pan without a lid
Heating the hob for a long time beforehand
Choosing a ring larger than the pan
108757.e: A lid keeps the heat in the pan, so the water boils faster. This means less electrical energy is needed.
108757.m: With a lid, you cook faster and more economically.

108758.q: A router draws 2 W round the clock. How much energy does it use in 30 days?
108758.m: Even devices that are always on with few watts add up kilowatt-hours.

108759.q: Which letters does the new energy label for household appliances use?
108759.e: Since 2021, the label for many appliances has been changed to the scale A to G. The confusing plus classes such as A+++ were dropped.
108759.m: The new energy label goes from A to G.

108760.q: What colour is the most economical class on the energy label?
108760.e: The bars range from dark green for very economical to red for high consumption. So green stands for the best efficiency.
108760.m: On the energy label, dark green means very economical.

108761.q: Which class is the worst on the new energy label?
108761.e: G is the class with the highest energy use. It is marked in red on the label.
108761.m: Class G stands for the highest consumption.

108762.q: Which information is found on a fridge’s energy label in addition to the class?
a: the year the factory was built
108762.e: Among other things, the label states roughly how many kilowatt-hours the appliance uses per year. This lets you compare appliances directly.
108762.m: The energy label also gives the annual consumption.

108763.q: Fridge X uses 150 kWh per year, fridge Y 250 kWh. How much does X save per year at 30 centimes per kWh?
108763.e: Difference: 250 minus 150 = 100 kWh. Saving: 100 kWh · 0.30 francs = 30 francs.
108763.m: An economical appliance saves money every year.

108764.q: For which vehicles is there also an energy label in Switzerland?
108764.e: In Switzerland, new cars must be offered for sale with an energy label. It gives information about consumption and efficiency.
108764.m: New cars in Switzerland also carry an energy label.

108765.q: Which federal office is responsible for the energy label in Switzerland?
108765.e: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE) regulates the energy label and gives information through the SwissEnergy programme. The aim is for people to buy economical appliances.
108765.m: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy is responsible for the energy label.

108766.q: What does standby mean for an electrical device?
a: It is switched on, waiting for a command.
It is completely disconnected from the mains.
It is running at full power.
108766.e: On standby, a device is not completely off but ready, for example for the remote control. It still uses some electricity.
108766.m: A device on standby still uses electricity.

108767.q: A television uses 5 W on standby. How much energy is that in a year (365 days, always on standby)?
108767.e: 8760 h in a year. E = 0.005 kW · 8760 h = 43.8 kWh.
108767.m: A few watts on standby become many kilowatt-hours over a year.

108768.q: How much does 43.8 kWh of standby consumption cost at 25 centimes per kWh?
108768.m: Standby costs money every year without giving you anything.

108769.q: What is the easiest way to avoid the standby consumption of several devices?
a: with an extension lead with a switch
108769.e: If you switch off the extension lead, all the devices plugged into it are completely disconnected from the mains. Then no standby current flows any more.
108769.m: A switchable extension lead stops standby consumption.

108770.q: How can you often tell that a device is on standby?
108770.e: Many devices show standby with a small red or orange light. It shows that the device is still connected to the power.
108770.m: A small light often gives away standby mode.

108771.q: A games console uses 3 W on standby for 20 hours a day. How many kWh is that in a year?
108771.e: Per day: 0.003 kW · 20 h = 0.06 kWh. Per year: 0.06 · 365 = 21.9 kWh.
108771.m: Standby adds up day by day.

108772.q: Does a charger plugged into the socket without a phone still use some electricity?
108772.e: Many power adapters draw a small amount of power even with no device connected and get slightly warm. That is why it is better to unplug them after charging.
108772.m: Unplugging chargers after charging saves electricity.

108773.q: In a household, 8 devices are on standby at 2 W each. What is the total standby power?
108773.e: The powers are added: 8 · 2 W = 16 W.
108773.m: The standby powers of all devices add up.

108774.q: Roughly how much power can a healthy person deliver over a longer time?
108774.e: Over a longer time, untrained adults deliver about 75 to 100 W. Well-trained endurance athletes manage much more.
108774.m: Over a long time, a person delivers about a hundred watts.

108775.q: In 30 squats in 60 s, 40 kg of body mass is lifted 0.4 m each time (g = 10 N/kg). What is the average power?
108775.e: Once: 40 kg · 10 N/kg · 0.4 m = 160 J. Thirty times: 4800 J. P = 4800 J : 60 s = 80 W.
108775.m: In squats too, the leg muscles do lifting work.

108776.q: Why do we get warm when we do sport?
a: Muscles give off a large part of their energy as heat.
The air gets hotter during sport.
The bones rub against each other.
108776.e: Muscles have an efficiency of only about a quarter. The rest of the energy becomes heat, which we feel during sport.
108776.m: A large part of muscle energy becomes heat.

108777.q: A muscle has an efficiency of 25 %. How much mechanical power comes from 400 W of energy use?
108777.e: 25 % of 400 W is 0.25 · 400 W = 100 W. The remaining 300 W become heat.
108777.m: Efficiency tells you what share becomes usable.

108778.q: When can a person deliver the highest muscle power?
108778.e: For a few seconds, muscles can deliver a great deal of power, well over 1000 W in sprinters. But this peak power cannot be kept up for long.
108778.m: Peak muscle power is only possible for a short time.

108779.q: Which figure is used in cycling to compare the power of light and heavy riders?
108779.e: On a climb, what counts is how much power a rider delivers per kilogram of body mass. That is why watts per kilogram is an important figure.
108779.m: On a climb, power per kilogram is what counts.

108780.q: A 70 kg cyclist delivers 280 W. How many watts per kilogram is that?
108780.m: Watts per kilogram is power divided by body mass.

108781.q: In 10 s you lift a 2 kg dumbbell 0.5 m twenty times (g = 10 N/kg). What average power do you deliver?
108781.e: Once: 2 kg · 10 N/kg · 0.5 m = 10 J. Twenty times: 200 J. P = 200 J : 10 s = 20 W.
108781.m: Many quick repetitions add up to a measurable muscle power.

a: an exercise bike that measures power
a bike with an electric motor
108782.e: A bicycle ergometer is a stationary training bike. It measures how many watts you deliver when pedalling.
108782.m: A bicycle ergometer measures pedalling power in watts.

108783.q: You pedal on the ergometer for 20 minutes at 150 W. How much work do you do?
108783.m: Work on the ergometer is watts times seconds.

108784.q: How many kilowatt-hours are 150 W for 20 minutes?
108784.e: 0.15 kW · 1/3 h = 0.05 kWh. That is less than a kettle uses in three minutes.
108784.m: Human muscle power supplies only a little electrical energy.

108785.q: How long would you have to pedal at 250 W to deliver 1 kWh?
108785.e: 250 W is 0.25 kW. Time = 1 kWh : 0.25 kW = 4 h. Muscle power is very small compared with the electricity grid.
108785.m: Producing a kilowatt-hour with your own strength takes a very long time.

108786.q: What do doctors often use the bicycle ergometer for?
108786.e: In an exercise ECG, you pedal on the ergometer while your heart and blood pressure are monitored. This shows how the heart reacts to effort.
108786.m: The ergometer is used to test the heart under effort.

108787.q: Nora pedals for 3 minutes at 200 W. How much work is that?
108787.m: For work, the time must be in seconds.

108788.q: Roughly how many kilocalories are 180 kJ of mechanical work (1 kcal ≈ 4.2 kJ)?
108788.e: 180 kJ : 4.2 kJ/kcal ≈ 43 kcal. However, because of heat losses, the body burns considerably more.

108789.q: Which quantities does a bicycle ergometer measure to work out power?
108789.e: Power comes from the force on the pedals and how fast you pedal. The higher the resistance and the pedalling rate, the more watts.
108789.m: More resistance and faster pedalling give more watts.

108790.q: Which plant zone of a lake lies between the reed belt and the submerged plant zone?
108790.e: From the shore to deep water come the reed belt, the floating-leaf zone and the submerged plant zone. In the floating-leaf zone, the leaves lie on the surface of the water.
108790.m: The floating-leaf zone lies between the reed belt and the submerged plant zone.

108791.q: What is the open water zone in the middle of a lake, far from the shore, called?
108791.e: The open water zone (pelagic zone) is the body of open water with no contact with the shore or the bottom. Mainly plankton and fish live there.
108791.m: The open water area of a lake is called the open water zone.

108792.q: Where in a lake can plants grow on the bottom?
a: In the shallow area near the shore
Only in the middle of the lake
108792.e: Plants need light. Only in the shallow area near the shore does enough light reach the lake bottom. The technical term for this zone is the littoral zone.
108792.m: Near the shore, light reaches the lake bottom.

108793.q: Which living things break down dead plants and animals on the dark bottom of a deep lake?
108793.e: Hardly any light reaches the depths, so no plants grow there. But bacteria and worms break down the remains that sink to the bottom.
108793.m: On the dark lake bottom, bacteria and worms break down dead matter.

108794.q: Which plants typically grow in the submerged plant zone of a lake?
108794.e: In the submerged plant zone, plants live completely underwater, for example pondweeds and Canadian waterweed. Water lilies, on the other hand, have leaves on the surface.
108794.m: Pondweeds live fully submerged in the submerged plant zone.

108795.q: Why do water plants stop growing below a certain depth in a lake?
108795.e: Plants need light for photosynthesis. The deeper you go, the more light the water swallows, until there is not enough.
108795.m: Without enough light, water plants cannot grow.

108796.q: Which tree is typical of the wet swamp forest on the shores of many lakes?
108796.e: The black alder copes with wet soils that are sometimes flooded. That is why it often forms the swamp forest on lake shores.
108796.m: The black alder likes to grow with wet feet on the shore.

108797.q: Why do water plants grow deeper in clear lakes than in murky ones?
a: Light reaches deeper into the water
There are no seeds in murky lakes
108797.e: In clear water, sunlight gets further down. That is why plants such as stoneworts can still grow at greater depths there.
108797.m: In clear lakes, plants grow deeper because more light gets down.

108798.q: Where is the water of a deep lake warmest in summer?
108798.e: The sun warms the surface water. Warm water is lighter and stays on top, while the cold water lies in the depths.
108798.m: In summer, warm water lies on top of the cold deep water.

108799.q: Which plant is typical of the floating-leaf zone of a lake?
108799.e: The white water lily is rooted in the bottom and spreads its round leaves on the water's surface. It is the best-known plant of the floating-leaf zone.
108799.m: The white water lily is the typical floating-leaf plant.

108800.q: Where are the stomata for gas exchange on water lily leaves?
a: On the upper side of the leaf
On the underside of the leaf
On the edge of the leaf
108800.e: The underside of the leaf lies in the water, where no air could be taken in. That is why water lilies have their stomata on top.
108800.m: Water lilies breathe through stomata on the upper side of the leaf.

108801.q: What is the air-filled tissue in the stalks of the water lily for?
a: It carries air to the roots
It stores sugar for the winter
It fends off animals that eat it
108801.e: The roots are stuck in mud that has little oxygen. Air travels down from the leaves through the airy tissue.
108801.m: Airy tissue brings air to the roots in the mud.

108802.q: Which yellow-flowering plant also grows in the floating-leaf zone?
108802.e: Like the water lily, the yellow water lily has floating leaves and is rooted in the bottom of the water. Marsh marigold and yellow iris, on the other hand, grow on the shore.
108802.m: The yellow water lily is the yellow relative of the water lily.

108803.q: Why does water roll off the upper side of a water lily leaf?
108803.e: A waxy layer makes the upper side of the leaf water-repellent. That way the stomata stay clear and the leaf does not sink.
108803.m: A waxy layer keeps water lily leaves dry.

108804.q: Which tiny floating plant can cover ponds like a green carpet?
108804.e: Duckweeds are only a few millimetres across and float freely on the water. They multiply very fast and form green blankets.
108804.m: Duckweed floats freely and covers ponds like a carpet.

a: In the bottom of the water
On tree roots on the shore
108805.e: Water lilies have a thick rootstock in the muddy bottom. Long stalks grow from there up to the surface.
108805.m: Water lilies are rooted in the bottom of the water.

108806.q: Why do water lilies have long, bendy leaf stalks?
a: So that the leaves stay on top when the water level changes
So that fish do not eat the leaves
So that they store warmth in winter
So that they get nutrients from the air
108806.e: When the water rises or falls, the bendy stalks give way. That way the leaves keep floating on the surface.
108806.m: Bendy stalks keep water lily leaves on the surface.

108807.q: Which plant most often forms the reed belt on Swiss lakes?
108807.e: Common reed forms dense stands in the shallow water by the shore. These stands are called reed beds or the reed belt.
108807.m: Common reed forms the reed belt on the lake shore.

108808.q: About how tall can common reed grow?
108808.e: Common reed usually grows 1 to 4 metres tall. This makes it one of the largest grasses in Europe.
108808.m: Common reed can grow taller than a person.

108809.q: Which reed bed plant has brown, club-shaped flower heads?
108809.e: The bulrush carries striking brown heads that look like sausages. It grows in the reed beds of ponds and lakes.
108809.m: The bulrush is easy to recognise by its brown heads.

108810.q: How does the reed belt protect the lake shore?
a: It slows down the waves and holds the ground together
It cools the water down a lot
It keeps fish away from the shore
108810.e: The dense stems slow down waves, and the rootstocks hold the ground together. That way the shore is worn away less.
108810.m: Reed beds protect the shore from waves and erosion.

108811.q: Which bird is named after its habitat in the reeds?
108811.e: The reed warbler builds its nest between reed stems. It is a typical breeding bird of reed beds.
108811.m: The reed warbler nests in the reeds.

108812.q: Why is entering reed areas often forbidden in spring and summer?
a: Because the reeds are poisonous then
Because the water is too cold then
108812.e: Many birds nest in reed beds. Disturbance can make them abandon their nests.
108812.m: During the breeding season, reed areas are quiet zones for birds.

108813.q: How does common reed mainly spread?
108813.e: Reed forms long underground runners (rhizomes) from which new stems grow. That is how large, dense stands form.

108814.q: How does a reed belt improve water quality?
a: It takes up nutrients and filters the water
It releases salt into the water
It makes the water clear by colouring it
108814.e: Reed takes up nutrients such as phosphate and nitrogen. Bacteria living on its stems break down dirt.
108814.m: Reed helps to clean the water.

108815.q: What does the Greek word “plankton” mean?
108815.e: Plankton are living things that float in water and are carried by the current. They cannot swim against it on purpose.
108815.m: Plankton drifts with the current in the water.

108816.e: Phytoplankton consists of tiny algae that carry out photosynthesis. “Phyton” means plant in Greek.

108817.q: Which animal belongs to the zooplankton in fresh water?
108817.e: The water flea is a tiny crustacean that floats in water. It belongs to animal plankton, the zooplankton.
108817.m: The water flea is a typical zooplankton animal.

108818.q: What does the water flea mainly feed on?
108818.e: Water fleas filter algae out of the water with their little legs. In this way they keep the water clearer.
108818.m: Water fleas eat algae and so clear the water.

108819.q: Why are fish not part of the plankton?
a: They can actively swim against the current
They live only by the shore
108819.e: Plankton drifts with the current. Fish are strong swimmers and decide for themselves where they swim.

108820.q: Which plankton do diatoms belong to?
108820.e: Diatoms carry out photosynthesis and therefore belong to the phytoplankton. They live in a shell made of silica.

108821.q: About what share of the Earth's oxygen does phytoplankton produce?
108821.e: The phytoplankton of the oceans carries out photosynthesis in huge amounts. It provides about half of the oxygen produced by the Earth's plants.
108821.m: Tiny ocean algae provide about half of the oxygen.

108822.q: Why does a lot of zooplankton rise to the water's surface at night?
a: To eat algae while protected by the dark
To warm up in the moonlight
108822.e: During the day, zooplankton hides from fish in the dark depths. At night it rises to eat algae at the surface.
108822.m: Zooplankton eats near the top at night and hides in the depths by day.

108823.q: Which nutrient limits the growth of algae in most Swiss lakes?
108823.e: In lakes, phosphorus is usually the scarcest nutrient. If more phosphorus gets into the water, more algae grow at once.
108823.m: Phosphorus is the main brake on algae growth in lakes.

108824.q: Which ban helped from 1986 to reduce the over-fertilisation of Swiss lakes?
108824.e: Since 1986, phosphates in laundry detergents have been banned in Switzerland. Together with the building of sewage treatment plants, this greatly improved water quality.
108824.m: The ban on phosphates in detergents helped Swiss lakes.

108825.q: What does a nutrient-poor lake usually look like?
a: Clear, with lots of oxygen in the water
Green and murky with lots of algae
108825.e: Only a few algae grow in a nutrient-poor lake. The water stays clear, and there is enough oxygen even at the bottom.
108825.m: A nutrient-poor lake is clear and rich in oxygen.

108826.q: Where does a large share of the nutrients entering Swiss waters come from today?
108826.e: Fertiliser and slurry can be washed off fields into streams and lakes. Sewage, on the other hand, is mostly cleaned in treatment plants today.
108826.m: Fertiliser from fields can over-fertilise waters.

108827.q: Why is there often a lack of oxygen at the bottom of over-fertilised lakes?
a: Breaking down dead algae uses it up
108827.e: Lots of algae die and sink to the bottom. Bacteria break them down there and use up a lot of oxygen in the process.
108827.m: When lots of algae die, oxygen runs short at the lake bottom.

108828.q: What do people say when an over-fertilised lake suddenly becomes hostile to life because of a lack of oxygen?
108828.e: When a lake “dies” (in German, it “tips over”), the oxygen runs out, fish die and foul-smelling gases form. This is the worst result of over-fertilisation.

108829.q: Which fish is caught less in many Swiss lakes since they were cleaned up, because there are fewer nutrients?
108829.e: Whitefish feed on plankton, which grows less when there are fewer nutrients. That is why whitefish catches have fallen in many places.
108829.m: Clean, nutrient-poor lakes provide fewer whitefish.

108830.q: What happens to how far you can see down into a lake when it is heavily over-fertilised?
108830.e: Lots of algae make the water murky. That is why you cannot see as deep in over-fertilised lakes.
108830.m: Lots of algae make the water murky.

108831.q: Which water can dissolve more oxygen?
108831.e: The colder water is, the more gas it can dissolve. That is why fish suffer from a lack of oxygen in hot summers.
108831.m: Cold water contains more oxygen than warm water.

108832.q: Which contains more oxygen: a litre of air or a litre of water?
108832.e: Air is about one fifth oxygen. Only very little oxygen dissolves in water, which is why fish need gills.
108832.m: Water contains much less oxygen than air.

108833.q: In our climate, when is a deep lake usually completely mixed and supplied with oxygen down to the bottom?
108833.e: In spring and autumn, the water at the top and bottom is about the same temperature. Then the wind can turn over the whole lake.
108833.m: A lake is mixed in spring and autumn.

108834.q: What is the layer called in which, in summer, the temperature drops quickly between warm and cold lake water?
108834.e: In the thermocline, the temperature drops sharply over just a few metres. It separates the warm surface water from the cold deep water.
108834.m: The thermocline separates warm and cold lake water.

108835.q: When is the oxygen level in a pond full of plants usually lowest?
108835.e: At night, plants carry out no photosynthesis, but they use oxygen to breathe. That is why the level is lowest just before sunrise.
108835.m: After the night, there is least oxygen in the pond.

108836.q: Which insect larvae indicate clean, oxygen-rich stream water?
108836.e: Stonefly larvae need a lot of oxygen and can hardly tolerate pollution. If you find them, the stream is usually clean.
108836.m: Stonefly larvae are indicators of clean water.

108837.q: Why is a fast-flowing mountain stream usually very rich in oxygen?
a: It is cold and very turbulent
108837.e: As it bubbles over stones, a lot of air gets into the water. And because the water is cold, it can dissolve a lot of oxygen.
108837.m: Cold, bubbling streams are rich in oxygen.

108838.q: What is the aim when a stream is restored to nature?
a: To bring back a near-natural state
To put the stream into pipes
108838.e: In a restoration, a built-up stream gets back space, bends and natural banks. This creates habitats for animals and plants.
108838.m: Restoring a stream means giving it back its natural state.

108839.q: Why are many streams and rivers in Switzerland being revitalised?
a: Many were straightened and built up in the past
They are too warm for swimming
They flow in the wrong direction
They have too few fish for angling
108839.e: In the past, many waters were straightened, squeezed into channels or put into pipes. Today thousands of kilometres are to become more natural again.
108839.m: Many built-up waters are to become more natural again.

108840.q: Which term is often used in Switzerland for restoring waters to nature?
108840.e: In laws and among authorities, improving waters is usually called revitalisation. It means bringing the water back to life.
108840.m: Revitalisation means bringing a body of water back to life.

108841.q: In which large water engineering project was the Aare diverted into Lake Biel from 1868?
108841.e: In the first Jura Water Correction, the Aare was led into Lake Biel to prevent floods in the Seeland. Today some built-up sections are being made more natural again.
108841.m: The Jura Water Correction led the Aare into Lake Biel.

108842.q: What helps fish to get past the weir of a river power station?
108842.e: A fish ladder consists of many small pools that rise like steps. That way fish can travel upstream.
108842.m: Fish ladders help fish past obstacles.

108843.q: Why are loose gravel banks important in a restored river?
a: Many fish lay their eggs there
They warm the water a lot
They keep algae away from the bank
108843.e: Trout and grayling need loose gravel with good water flow for their eggs. In built-up rivers, such places are often missing.
108843.m: Loose gravel is a nursery for fish.

108844.q: Why does it harm fish when a power station changes a river's water level sharply several times a day?
a: Young fish are stranded on dry land
108844.e: Storage power stations release a lot or a little water depending on electricity demand. If the level suddenly drops, young fish and small creatures are left stranded on the bank. This is called hydropeaking.
108844.m: Rapid changes in water level from power stations harm fish.

a: A stream that flows in pipes under the ground
A stream that flows only in spring
A stream that flows into a valley
108845.e: Many streams were put into pipes in the past to gain land. When they are brought back to the surface, this is called daylighting.
108845.m: A culverted stream flows unseen in pipes.

108846.q: Which trees are typical of the often flooded softwood floodplain forest?
108846.e: Willows and poplars can stand long floods and grow fast. Their wood is soft, hence the name softwood floodplain.
108846.m: Willows and poplars grow in the softwood floodplain.

108847.q: Which trees typically grow in the less often flooded hardwood floodplain forest?
a: Swiss stone pines, larches and mountain pines
108847.e: The hardwood floodplain lies a little higher and is only flooded by big floods. Trees with hard wood such as oaks, ashes and elms grow there.
108847.m: Trees with hard wood grow in the hardwood floodplain.

108848.q: Which rodent dams streams in Swiss floodplains and so creates new habitats?
108848.e: The beaver fells trees and builds dams, creating pools and wetlands. It had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1956.
108848.m: The beaver reshapes floodplains with its dams.

108849.q: Why are floodplains useful during floods?
a: They hold back water like a sponge
They make the water flow away faster
They evaporate the water at once
They divert the water to the sea
108849.e: Floodplains give the river room to spread out. The water is held back, and the flood peak further downstream is smaller.

108850.q: On which river is the Pfyn forest, a valuable floodplain in the Valais?
108850.e: In the Pfyn forest between Sierre and Leuk, the Rhône can still flow relatively freely. The area is one of the most important floodplains in Switzerland.
108850.m: The Pfyn forest is a valuable floodplain on the Rhône.

108851.q: Which bird nests on open gravel banks in river floodplains?
108851.e: The little ringed plover lays its well-camouflaged eggs directly on the gravel. That is why it needs open gravel areas with few plants.
108851.m: The little ringed plover nests on bare gravel.

108852.q: Why have many floodplains in Switzerland disappeared?
108852.e: River corrections and dams meant rivers could no longer burst their banks. The land was used for farming and settlements.

108853.q: Which waters does the brown trout prefer to live in?
108853.e: The brown trout needs cool, clear and oxygen-rich water. That is why it lives mainly in streams and the upper reaches of rivers.
108853.m: The brown trout needs cool, clean water.

108854.q: Which spots are typical of the brown trout?
a: Red spots with a pale ring
108854.e: The brown trout has black and red spots, the red ones often ringed with pale colour. The colouring can vary greatly depending on the water.
108854.m: Red spots with pale rings mark the brown trout.

108855.q: In which season does the brown trout spawn?
108855.e: Brown trout spawn from about October to January. The eggs develop slowly in the cold water over the winter.
108855.m: Brown trout spawn in the cold season.

108856.q: Where does the brown trout lay its eggs?
a: In hollows in the gravel bed
108856.e: The female beats a hollow into the gravel with her tail. There the eggs are protected and washed by oxygen-rich water.
108856.m: Trout bury their eggs in the gravel.

108857.q: Which fish family does the brown trout belong to?
108857.e: Like the salmon and the grayling, the brown trout belongs to the salmon family. A typical feature is the small fatty fin on its back.
108857.m: The brown trout belongs to the salmon family.

108858.q: Why does water that is too warm cause problems for brown trout in Swiss rivers?
a: It contains less oxygen and encourages disease
It makes the fish too heavy
108858.e: Warm water contains less oxygen. In addition, a kidney disease of trout is often fatal above about 15 degrees.
108858.m: Warm water makes brown trout prone to disease.

108859.q: What does the brown trout mainly feed on?
108859.e: The brown trout is a predator. It eats insect larvae, insects from the surface and freshwater shrimps, and larger trout also eat small fish.
108859.m: The brown trout is a predator that mainly eats insects.

108860.q: What is the form of trout called that lives in lakes and swims up rivers to spawn?
108860.e: Lake trout and brown trout belong to the same species. The lake trout grows into a large fish in the lake and travels into the inflowing rivers to spawn.
108860.m: The lake trout travels from the lake into rivers to spawn.

108861.q: Where does the rainbow trout, which was introduced to Switzerland, come from?
108861.e: The rainbow trout originally comes from North America. It has a shimmering pink stripe along its side.
108861.m: The rainbow trout comes from North America.

108862.q: In Switzerland, what is the abbreviation for a sewage treatment plant?
108862.e: ARA stands for Abwasserreinigungsanlage, sewage treatment plant. KVA, on the other hand, is a waste incineration plant.
108862.m: In Switzerland, the sewage treatment plant is called the ARA.

108863.q: What does the screen at the entrance of a sewage treatment plant do?
108863.e: The screen is a grid that fishes rags, paper and other coarse material out of the sewage. This protects pumps and pipes.
108863.m: The screen fishes coarse rubbish out of the sewage.

108864.q: What is the grit chamber in a sewage treatment plant for?
a: Sand and small stones settle there
108864.e: In the grit chamber, the water flows more slowly. Heavy particles such as sand sink and are removed.
108864.m: In the grit chamber, sand sinks to the bottom.

108865.q: What cleans the sewage in the aeration tank of a sewage treatment plant?
108865.e: In the aeration tank, countless bacteria and other microorganisms break down the dissolved dirt. This is the biological cleaning stage.
108865.m: Bacteria eat the dirt in the aeration tank.

108866.q: Why is air blown into the aeration tank?
a: So that the water does not freeze
So that the sand floats up
108866.e: The bacteria that break down the dirt breathe oxygen. Without air being blown in, they would not do enough work.
108866.m: Blowing in air gives the bacteria in the tank oxygen.

108867.q: Why is phosphate removed from sewage in the treatment plant?
a: Otherwise too many algae grow in the lakes
Otherwise the water becomes too salty
Otherwise the water smells of smoke
108867.e: Phosphate is a fertiliser. If too much of it gets into lakes, algae grow in huge numbers, and as the algae are broken down, oxygen in the water runs short.
108867.m: Phosphate in sewage fertilises algae in the lakes.

108868.q: Which gas is produced from sewage sludge in the digester tower of a treatment plant?
108868.e: In the digester tower, bacteria break down the sludge without oxygen. This produces biogas with a lot of methane, which provides electricity and heat.
108868.m: Biogas is made from sewage sludge in the digester tower.

108869.q: Since 2006, what happens to sewage sludge in Switzerland instead of it being spread on fields?
a: It is taken to the sea
108869.e: Because sewage sludge can contain pollutants, it has not been allowed as fertiliser since 2006. Instead it is burnt.
108869.m: In Switzerland, sewage sludge is burnt.

108870.q: What are many Swiss sewage treatment plants meant to remove from sewage with an extra cleaning stage?
a: Traces of medicines and other micropollutants
108870.e: Traces of medicines, pesticides and cosmetics are hardly broken down in a normal treatment plant. An extra stage removes most of these micropollutants.
108870.m: An extra stage in the treatment plant removes traces of medicines.

108871.q: Why should leftover paint and oil not go down the sink?
a: Treatment plants cannot remove them completely
They make the water too warm
They are banned from the sink because they smell
108871.e: Paints, oils and solvents are only partly broken down in the treatment plant and can get into streams and lakes. They should be taken to a collection point.
108871.m: Leftover paint and oil belong at a collection point, not down the sink.

108872.q: Where does most of Switzerland's drinking water come from?
108872.e: About 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and spring water. The rest is mainly taken from lakes.
108872.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from the ground.

a: Water that must stay in a stream after water is taken out
Water left over after a shower
108873.e: When power stations take water, a minimum amount must stay in the streambed. That way fish and other animals can go on living there.
108873.m: Residual flow keeps a stream alive below a power station.

108874.e: Medicines in sewage are only partly broken down in treatment plants. Pharmacies take back old medicines and dispose of them safely.
108874.m: Old medicines are taken back to the pharmacy.

108875.q: Why were many sewage treatment plants built in Switzerland from the 1950s?
a: Lakes and rivers were badly polluted
People wanted to produce more electricity
108875.e: At that time, a lot of sewage flowed untreated into the waters, and swimming was banned in many places. In 1953, voters accepted a water protection article, and after that treatment plants were built everywhere.
108875.m: Sewage treatment plants made Swiss waters clean again.

a: A strip along a body of water that must be kept free
The water volume of a lake
A pool in an indoor swimming pool
108876.e: Along streams, rivers and lakes, a space must be kept free for natural functions and flood protection. As a rule, no building is allowed there.
108876.m: Waters need free space along their banks.

108877.q: Why must you not wash a car with cleaning products over a street drain?
a: The water often flows untreated into a stream
The water freezes in the drain
108877.e: Many street drains lead rainwater directly into streams without a treatment plant. Soap, oil and dirt would then pollute the water.
108877.m: Street drains often lead straight into the nearest stream.

108878.q: What can happen if sewage gets into drinking water?
108878.e: Sewage can contain germs. In Zermatt in 1963, hundreds of people fell ill with typhoid because sewage had got into the drinking water.
108878.m: Polluted water can spread dangerous diseases.

a: A flower that grows in water
A festival on the lake shore
108879.e: In an algal bloom, algae multiply so much that the water changes colour. It has nothing to do with flowers.
108879.m: In an algal bloom, algae multiply in huge numbers.

108880.q: Which living things, once called “blue-green algae”, can produce toxins during an algal bloom?
108880.e: Blue-green algae are really bacteria that carry out photosynthesis. Some species produce toxins that are dangerous for people and animals.

108881.q: Which battle is the “Burgundian blood alga”, which can turn lakes red, named after?
108881.e: According to legend, the blood of the defeated Burgundians in 1476 turned Lake Murten red. In fact, the red colour came from this alga.
108881.m: The Burgundian blood alga recalls the Battle of Murten.

108882.q: Why should dogs not drink from the lake during an algal bloom?
a: Algal toxins can be deadly for them
They could burn themselves on it
108882.e: Certain algae produce strong toxins. Dogs take in a lot of them when drinking and licking their fur, which can be fatal.
108882.m: During algal blooms, dogs should not drink lake water.

108883.q: Which conditions encourage an algal bloom?
a: Lots of nutrients, warmth and sun
Lots of ice and little light
108883.e: Algae grow particularly fast when there is a lot of phosphate and the water is warm and sunny. That is why algal blooms often happen in summer.
108883.m: Nutrients and warmth make algae bloom.

108884.q: What is an algal bloom in the sea that turns the water reddish called?
108884.e: In a red tide, certain sea algae multiply so much that the water turns red or brown. Their toxins can affect fish and shellfish.
108884.m: A red tide is an algal bloom in the sea.

108885.q: What often forms on the water's surface during a bloom of blue-green algae?
108885.e: Many cyanobacteria have tiny gas bubbles and rise to the surface. There they form green or blue-green streaks and carpets.
108885.m: Green streaks on the water can show a blue-green algae bloom.

108886.q: Which pigment is measured to estimate the amount of algae in water?
108886.e: All algae contain the green pigment chlorophyll. The more chlorophyll in the water, the more algae.
108886.m: Chlorophyll in the water shows how many algae there are.

108887.q: What does the abbreviation DNA stand for?
108887.e: DNA is short for “deoxyribonucleic acid”. It carries the genetic information.
108887.m: Written out in full, DNA is deoxyribonucleic acid.

108888.q: What shape is the DNA molecule?
108888.e: DNA consists of two strands that are wound around each other like a twisted rope ladder. This shape is called a double helix.
108888.m: DNA is a twisted double rope ladder.

108889.q: What is the sugar in the building blocks of DNA called?
108889.e: Each building block of DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a base. The sugar also gave DNA its name.

108890.q: Which substance, together with the sugar, forms the two sides of the DNA ladder?
108890.e: Sugar and phosphate take turns and form the side strands of DNA. The base pairs are the rungs in between.
108890.m: Sugar and phosphate form the backbone of DNA.

108891.q: In DNA, which base does adenine pair with?
108891.e: In DNA, only certain bases fit together. Adenine always pairs with thymine.
108891.m: In DNA, adenine always pairs with thymine.

108892.q: In DNA, which base does guanine pair with?
108892.e: Guanine and cytosine fit together chemically and are joined by three hydrogen bonds. This forms one rung of the DNA ladder.
108892.m: In DNA, guanine always pairs with cytosine.

108893.q: Where is most of the DNA in a human cell?
108893.e: Almost all the DNA is packed into the nucleus. Only a small part is in the mitochondria.
108893.m: DNA is well packed in the nucleus.

108894.q: How many different bases are found in DNA?
108894.e: DNA contains the four bases adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Their order makes up the genetic information.
108894.m: DNA writes its information with four bases.

a: A section of DNA carrying genetic information
108895.e: A gene is a particular section of DNA. It contains the information for a characteristic or a protein.
108895.m: A gene is a section of DNA.

108896.q: What does a gene usually contain the building instructions for?
108896.e: Most genes describe how a particular protein is built. Proteins do many jobs in the body.
108896.m: Genes are building instructions for proteins.

108897.q: Roughly how many genes containing building instructions for proteins do humans have?
108897.e: Humans have about 20,000 such genes. That is fewer than scientists used to think.
108897.m: Humans have about 20,000 genes for proteins.

108898.q: Why do brothers and sisters often have different eye colours?
a: They have inherited different versions of the genes
Eye colour depends on the weather
108898.e: A gene can come in different versions. Each child inherits their own mix of these versions from the parents.

108899.q: How many different bases, often written as the letters A, C, G and T, are there in DNA?
108899.e: DNA is made of four bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine. Their order contains the genetic information.

108900.q: In which part of the cell are most human genes found?
108900.e: The DNA with the genes is in the nucleus. It is the control centre of the cell.
108900.m: The genes are in the nucleus.

108901.q: How do genes get from parents to their children?
108901.e: Children inherit about half of their genes from their mother and half from their father. That is why they are similar to both parents.
108901.m: Genes are inherited from the parents.

108902.q: What can a mutation in a gene be?
a: A change in the genetic information
108902.e: In a mutation, the order of the building blocks in the DNA changes. Often this has no effect, but sometimes it changes a characteristic.
108902.m: A mutation is a change in the genetic information.

108903.q: What happens to the chromosomes before a cell divides?
108903.e: Before division, each chromosome is copied. This way, each of the two new cells receives the complete genetic information.
108903.m: Before cell division, the chromosomes are doubled.

108904.q: What is special about the chromosomes in Down syndrome?
108904.e: In Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice. That is why it is also called trisomy 21.
108904.m: Down syndrome is also called trisomy 21.

108905.q: How many chromosomes does a normal human body cell have?
108905.e: Humans have 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs. Chimpanzees have 48, one pair more.

108906.q: How are the chromosomes arranged in a human body cell?
108906.e: There are two similar copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. That is why humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes.

108907.q: When are chromosomes easy to see under a light microscope?
108907.e: Before division, the chromosomes become very compact. Only then are they visible as separate structures under the microscope.
108907.m: Chromosomes are easiest to see during cell division.

108908.q: In which part of the cell are the chromosomes?
108908.e: The chromosomes are well protected in the nucleus. It is the control centre of the cell.

108909.q: What is stored on the chromosomes?
108909.e: Chromosomes carry the genes. For example, they help to decide what colour eyes a person has.

108910.q: What are chromosomes mainly made of?
108910.e: DNA is a very long thread. So that it fits into the nucleus, it is tightly wound around proteins, forming the chromosomes.
108910.m: Chromosomes are made of wound-up DNA.

108911.q: Does a living thing with more chromosomes automatically have a more complicated body?
a: No, a dog, for example, has more chromosomes than a human
No, all living things have the same number
108911.e: Dogs have 78 chromosomes, humans 46. The number says nothing about how complex a living thing is.
108911.m: The number of chromosomes does not show how complex a living thing is.

108912.q: How many Mendel’s laws are there?
108912.e: They are the law of uniformity, the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment. They describe how characteristics are inherited.

108913.q: What does the law of uniformity say?
a: The first generation of offspring from purebred parents is all the same
Only one parent passes on characteristics
108913.e: If you cross two purebred parents that differ in one characteristic, all the offspring in the first generation look the same. Uniform means all alike.
108913.m: The first generation of offspring from purebred parents is uniform.

108914.q: According to the law of segregation, in what ratio do the characteristics split in the second generation of offspring with dominant and recessive inheritance?
108914.e: If you cross two hybrid animals or plants from the first generation, three quarters show the dominant and one quarter the recessive characteristic. That gives 3 to 1.
108914.m: With dominant inheritance, the law of segregation gives 3 to 1.

108916.q: What is the kind of inheritance called in which red and white four o’clock flowers produce pink offspring?
108916.e: In intermediate inheritance, neither of the two alleles wins out. The offspring show a mixed form, here pink.
108916.m: Intermediate inheritance produces a mixed form.

108917.q: How is the first generation of offspring abbreviated in genetics?
108917.e: F stands for “filia”, Latin for daughter. The first generation of offspring is called F1, the second F2.
108917.m: The first generation of offspring is called F1.

108918.q: What does the letter “P” stand for in a cross diagram?
108918.e: P comes from the Latin “parentes”, meaning parents. The parent generation is at the start of every cross.
108918.m: In a cross diagram, P stands for the parents.

108920.q: With which plant did Gregor Mendel carry out his famous experiments on inheritance?
108920.e: For years Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants. From his counts he worked out the laws of inheritance.
108920.m: Mendel discovered the laws of inheritance using peas.

108921.q: Which office did Gregor Mendel take on in his monastery in 1868?
108921.e: In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of his monastery. After that he hardly had any time left for his research.
108921.m: Mendel became abbot of his monastery in 1868.

108922.q: Where did Gregor Mendel carry out his pea experiments?
a: In the garden of his monastery
On a farm in the Alps
108922.e: Mendel was a monk. In the garden of his monastery he grew thousands of pea plants and counted their characteristics.
108922.m: Mendel did his research in the monastery garden.

108923.q: How did other scientists react to Mendel’s results at first?
a: They were laughed at and burnt
108923.e: Mendel published his experiments in 1866, but hardly anyone realised how important they were. Only around 1900 were they rediscovered.
108923.m: Mendel’s discoveries only became famous after his death.

108924.q: What are the laws of inheritance discovered by Gregor Mendel called today?
108924.e: The laws describe how characteristics are passed on from parents to offspring. They bear Mendel’s name.
108924.m: Mendel’s laws of inheritance are called Mendel’s laws.

108925.q: Why were peas well suited to Mendel’s experiments?
a: They have clearly different characteristics and many offspring
They live for several hundred years
108925.e: Peas show clear characteristics such as yellow or green and produce many seeds. This meant Mendel could count large numbers.
108925.m: Peas have clear characteristics and many seeds.

108926.q: Which characteristic did Mendel study in his peas?
108926.e: Mendel studied characteristics that were easy to see, including flower colour. He only chose characteristics with two clearly separate forms.
108926.m: Mendel chose clearly visible characteristics such as flower colour.

108927.q: Which seed shape was dominant in Mendel’s peas?
108927.e: When Mendel crossed round peas with wrinkled ones, all the offspring were round. So the round shape is dominant.
108927.m: In peas, the round seed shape is dominant.

108928.q: Which title of honour is Gregor Mendel often given today?
108928.e: With his pea experiments, Mendel laid the foundations of genetics. That is why he is called the father of genetics.
108928.m: Mendel is regarded as the father of genetics.

108929.q: What does it mean if an allele is dominant?
a: It wins out in the appearance
108929.e: A dominant allele decides the characteristic even if only one copy is present. The other allele is masked.

108930.q: How is a dominant allele written in a cross diagram?
108930.e: Dominant alleles are written with capital letters, for example A. Recessive alleles get the same letter in lower case.
108930.m: Dominant alleles are written with a capital letter.

108931.q: Which blood group alleles are dominant over the O allele?
108931.e: The alleles A and B win out over O. So someone who carries A and O has blood group A.
108931.m: A and B are dominant over O.

108932.q: Which blood group does a person have who carries the alleles A and B?
108932.e: A and B both show up, which is called codominance. That is why both characteristics appear on the red blood cells.
108932.m: With A and B, you have blood group AB.

108933.q: Who introduced the terms “dominant” and “recessive” into genetics?
108933.e: Mendel called the characteristic that wins out dominating and the hidden one recessive. These terms are still used today.
108933.m: The terms dominant and recessive come from Mendel.

108934.q: What is a genotype with one dominant and one recessive allele, for example Aa, called?
108934.e: Heterozygous means that two different alleles are present. The appearance matches the dominant allele.

108935.q: When AA is crossed with aa and A is dominant, how many offspring show the dominant characteristic?
108935.e: All the offspring get one A and one a, so they have the genotype Aa. Because A is dominant, they all show the dominant characteristic.
108935.m: AA and aa produce only offspring with Aa.

108936.q: Suppose black fur (S) is dominant over white fur (s). Which genotype gives white fur?
108936.e: White fur only shows if there is no dominant S. That is only the case with the genotype ss.
108936.m: A recessive characteristic needs two recessive alleles.

108937.q: When does a recessive characteristic show in the appearance?
a: Only when two recessive alleles are present
Always, as soon as one recessive allele is present
108937.e: A recessive allele is masked by a dominant one. Only when both alleles are recessive does the characteristic become visible.
108937.m: Recessive characteristics only show with two identical alleles.

108938.q: What do you call someone who carries a recessive allele for a disease but is healthy themselves?
108938.e: Carriers have one healthy dominant allele and one recessive allele for the disease. They are healthy, but they can pass the allele on.
108938.m: Carriers have an allele for a disease without being ill.

108939.q: When Aa is crossed with Aa, what is the probability of an offspring with aa?
108939.e: AA, Aa, aA and aa are possible, each with the same probability. Only one of the four combinations is aa, so 1 in 4 or 25 per cent.
108939.m: Aa and Aa produce aa in a quarter of cases.

108940.q: Which inherited disease is passed on recessively and mainly affects the lungs and digestion?
108940.e: In cystic fibrosis, the body makes thick mucus that puts a strain on the lungs and digestive organs. Only people with two altered alleles have the disease.

108941.q: Why can a recessive characteristic skip a generation?
a: Parents can carry the allele hidden
Only every second generation has genes
108941.e: Heterozygous parents do not show the recessive characteristic, but they pass on the allele. When two such alleles come together, the characteristic appears again.
108941.m: Recessive alleles can be passed on unnoticed.

108942.q: Which recessively inherited disease means that the blood does not clot well?
108942.e: In haemophilia, a clotting factor is missing, so wounds have trouble stopping bleeding. The gene is on the X chromosome, which is why almost only boys get the disease.
108942.m: Haemophilia is inherited recessively via the X chromosome.

108943.q: When Aa is crossed with aa, what is the probability that an offspring shows the recessive characteristic?
108943.e: Aa, Aa, aa and aa are possible. Two out of four combinations are aa, which is 50 per cent.
108943.m: Aa and aa produce aa in half of cases.

108944.q: What is an allele called that is masked by another allele?
108944.e: Recessive comes from the Latin “recedere”, to step back. The recessive allele steps back behind the dominant one.

108945.q: What are mutations called that arise without any obvious outside influence?
108945.e: When DNA is copied, random mistakes happen now and then. Mutations like these with no outside cause are called spontaneous mutations.
108945.m: Spontaneous mutations arise by chance when DNA is copied.

108946.q: Which radiation can cause mutations in skin cells?
108946.e: UV radiation from the sun can damage the DNA in skin cells. That is why sun cream also protects against skin cancer.
108946.m: Too much UV light can damage the genetic material of the skin.

108948.q: What are substances or influences that cause mutations called?
108948.e: Mutagens include certain chemicals, radioactive radiation or UV light. They increase the number of mutations.

108949.q: What is a mutation that affects only a single base pair called?
108949.e: In a point mutation, a single base is swapped, inserted or removed. So it affects only a tiny point in the DNA.
108949.m: A point mutation affects only one base.

108950.q: Why are mutations important for evolution?
a: They create new variants for selection
They make all living things the same
108950.e: Mutations produce new alleles and so differences between living things. Natural selection then picks out the useful ones.
108950.m: Without mutations there would be no evolution.

108952.q: What feature do animals with albinism show?
108952.e: With albinism, a mutation means the pigment melanin cannot be made. Fur or skin is white, and the eyes look reddish because of the blood vessels.

108953.q: What is meant by the genome?
a: All the genetic information of a living thing
108953.e: The genome includes all the DNA of a living thing with all its genes. It is a bit like the complete library of genetic information.
108953.m: The genome is all the genetic information.

108954.q: Roughly how many DNA letters does human genetic information contain?
108954.e: A single set of human DNA contains about 3 billion building blocks. Printed out, it would fill thousands of books.

108955.q: What was the aim of the great Human Genome Project?
a: To read all human genetic information
To get rid of all diseases
108955.e: From 1990 to 2003, researchers from many countries decoded most of human DNA. Today this helps medicine.
108955.m: The Human Genome Project decoded human DNA.

108956.q: Roughly how much of their genetic material do humans and chimpanzees share?
108956.e: If you compare the sequence of bases, humans and chimpanzees match by about 98 to 99 per cent. Chimpanzees are our closest living relatives.
108956.m: Humans and chimpanzees have very similar genetic material.

108957.q: What share of the human genome directly contains instructions for building proteins?
108957.e: Only a very small part of DNA codes for proteins. The rest has other jobs, such as controlling genes, or is still poorly understood.
108957.m: Only a small part of the genome codes for proteins.

108958.q: What is decoding the sequence of bases in DNA called?
108958.e: Sequencing works out the order of the bases. Modern machines can now do this very quickly and cheaply.
108958.m: Sequencing means reading the base sequence of DNA.

108959.e: All living things have genetic information, from bacteria to plants to humans. All of this genetic information together is called the genome.
108959.m: Every living thing has a genome.

a: A DNA pattern that tells people apart
A print of a finger on paper
108960.e: Certain sections of DNA differ a lot from person to person. The police use their pattern to link traces to a person.
108960.m: A genetic fingerprint identifies a person by their DNA.

a: The appearance with all its features
The combination of alleles of a gene
108961.e: The phenotype includes all the features you can observe, such as appearance, body build or behaviour. It comes from genes and environment.
108961.m: The phenotype is what you can observe about a living thing.

108962.q: Besides genes, what influences the phenotype?
108962.e: Diet, climate, light or training affect how a living thing looks. So the phenotype is the result of genes and environment.
108962.m: Genes and environment shape the phenotype together.

108963.q: Which example shows that the environment changes the phenotype?
a: Hydrangeas flower blue or pink depending on the soil
108963.e: The flower colour of a hydrangea depends on how acidic the soil is and how much aluminium the plant takes up. The genes stay the same.
108963.m: The soil can change the flower colour of a hydrangea.

108964.q: Is a person's height decided only by their genes?
a: No, diet and environment play a part too
Yes, only by the year of birth
108964.e: Genes set a range for how tall someone can grow. Good food and health help decide how much of this range is reached.
108964.m: Height depends on genes and environment.

108965.q: Why do Siamese cats have dark ears, paws and tail tips?
a: More pigment is made in cooler parts of the body
They often lie in the sun
108965.e: In Siamese cats, the enzyme for fur pigment only works at lower temperatures. The ears, paws and tail are cooler and so turn dark.
108965.m: In Siamese cats, temperature helps decide fur colour.

108966.q: In a plant, red flower colour (R) is dominant over white (r). What colour are plants with RR and with Rr?
108966.e: The dominant allele R wins in both. Despite different genotypes, they have the same phenotype.
108966.m: Different genotypes can look the same.

108968.q: Which of these features belongs to the phenotype?
a: The base sequence of a gene
108968.e: You can see eye colour directly, so it is part of the appearance. Alleles and base sequences, on the other hand, are part of the genetic information.
108968.m: Visible features such as eye colour belong to the phenotype.

108969.e: The genotype describes the genetic information, such as which alleles a living thing has for a feature. You usually cannot see it directly.
108969.m: The genotype is the genetic make-up of a living thing.

108970.q: What is one difference between the genotype and the appearance of a living thing?
a: You cannot see the genotype directly, but you can see the appearance
Appearance is always inherited, the genotype never
108970.e: The genotype is the genetic information in the cells. The appearance comes from it, but is also influenced by the environment.
108970.m: The genotype is in the genes, the appearance is what you see.

108971.q: How many alleles of a gene does a person normally have in their body cells?
108971.e: Body cells have two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. That is why each gene usually exists as two alleles.
108971.m: In body cells, each gene is usually present twice.

108972.q: Can you always tell the genotype from the appearance of a living thing?
a: No, dominant alleles can hide recessive ones
108972.e: A living thing with AA looks the same as one with Aa if A is dominant. You cannot tell the difference from appearance alone.
108972.m: Appearance does not always give away the genotype.

108973.q: Who does a child inherit its genes from?
108973.e: Half of the genetic make-up comes from the mother and half from the father. That is why a child resembles both parents.
108973.m: A child inherits from both parents.

108974.q: Why do children often look like their parents?
a: They have inherited genes from them
They live in the same house
108974.e: Features such as hair colour or face shape are passed on through genes. That is why children resemble their parents.
108974.m: Family likeness comes from the genes.

108975.q: How can a person's genotype be determined directly today?
108975.e: In a genetic test, DNA from blood or saliva is examined. This shows which alleles a person carries.
108975.m: A genetic test reads the genotype from DNA.

108976.q: From what can a person's DNA be obtained for a genetic test?
a: From the air in the room
108976.e: Saliva and blood contain body cells. DNA can be extracted from them and examined.

108977.q: Why do researchers compare identical and non-identical twins?
a: To tell apart the influence of genes and environment
108977.e: Identical twins have practically the same genes, non-identical twins only about half. If identical twins are more alike in a feature, this points to an influence of the genes.
108977.m: Twin studies separate the influence of genes and environment.

108978.q: What do identical twins have in common?
108978.e: Identical twins develop from the same beginning and so have almost identical genes. Their hobbies and tastes can still differ.
108978.m: Identical twins have almost the same genetic material.

108979.q: Do identical twins have the same fingerprints?
a: Yes, they are exactly the same
Only until the age of ten
108979.e: Fingerprints form before birth, partly through random influences such as pressure and position. That is why they differ even in identical twins.
108979.m: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

108980.q: On average, how much of their genetic material do non-identical twins share?
a: About half, like other brothers and sisters
108980.e: Genetically, non-identical twins are like ordinary siblings born at the same time. On average they match by about half.
108980.m: Non-identical twins are as genetically alike as siblings.

108981.q: Which question can twin research help to answer?
a: Whether a feature is more inherited or learned
108981.e: By comparing twins, researchers estimate how strongly genes and how strongly environment affect a feature, for example in diseases.
108981.m: Twin research studies nature and nurture.

108982.q: Why are identical twins who grew up apart especially revealing for research?
a: They have the same genes but different environments
They have different genes but the same environment
108982.e: In identical twins raised apart, similarities cannot be explained by the same upbringing. This makes it possible to estimate the influence of genes well.
108982.m: Twins raised apart show the effect of genes.
