108983.q: Identical twins who grew up apart often have similar tastes. What does that suggest?
a: That they secretly agree on things
That tastes depend only on the weather
108983.e: Because these twins grew up in different families, their similarities cannot be explained by the same upbringing. This points to an influence of the genes.
108983.m: Similarities between twins raised apart show the effect of genes.

108984.q: What is the share of differences in a feature that comes from genes called?
108984.e: Heritability shows how much of the differences between people can be explained by genes. Twin studies help to estimate it.
108984.m: Heritability measures the influence of genes on differences.

108985.q: Which feature is practically always the same in identical twins?
108985.e: Blood group is fully set by the genes. Since identical twins have practically the same genes, it matches.
108985.m: Identical twins have the same blood group.

108986.q: Which simple sugar is carried in the blood to the cells and is their most important source of energy?
108986.e: Glucose, also called grape sugar, is blood sugar. The cells get energy from it.
108986.m: Glucose is the sugar that reaches the cells in the blood.

108987.q: In which form do plants such as the potato store their carbohydrates?
108987.e: Plants link many glucose units together to form starch and store it in tubers, grains and seeds.
108987.m: Potatoes, rice and cereals are rich in starch.

108988.q: What is the double sugar made of two glucose units called, which forms in germinating grain for malt?
108988.e: Maltose is also called malt sugar. It forms when germinating grain breaks down its starch.

108989.q: What is the sugar called that is found naturally in milk?
108989.e: Lactose is also called milk sugar. People with lactose intolerance find it hard to digest.

108990.q: From which plant do the sugar factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld make household sugar?
108990.e: In Switzerland, sugar is made from sugar beet grown in Swiss fields. Sugar cane only grows in warm countries.
108990.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

108991.q: Which food makes blood sugar rise especially quickly?
108991.e: Glucose goes straight into the blood without needing to be digested. Thanks to their fibre, wholegrains, lentils and nuts make blood sugar rise slowly.
108991.m: Glucose gets into the blood very quickly.

108992.q: Roughly how much energy does 1 gram of carbohydrate provide?
108992.e: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal or 17 kJ. One gram of protein provides the same amount.
108992.m: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories.

108993.q: According to dietary recommendations, roughly what share of daily energy should carbohydrates provide?
108993.e: It is recommended that about half of your energy comes from carbohydrates, ideally from wholegrains, potatoes, pulses and fruit.
108993.m: Carbohydrates are the biggest source of energy in the diet.

108994.q: Which sugar is found mainly in fruit and honey?
108994.e: Fructose is also called fruit sugar. It is sweeter than household sugar.

108995.q: What building blocks are proteins made of?
108995.e: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. The order of the amino acids decides the shape and job of the protein.
108995.m: Proteins are made of amino acids.

108996.q: What does it mean when an amino acid is “essential”?
a: The body cannot make it itself
It is found only in meat
It provides especially lots of energy
It is poisonous in large amounts
108996.e: Essential amino acids must come from food, because the body cannot make them.
108996.m: Essential amino acids must come from food.

108997.q: Which foods are good plant sources of protein?
108997.e: Lentils, beans, peas and chickpeas contain a lot of protein. Salad, fruit and oil provide hardly any protein.
108997.m: Pulses are rich in plant protein.

108998.q: In which organ does the enzyme pepsin start digesting protein?
108998.e: Stomach acid makes proteins swell, and pepsin breaks them into shorter pieces. Digestion continues in the small intestine.
108998.m: Protein digestion begins in the stomach.

108999.q: Which protein are hair and fingernails mainly made of?
108999.e: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein. It is also found in horns, feathers and the top layer of the skin.
108999.m: Hair and nails are made of keratin.

109000.q: What does the body mainly need protein for?
109000.e: Proteins are the body's building materials. Muscles, skin, hair and many other parts of the cells are made from them.
109000.m: Protein is the building material for muscles and cells.

109001.q: What job do enzymes, which are mostly proteins, do?
109001.e: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they make chemical reactions in the body happen quickly, for example in digestion.
109001.m: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in the body.

109002.q: What can happen to children with a severe lack of protein?
a: They grow poorly and become weak
109002.e: Without enough protein, the body lacks building materials. Children then grow poorly, become weak and are often ill.
109002.m: Children need enough protein to grow.

109003.q: A yoghurt contains 4 g of protein per 100 g. How much protein is in a 180 g pot?
109003.e: You calculate 4 g times 1.8, because 180 divided by 100 is 1.8. That makes 7.2 g of protein.
109003.m: Convert nutrition values per 100 g using the amount in the pack.

109004.q: Which of these vitamins is fat-soluble?
109004.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat. Vitamin C, on the other hand, dissolves in water.
109004.m: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

109005.q: What does the body need fat from food for?
a: As an energy store and to absorb certain vitamins
To carry oxygen in the blood
109005.e: Fat provides a lot of energy and is stored as a reserve. The body also needs fat to absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
109005.m: Fat provides energy and helps absorb vitamins.

109006.q: Which fatty acids are especially common in butter and make it solid at room temperature?
109006.e: Saturated fatty acids have straight chains that pack closely together. That is why animal fats such as butter tend to be solid and oils tend to be liquid.
109006.m: Saturated fatty acids make fats solid.

109007.q: Which food is especially rich in omega-3 fatty acids?
109007.e: Oily sea fish such as salmon, herring or mackerel contain a lot of omega-3 fatty acids. They are important for the heart and brain.
109007.m: Oily fish provides lots of omega-3 fatty acids.

109008.q: Which body fluid breaks fat in the gut into fine droplets so that it is digested better?
109008.e: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It emulsifies fat so that enzymes can break it down more easily.

109009.q: Which fats are considered especially unhealthy, partly because they form when oils are hardened industrially?
109009.e: Trans fatty acids raise the unhealthy LDL cholesterol. Switzerland limits their amount in cooking oils and fats by law.
109009.m: Trans fats are bad for the heart and blood vessels.

109010.q: Besides storing energy, what job does the fatty tissue under the skin do?
109010.e: The fat under the skin insulates the body against heat loss and cushions it against knocks.
109010.m: Fat under the skin keeps you warm and cushions the body.

109011.q: What happens to most fibre in the small intestine?
109011.e: Humans lack the enzymes to break down fibre. So it moves on into the large intestine.

109012.q: Which type of fibre forms the cell walls of plants?
109012.e: Cellulose is the most common plant substance and gives plant cells their strength. Paper and cotton are also mostly made of it.
109012.m: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

109013.q: According to recommendations, how much fibre should adults eat at least each day?
109013.e: At least about 30 g a day is recommended. Many people eat much less.
109013.m: Adults should eat about 30 grams of fibre a day.

109014.q: Which bread contains the most fibre?
109014.e: For wholemeal bread, the whole grain is ground including its outer layers. That is exactly where most of the fibre is.
109014.m: Wholegrain products contain lots of fibre.

109015.q: Which fibre from apples and quinces makes jam and jelly set?
109015.e: Pectin is a soluble fibre from the cell walls of fruit. With sugar and acid it forms a gel.
109015.m: Pectin from fruit makes jam set.

109016.q: Why should you drink enough when eating a high-fibre diet?
a: Because fibre binds water and swells
Because it draws salt out of the body
Because it raises the pulse a lot
Because it makes acid in the stomach
109016.e: Fibre soaks up water and so increases the volume of the gut contents. Without enough fluid, constipation can result.
109016.m: If you eat lots of fibre, you should drink plenty.

109017.q: What breaks down some of the fibre in the large intestine?
109017.e: Bacteria in the large intestine ferment certain kinds of fibre. This produces substances that are good for the gut lining, but also gases.

109018.q: What are the outer layers of the cereal grain called, which are separated during milling and contain lots of fibre?
109018.e: Bran is made of the husk and outer layers of the grain. You can mix it into muesli, for example.

109019.q: How does fibre affect the feeling of being full?
a: It keeps you full for longer
109019.e: High-fibre food has to be chewed for longer, fills the stomach and makes blood sugar rise more slowly. That is why the full feeling lasts longer.
109019.m: Fibre keeps you full for a long time.

109020.q: Which mineral is the main building block of bones and teeth and is found in large amounts in milk?
109020.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard. Dairy products such as cheese and yoghurt are good sources of calcium.
109020.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

109021.q: Chemically, table salt is made of sodium and which other substance?
109021.e: Table salt is sodium chloride, with the formula NaCl. It provides the body with sodium and chloride.

109022.q: According to the World Health Organization, what is the most salt adults should eat per day?
109022.e: The WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day, about a teaspoon. In Switzerland, people eat much more on average.
109022.m: You should not eat more than 5 grams of salt a day.

109023.q: Which mineral sits at the centre of the green leaf pigment chlorophyll?
109023.e: Every chlorophyll molecule contains a magnesium atom in its centre. That is why green leafy vegetables such as spinach are a good source of magnesium.
109023.m: There is magnesium in the green of leaves.

109024.q: What makes major minerals such as calcium different from trace elements?
a: The body contains more of them
They provide a lot of energy
They are found only in meat
109024.e: Major minerals are found in the body in larger amounts, trace elements only in tiny traces. Both must be taken in with food.
109024.m: The body contains larger amounts of major minerals than of trace elements.

109025.q: Which vitamin does the gut need to absorb calcium well?
109025.e: Vitamin D helps calcium be absorbed from the gut. The skin makes it with the help of sunlight.
109025.m: Without vitamin D, the body absorbs little calcium.

109026.q: Which mineral do you lose especially when you sweat?
109026.e: Sweat tastes salty because it contains sodium chloride. During long sport, you may therefore need to replace salt as well.
109026.m: Sweating mainly makes you lose sodium.

109027.q: Which mineral is important for relaxing the muscles and is often taken for calf cramps?
109027.e: Magnesium plays a part in muscle relaxation and in passing signals along nerves. It is found in nuts, wholegrains and green vegetables.

109028.q: Which gland grows larger when there is a lack of iodine and forms a goitre?
109028.e: The thyroid gland needs iodine for its hormones. If iodine is missing, the gland grows to catch more iodine, and a goitre forms.
109028.m: A lack of iodine makes the thyroid gland grow.

109029.q: Why is iodine added to table salt in Switzerland?
a: Because the soil and food contain little iodine
109029.e: The soils in the Alps are low in iodine. In the past, many people therefore suffered from a lack of iodine and goitre. Iodised salt has been available in Switzerland since 1922.
109029.m: Iodised salt protects against a lack of iodine.

109030.q: Which trace element is contained in the red blood pigment haemoglobin?
109030.e: In haemoglobin, an iron atom binds the oxygen. This is how the blood can carry oxygen.
109030.m: The blood needs iron to carry oxygen.

109031.q: What is a common result of a lack of iron?
109031.e: Without enough iron, the body makes too little red blood pigment. You become pale, tired and less able to perform.
109031.m: A lack of iron makes you tired and pale.

109032.q: Which metal, also found in electric cables, does the body need as a trace element?
109032.e: Copper is part of important enzymes, for example for making blood. Lead, mercury and cadmium, on the other hand, are poisonous heavy metals.
109032.m: Copper is a vital trace element.

109033.q: Which trace element is found in many toothpastes and protects tooth enamel against decay?
109033.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acids. In Switzerland there is also fluoridated table salt.

109034.q: Which trace element is important for the immune system and wound healing and is found in large amounts in oysters?
109034.e: Zinc is part of many enzymes and supports the immune system and wound healing. Good sources are oysters, meat, cheese and wholegrains.

109035.q: Why are some minerals called “trace elements”?
a: The body needs only tiny amounts of them
They leave traces on the skin
They are found only in animal tracks
They are found only in snow
109035.e: The body needs trace elements such as iron, iodine or zinc only in very small amounts. Even so, they are vital.
109035.m: The body needs trace elements only in the tiniest amounts.

109036.q: Which food is a good natural source of iodine?
109036.e: Sea water contains iodine, so sea fish and seaweed are rich in it. Soils in the Alps, on the other hand, tend to be low in iodine.
109036.m: Sea fish provides lots of iodine.

109037.q: What was the kilocalorie originally defined as?
a: Bringing 1 litre of water to the boil
109037.e: A kilocalorie is the amount of heat that warms 1 kg of water by 1 °C. A calorie is enough for 1 g of water.
109037.m: One kilocalorie warms a litre of water by one degree.

109038.q: 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ. Roughly how many kilojoules are 500 kcal?
109038.e: You calculate 500 times 4.2 and get 2,100 kJ. Exactly, it is 500 times 4.184, which is about 2,092 kJ.
109038.m: To convert kilocalories into kilojoules, multiply by 4.2.

109039.q: What is the official unit of energy that now appears alongside kcal on food packaging?
109039.e: The joule is the SI unit of energy. On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and kilocalories.

109041.q: What do the nutrition values on Swiss food packaging usually refer to?
109041.e: Giving the values per 100 g or 100 ml is required. This makes it easy to compare different products.
109041.m: Nutrition values are given per 100 grams on the pack.

109042.q: What happens if, over a long time, you eat more energy than you use?
109042.e: The body stores extra energy mainly as fat. That is why you put on weight.
109042.m: If you always eat more energy than you use, you put on weight.

109043.q: An apple has about 50 kcal, a slice of cake 350 kcal. How many apples provide as much energy as the cake?
109043.e: You calculate 350 divided by 50 and get 7. So seven apples have as much energy as one slice of cake.
109043.m: Comparing kilocalories shows how energy-rich a food is.

109044.q: Which device is used in the laboratory to find the energy content of a food by burning it?
109044.e: In a calorimeter, the sample is burned and the heat released is measured by how much it warms water.
109044.m: A calorimeter measures energy through the heat produced.

109045.q: What is meant by basal metabolic rate?
109045.e: The basal metabolic rate is the energy the body needs at rest for breathing, heartbeat, body heat and the organs.
109045.m: Even at complete rest, the body uses energy.

109046.q: A rule of thumb says the body needs 1 kcal per kg of body weight per hour at rest. By this rule, what is the basal metabolic rate of a 60 kg person per day?
109046.e: You calculate 60 kg times 24 hours times 1 kcal. That makes 1,440 kcal a day.
109046.m: Basal metabolic rate can be estimated with a simple rule of thumb.

109047.q: What is the extra energy called that the body needs for movement, work and sport?
109047.e: Activity energy expenditure is added to the basal metabolic rate. It is much higher in physically active people.

109048.q: What is the sum of basal metabolic rate and activity energy expenditure called?
109048.e: Total energy expenditure is the whole energy need of a day. Only if you eat that much does your weight stay the same.
109048.m: Basal metabolic rate and activity energy expenditure together make total energy expenditure.

109049.q: How does basal metabolic rate usually change in adults as they get older?
109049.e: With age, muscle mass usually decreases and metabolism slows down. That is why the basal metabolic rate falls.
109049.m: In old age, the body needs less energy at rest.

109050.q: Why do people with a lot of muscle have a higher basal metabolic rate?
a: Muscles use energy even at rest
Muscles store a lot of sugar
109050.e: Muscle tissue is metabolically active and uses energy even when you are sitting or lying down. Fatty tissue, on the other hand, needs little.
109050.m: More muscle means a higher basal metabolic rate.

109051.q: Which organ uses about 20 per cent of the energy at rest, although it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight?
109051.e: The nerve cells in the brain work all the time and need a great deal of energy for this, even during sleep.
109051.m: The brain uses a lot of energy.

109052.q: What makes the basal metabolic rate rise for a while?
109052.e: With a fever, metabolic processes run faster. For every degree of fever, the energy need rises noticeably.
109052.m: A fever increases the body's energy needs.

109053.q: Which sight problem can a lack of vitamin A cause?
109053.e: Without enough vitamin A, the eyes see poorly at dusk. In poor countries this deficiency is still common today.
109053.m: A lack of vitamin A leads to night blindness.

109054.q: Which orange pigment in carrots is a precursor of vitamin A?
109054.e: The body turns beta-carotene into vitamin A when needed. It is also found in pumpkin, apricots and peppers.
109054.m: Beta-carotene is a precursor of vitamin A.

109055.q: Why should you prepare carrots with a little oil or butter?
a: So the vitamin is absorbed better
109055.e: Vitamin A and its precursor are fat-soluble. With a little fat, the gut can absorb them much better.
109055.m: Carrots are best eaten with a little fat.

109056.q: For which sense organ is vitamin A especially important?
109056.e: Vitamin A is needed in the retina for seeing, especially in dim light. Its chemical name, retinol, also reminds us of the retina.
109056.m: Vitamin A is important for the eyes.

109057.q: In which organ does the body store vitamin A, which is why this organ is very rich in it as a food?
109057.e: The liver builds up large stores of vitamin A. So liver as a food contains a great deal of it.

109058.q: Why can too much vitamin A from supplements be harmful?
a: It is stored and builds up
It is removed from the body immediately
109058.e: What the body does not need is not simply passed out in urine but stored. Very large amounts can be poisonous.
109058.m: With vitamin A, too much can do harm.

109059.q: What is the genetically modified rice called that is meant to help against vitamin A deficiency and was partly developed at ETH Zurich?
109059.e: Golden Rice makes a precursor of vitamin A in the grain and is therefore yellowish. It was developed by Ingo Potrykus of ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer.
109059.m: Golden Rice is meant to fight vitamin A deficiency.

109060.q: Which sensory cells in the retina need vitamin A to see at dusk?
109060.e: The rods in the retina are responsible for seeing in dim light. Their visual pigment is made with vitamin A.
109060.m: The rods need vitamin A for seeing at dusk.

109061.q: What makes vitamin B12 in nature?
109061.e: Only microorganisms such as bacteria can make vitamin B12. Animals take it in through their food or from bacteria in their digestive tract.
109061.m: Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria.

109062.q: Which foods mainly contain vitamin B12?
109062.e: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods. Plants provide practically no usable B12.
109062.m: Vitamin B12 is mainly found in animal foods.

109063.q: What can a long-lasting lack of vitamin B12 lead to?
109063.e: Vitamin B12 is needed to make red blood cells and for healthy nerves. A lack leads to anaemia and can permanently damage nerves.
109063.m: A lack of B12 harms the blood and nerves.

109064.q: In which unit is the daily need for vitamin B12 given?
109064.e: The body needs only a few micrograms a day, that is millionths of a gram. Even so, the vitamin is vital.
109064.m: You need only tiny amounts of vitamin B12.

109065.q: Why can some people get a vitamin B12 deficiency despite eating well?
a: Because their body cannot absorb the vitamin properly
Because they drink too much water
Because they are outside too often
109065.e: A special substance from the stomach is needed to absorb vitamin B12. If it is missing or the gut is ill, a deficiency develops even if you eat enough B12.
109065.m: B12 deficiency can also come from poor absorption in the gut.

109066.q: Which group does vitamin B12 belong to?
109066.e: All B vitamins are water-soluble. Vitamin B12 is still an exception, because the body can store larger reserves of it.
109066.m: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin.

109067.q: Why does a vitamin B12 deficiency often show only after years?
a: Because the body has reserves for years
Because B12 only works at night
Because you only need it in old age
Because it is in every vegetable
109067.e: The body stores a few milligrams of vitamin B12. These reserves often last several years before a deficiency appears.
109067.m: B12 deficiency develops slowly because the body has reserves.

109068.q: How is a severe vitamin B12 deficiency often treated when absorption in the gut does not work properly?
109068.e: Injections bypass the gut, so the vitamin goes straight into the blood. The treatment is given by a doctor.

109069.q: A lack of which vitamin causes scurvy?
109069.e: Scurvy develops when the body gets too little vitamin C for weeks. With fresh fruit and vegetables it heals quickly.
109069.m: Scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency disease.

109070.q: Who used to suffer from scurvy especially often?
109070.e: On voyages lasting months there was no fresh fruit or vegetables. Many sailors fell ill or died.

109071.q: Which of these is a typical sign of scurvy?
109071.e: In scurvy, blood vessels and connective tissue become fragile. The gums bleed, wounds heal poorly and teeth can fall out.
109071.m: Bleeding gums are a sign of scurvy.

109072.q: Which remedy worked against scurvy in the ship's doctor James Lind's experiment of 1747?
109072.e: Lind divided sick sailors into groups with different remedies. Only the group with citrus fruit recovered quickly.

109073.q: Which pet, like humans, cannot make the vitamin that protects against scurvy itself?
109073.e: Like humans, guinea pigs lack an enzyme to make this vitamin. That is why they need fresh vegetables every day.
109073.m: Guinea pigs need fresh vegetables every day.

109074.q: Which long-lasting food did the explorer James Cook take on his voyages against scurvy?
109074.e: Sauerkraut keeps for a long time and still contains enough of the protective vitamin. As a result, Cook's crews were largely spared from scurvy.

109075.q: Why is some of the protection against scurvy lost when vegetables are cooked for a long time?
a: The vitamin is sensitive to heat
109075.e: The vitamin is destroyed by heat and oxygen and dissolves into the cooking water. Steaming briefly protects it.

109076.q: Which foods protect especially well against scurvy?
109076.e: Peppers, kiwis, citrus fruit, cabbage and berries contain a lot of the vitamin that protects against scurvy. Cereals, fat and sugar contain hardly any of it.
109076.m: Fresh fruit and vegetables prevent scurvy.

109077.q: Besides meat and fish, what do people who eat a vegan diet also go without?
109077.e: Vegetarians do not eat meat or fish. Vegans leave out all products from animals, so also milk, eggs and honey.
109077.m: Vegan means completely without animal products.

109078.q: Which plant is tofu made from?
109078.e: To make tofu, soya milk is made from soya beans and then made to curdle, similar to making cheese.
109078.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

109079.q: What is the meat substitute seitan mainly made of?
109079.e: Seitan is made from gluten, the sticky protein in wheat. That is why it is unsuitable for people with coeliac disease.
109079.m: Seitan is made of wheat protein.

109080.q: Which vitamin should people who eat a vegan diet take as a supplement or through fortified foods?
109080.e: Plant foods provide practically no usable vitamin B12. Expert bodies therefore recommend a supplement for vegans.
109080.m: A vegan diet needs a vitamin B12 supplement.

109081.q: Why are many jelly sweets not vegan?
109081.e: Gelatine is made from the skin and bones of animals. Vegan jelly sweets use plant-based gelling agents instead.

109082.q: Which plant ingredient provides lots of omega-3 fatty acids?
109082.e: Linseed, linseed oil, walnuts and algae oil contain omega-3 fatty acids. For vegans they replace fish.
109082.m: Linseed is a plant source of omega-3.

109083.q: Which word was the word “vegan” formed from?
109083.e: The word was formed in England in 1944 from the first and last letters of “vegetarian”.

109084.q: Which of these plant foods is a good source of calcium for vegans?
109084.e: Kale, broccoli, almonds and plant drinks fortified with calcium provide lots of calcium. Cucumbers, rice and apples contain only a little.
109084.m: Green cabbage vegetables provide calcium without milk.

109085.q: How is energy transferred in conduction?
a: From particle to particle without any material moving
By sound waves in the air
109085.e: In conduction, faster vibrating particles bump into their neighbours and so pass energy on. The material itself stays in place.
109085.m: In conduction, energy travels, not the material.

109087.q: How does the handle of a metal spoon standing in hot soup get warm?
a: By friction of the particles with the air
109087.e: The heat travels step by step through the solid metal from the hot end to the handle. In solids, this is the most important way heat travels.
109087.m: In solids, heat travels by conduction.

109088.q: Why do cooking spoons and pan handles often have parts made of wood or plastic?
a: Because these materials conduct heat poorly
Because these materials conduct heat well
109088.e: Wood and plastic conduct heat only poorly. This keeps the handle cool even when the pan is hot.
109088.m: Wooden or plastic handles protect against burns.

109089.q: What are materials called that conduct heat only poorly?
109089.e: Insulators such as wood, cork, wool or polystyrene slow down the flow of heat. They are used to keep things warm or cool.

109090.q: Which of these materials is a very good conductor of heat?
109090.e: Metals conduct heat well because their freely moving electrons carry the energy on quickly. Copper is one of the best.
109090.m: Metals such as copper conduct heat very well.

109091.q: Why do you put a thick mat under your sleeping bag when camping in winter?
a: So that less body heat flows into the ground
So that the ground conducts heat better
So that the Sun warms the ground
So that cold air escapes faster
109091.e: The cold ground would draw a lot of heat from the body by conduction. The mat interrupts this flow of heat.
109091.m: An insulating mat protects you from the cold of the ground.

109092.q: What does the amount of heat conducted through a wall per second depend on?
a: On material, thickness, area and temperature difference
Only on the colour of the wall
Only on the height of the house
Only on the age of the building
109092.e: More heat flows with a large area, a thin wall, a material that conducts well and a large temperature difference.
109092.m: The thickness and material of a wall decide the heat loss.

109093.q: Why do you cool down much faster in water at 15 °C than in air at 15 °C?
a: Water conducts heat much better than air
Water is always colder than air
Air contains more energy than water
109093.e: Water conducts heat about twenty times better than air. At the same temperature, it therefore draws much more heat from the body.
109093.m: Cold water cools you down much more than cold air.

109094.q: What does the thermal conductivity of a material tell you?
109094.e: Materials with a high thermal conductivity, such as metals, conduct heat quickly. Insulating materials have a very low thermal conductivity.
109094.m: Thermal conductivity shows how well a material conducts heat.

109095.q: Insulating materials carry a lambda value, which gives the thermal conductivity. Which insulating material insulates better?
a: The one with the smaller lambda value
The one with the larger lambda value
The lambda value makes no difference
The one with the lighter colour
109095.e: A small lambda value means that the material conducts heat poorly. That is why it insulates better.
109095.m: The smaller the lambda value, the better a material insulates.

109096.q: Which metal has the highest thermal conductivity?
109096.e: Silver conducts heat slightly better than copper and much better than iron or lead.
109096.m: Silver is the metal with the best thermal conductivity.

109097.q: Copper has a thermal conductivity of about 400 W/(m·K), polystyrene about 0.035 W/(m·K). Roughly how many times better does copper conduct?
109097.e: You calculate 400 divided by 0.035 and get about 11,400. So copper conducts about 11,000 times better.
109097.m: Metals and insulating materials differ enormously in thermal conductivity.

109098.q: Which material conducts heat even better than copper?
109098.e: Diamond has a thermal conductivity of up to about 2000 W/(m·K), about five times more than copper. That is why a real diamond feels cool.
109098.m: Diamond is an excellent conductor of heat.

109099.q: Why do good frying pans often have a base made of aluminium or copper?
a: They spread the heat quickly and evenly
They make the pan especially heavy
They keep the heat away from the food
They stop anything from ever burning
109099.e: Aluminium and copper conduct heat very well. The heat from the hob spreads evenly over the whole base of the pan.
109099.m: Pan bases that conduct well heat the food evenly.

109100.q: Which of these building materials has the lowest thermal conductivity?
109100.e: Wood conducts heat more than ten times worse than concrete and much worse than steel. That is why wooden floors feel warm.
109100.m: Wood is a building material with low thermal conductivity.

109101.q: A wall is made of a material with twice the thermal conductivity, and everything else stays the same. How much heat flows through it now?
109101.e: The heat flow is proportional to the thermal conductivity. If you double it, the heat loss doubles too.
109101.m: Twice the thermal conductivity means twice the heat flow.

a: Heat transfer by flowing liquids or gases
109102.e: In convection, the warm water or warm air itself moves and carries the energy with it.
109102.m: In convection, the warm material flows along.

a: It is heavier than cold air
It is pushed away by the ground
109103.e: When air is heated, it expands and becomes less dense. The denser cold air pushes it upwards.
109103.m: Warm air rises because it is lighter.

109104.q: Why are radiators often placed right under the window?
a: The rising warm air catches cold air from the window
The Sun shines most strongly there
So that the window does not open
109104.e: At the cold window, cooled air sinks downwards. The warm air from the radiator rises there and prevents a cold draught.
109104.m: Radiators under the window prevent cold draughts.

109105.q: In which materials is convection not possible?
109105.e: Convection needs particles that can move freely and flow. In solids, there is only conduction.
109105.m: Convection only happens in liquids and gases.

109106.q: On a sunny day, a wind often blows from the lake to the shore at large lakes. Why?
a: The land warms up faster, and air rises there
The lake is warmer than the land during the day
The mountains push the air to the shore
109106.e: Warm air rises above the land, which heats up quickly. Cooler air from the lake flows in, and this creates the lake breeze.
109106.m: A lake breeze forms because land warms up faster than water.

a: A hair dryer blows warm air
A spoon in tea gets hot
A stone lies in the shade
109107.e: In forced convection, a device such as a fan or a pump moves the gas or liquid.
109107.m: Fans and pumps produce forced convection.

109108.q: Why do you feel colder in the wind than in still air, even though the air temperature is the same?
a: The wind carries away the warm layer of air around the body
The wind makes the air colder
The wind brings moisture into the skin
The wind slows down the heartbeat
109108.e: A thin, warm layer of air forms around the body. The wind keeps blowing it away, so the body loses more heat.
109108.m: Wind makes us cool down faster.

109109.q: According to current thinking, what drives the movement of the Earth’s plates?
a: Convection currents in the Earth’s mantle
The tides caused by the Moon
109109.e: In the hot mantle, rock rises very slowly and sinks again elsewhere. These currents carry the plates along with them.
109109.m: There is convection inside the Earth too.

109110.q: What is rising warm air called that glider pilots and birds of prey use?
109110.e: Above sunlit surfaces, the air warms up and rises in bubbles. Glider pilots circle in them and gain height.

109111.q: In physics, what is an ideal object called that completely absorbs all radiation that hits it?
109111.e: A black body swallows all radiation and is at the same time the best possible emitter. It serves as a model for the laws of heat radiation.
109111.m: A black body absorbs all radiation.

109112.q: Why is it more pleasant under a sunshade, even though the air there is almost as warm?
a: It sucks the heat out of the ground
109112.e: In the Sun, the skin is warmed mainly by radiation. The shade catches this radiation, even if the air temperature stays the same.
109112.m: Shade protects you from the Sun’s radiation.

109113.q: A researcher held a thermometer next to the red end of a rainbow made by a prism. What did he find?
a: It got warm, even though no light could be seen
109113.e: This is how William Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800. It is invisible, but we feel it as heat.
109113.m: Infrared radiation is invisible, but you can feel it as heat.

109114.q: Why does a silver emergency blanket keep an injured person warm?
a: It reflects the body’s heat radiation back
109114.e: The thin metal layer reflects the heat radiation back to the body. The foil also keeps the wind off.
109114.m: Shiny surfaces reflect heat radiation back.

109115.q: Which objects give off heat radiation?
a: All objects, depending on their temperature
109115.e: Every object that is warmer than absolute zero radiates heat. The hotter it is, the more it radiates.
109115.m: Everything that has a temperature gives off heat radiation.

109116.q: The power radiated by an object increases with the fourth power of its absolute temperature. By what factor does it rise if the absolute temperature doubles?
109116.e: You calculate 2 to the power of 4, that is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2. That gives 16.
109116.m: Hot objects radiate much more energy than cool ones.

109117.q: Why does a car standing in the Sun get so hot inside?
a: Light gets in, but the heat radiation hardly gets out
The engine keeps heating while it is parked
The tyres conduct heat in from the ground
The air in the car is compressed
109117.e: Sunlight passes through the windows and warms the seats. These radiate heat that the glass hardly lets through, and the warm air stays trapped.
109117.m: In a closed car, heat builds up as in a greenhouse.

109118.q: Why do you feel the heat of a campfire on your face, even though the hot air rises upwards?
a: Because of the fire’s heat radiation
Because of conduction through the air
Because of the moisture in the air
109118.e: The flames and embers send out heat radiation in all directions. It also reaches people sitting to the side of the fire.
109118.m: You feel the warmth of a fire mainly as radiation.

109119.q: Why do materials such as polystyrene or rock wool insulate so well?
a: They trap a lot of air in tiny pores
They are especially heavy and dense
They contain a lot of metal
109119.e: Still air conducts heat poorly. In the tiny pores, it cannot flow, so there is hardly any convection either.
109119.m: Trapped air makes insulating materials effective.

109120.q: What does a well-insulated house wall do in winter?
a: It lets a lot of heat out
It draws cold into the house
109120.e: Good insulation slows down the flow of heat. This keeps the warmth in the house, and less heating energy is needed.
109120.m: Good insulation keeps the warmth in the house.

109121.q: Which window keeps the heat in the house best?
a: A window with three panes of glass
A window with one pane of glass
A window with especially thin glass
A window that is tilted open
109121.e: A gas that conducts heat poorly is trapped between the panes. The more panes, the better the window insulates.

109122.q: What is a spot in a building’s outer shell called where heat flows out especially fast, for example at a balcony slab?
109122.e: At thermal bridges, the insulation is interrupted or a material that conducts well leads outside. Damp and mould can form on the inside there.
109122.m: Thermal bridges are weak points in the insulation.

109123.q: Which of these insulating materials is a natural product?
109123.e: Sheep’s wool, wood fibre, hemp or cellulose are natural insulating materials. Polystyrene and other foams are made from crude oil.
109123.m: Sheep’s wool can insulate a house too.

109124.q: What does good thermal insulation do in summer?
a: The house stays cool for longer
It has no effect in summer
The windows mist up more often
109124.e: Insulation slows down the flow of heat in both directions. In summer, it keeps the heat outside.
109124.m: Insulation protects against cold in winter and heat in summer.

109125.q: Why do the Confederation and the cantons give homeowners money when they insulate their houses better?
a: So that less energy is used for heating
So that the houses look nicer
So that the houses get lighter
So that more houses are built
109125.e: Well-insulated houses need less heating energy and cause less CO2. That is why Switzerland has the Buildings Programme.

109126.q: Why must insulating materials stay dry?
a: Wet insulating materials conduct heat much better
Wet insulating materials become very light
109126.e: If water gets in, it pushes the insulating air out of the pores. As a result, much of the insulating effect is lost.

a: A Swiss building standard for energy-efficient buildings
109127.e: Minergie is a building label for new buildings and renovations with low energy use and high comfort.
109127.m: Minergie stands for energy-saving buildings in Switzerland.

109128.q: What does a Minergie house need much less of than an ordinary house?
109128.e: Thanks to good insulation and comfort ventilation, a Minergie house needs only a little heating energy. The standard has existed since 1998.
109128.m: Minergie houses need little heating energy.

109129.q: What does the Minergie-P standard require compared with the normal Minergie standard?
109129.e: Minergie-P requires especially good insulation and airtightness. This means the house hardly needs any heating energy.
109129.m: Minergie-P is the especially economical Minergie standard.

109130.q: What does the Minergie-ECO addition pay attention to besides energy use?
a: Healthy and environmentally friendly building materials
109130.e: With Minergie-ECO, healthy indoor air, daylight, noise protection and environmentally friendly building materials also count.
109130.m: Minergie-ECO also pays attention to health and the environment.

109131.q: Which system is typical of Minergie buildings and provides fresh air without you having to open the windows?
109131.e: Comfort ventilation swaps stale air for fresh air and uses the heat of the outgoing air to pre-warm the incoming air.
109131.m: Comfort ventilation brings fresh air without much heat loss.

109132.q: Besides low energy use, what does Minergie explicitly set as a goal?
109132.e: Minergie buildings are meant to be comfortable: pleasant temperatures, good air and little noise are part of the concept.
109132.m: Minergie combines saving energy with living comfort.

a: The Confederation, the cantons and the business world
109133.e: Minergie is an association supported by the Confederation, the cantons and the business world. It awards the certificates.
109133.m: Behind Minergie are the Confederation, the cantons and business.

109134.q: Which feature of the building shell is especially important for a Minergie house?
a: As many open joints as possible
109134.e: Only with a well-insulated and airtight shell can the heating energy needed be lowered as much as Minergie requires.
109134.m: A Minergie house needs a well-insulated shell.

109135.q: Which gas usually fills the gaps in triple glazing?
109135.e: The noble gas argon is usually used, and krypton in very good windows. Both are non-toxic and do not react.
109135.m: Modern insulated windows are filled with noble gas.

109136.q: How many gaps does triple glazing have?
109136.e: Between three panes of glass, there are two sealed gaps.

109137.q: Why are the gaps filled with a noble gas instead of air?
a: It conducts heat worse than air
It tints the glass slightly blue
109137.e: Noble gases such as argon conduct heat worse than air. This means less heat is lost through the window.
109137.m: Noble gas in the window reduces heat loss.

109138.q: Why does triple glazing save heating energy?
a: It lets more cold air in
109138.e: Three panes with gas-filled gaps conduct heat much worse than a single pane. So the warmth stays in the house.
109138.m: Triple glazing lets far less heat through than a single pane.

109139.q: What does the wafer-thin metal coating on modern heat-protection glass do?
a: It reflects heat radiation back into the room
109139.e: The invisible coating lets light through but reflects the heat radiation from the heating and the furniture back into the room.
109139.m: A heat-protection coating keeps radiant heat in the room.

109140.q: What disadvantage does triple glazing have compared with double glazing?
a: It is more often cold on the inside
109140.e: The third pane adds extra weight. That is why frames and fittings have to be built more sturdily.
109140.m: Triple glazing is heavier than double glazing.

109141.q: Why does triple glazing sometimes mist up on the outside on cold mornings?
a: Because the outer pane gets hardly any heat from inside
Because the window has started to leak
Because the noble gas escapes outwards
Because the heating is too weak
109141.e: The good insulation lets hardly any heat reach the outer pane. It gets very cold, and moisture from the air condenses on it. This is a sign of good insulation.
109141.m: Windows that mist up on the outside show good insulation.

109142.q: Why is the window frame insulated as well in good windows?
a: Otherwise a lot of heat is lost at the edge
So that the window is lighter
So that the glass does not break
So that more light comes in
109142.e: Heat finds the easiest way outside. A poorly insulated frame or glass edge would be a weak point.
109142.m: The frame and glass edge must insulate well too.

109143.q: What does a thermal imaging camera make visible?
109143.e: The camera measures the radiation that surfaces give off depending on their temperature and shows it as a coloured image.
109143.m: A thermal imaging camera shows temperatures as colours.

109144.q: What do red and yellow areas on a thermal image usually show?
109144.e: Thermal images use false colours. Usually red, yellow and white stand for warm, blue and purple for cold.
109144.m: On thermal images, red usually means warm.

109145.q: When is the best time for a thermal survey of the outside of a house?
109145.e: You need a large difference in temperature between inside and outside. Sun and rain would distort the result.
109145.m: Buildings are thermally surveyed on cold nights.

109146.q: What can you find with a thermal survey of a house?
a: The age of the roof tiles
109146.e: Where a lot of heat escapes, the outside surface is warmer and lights up on the image. This shows the weak points.
109146.m: A thermal survey shows where a house loses heat.

109147.q: What does the fire brigade use thermal imaging cameras for?
109147.e: Smoke blocks the view, but the heat radiation from people and pockets of embers gets through.
109147.m: Thermal imaging cameras help the fire brigade in thick smoke.

109148.q: What were thermal imaging cameras used for at airports during epidemics, for example?
109148.e: People with a fever have a warmer skin surface. The camera can pick them out without touching them.
109148.m: Thermal images can detect fever without contact.

109149.q: Why can a thermal imaging camera not see through an ordinary windowpane?
a: Glass hardly lets this radiation through
Glass is too cold for the camera
Glass is too thin for it
109149.e: Glass is transparent to visible light, but almost opaque to long-wave heat radiation. The camera only sees the surface of the glass.
109149.m: Window glass is opaque to thermal imaging cameras.

109150.q: What can an electrician track down with a thermal imaging camera?
109150.e: Loose or overloaded contacts get warm before they fail or start a fire. On the thermal image, they stand out at once.
109150.m: Thermal imaging finds hot spots in electrical installations.

109151.q: What is the technical term for an image taken with a thermal imaging camera?
109151.e: The image from a thermal survey is called a thermogram. Each pixel corresponds to a measured surface temperature.
109151.m: A thermal image is called a thermogram.

109152.q: Why do heat sinks have many thin fins?
a: The larger surface gives off more heat
The fins make the device lighter
109152.e: The larger the surface, the more heat can be given off to the surrounding air.

109153.q: Which metal are heat sinks often made of because it is light and conducts heat well?
109153.e: Aluminium conducts heat well and is light and cheap. Copper is also used for especially powerful coolers.
109153.m: Heat sinks are often made of aluminium.

109154.q: Where are cooling fins typically found?
109154.e: Processors produce a lot of heat in a small area. A heat sink with fins stops them from overheating.

109155.q: What is spread between the processor and the heat sink so that the heat passes across well?
109155.e: Tiny air gaps remain between two metal surfaces. Thermal paste fills them and improves the transfer of heat.
109155.m: Thermal paste fills air gaps between the chip and the cooler.

109156.q: Why is there a fan on many heat sinks?
a: It blows the warmed air away
It produces electricity for the computer
109156.e: The fan keeps moving cool air past the fins. This lets the heat sink give off much more heat.
109156.m: A fan boosts the effect of cooling fins.

109157.q: Which animal uses its large ears, which have a good blood supply, rather like cooling fins?
109157.e: A lot of blood flows through the thin ears and gives off heat to the air there. By flapping them, the elephant strengthens the effect.
109157.m: Elephants cool down through their large ears.

109158.q: What happens if a computer’s cooling fins are very dusty?
109158.e: Dust acts like an insulating layer and blocks the airflow. The computer gets hotter and the fan gets louder.

109159.q: How should cooling fins without a fan best be positioned?
a: Vertically, so that warm air can rise
Horizontally, so that the air stays put
109159.e: Without a fan, the warmed air rises on its own. Vertical fins let it flow through freely.
109159.m: Vertical cooling fins let warm air escape well.

109160.q: What is typical of central heating?
a: One heat source heats all the rooms
Each room has its own stove
The heat comes from the television
109160.e: With central heating, heat is produced in one place, for example in the cellar, and spread around the house through pipes.
109160.m: Central heating supplies the whole house from one place.

109161.q: How is the heat usually spread in central heating?
a: With heating oil in the radiators
109161.e: The heated water flows through pipes to the radiators, gives off heat there and returns cooled down.
109161.m: Heating water carries the heat to the radiators.

109162.q: Which pump makes the heating water flow round the circuit?
109162.e: The circulation pump pushes the heating water through the boiler, pipes and radiators. Modern pumps need little electricity for this.
109162.m: The circulation pump keeps the heating water moving.

109163.q: What is the pipe called in which the hot water flows to the radiators?
109163.e: In the flow pipe, the warm water flows to the radiators, and in the return pipe, the cooled water comes back.
109163.m: Warm heating water flows in the flow pipe.

109164.q: Why does central heating need an expansion vessel?
a: Because water expands when it is heated
Because the water would otherwise freeze
109164.e: Warm water needs more space than cold water. The expansion vessel takes up the extra volume, otherwise the pressure would rise too much.
109164.m: The expansion vessel protects the heating from too much pressure.

109165.q: Why does underfloor heating go especially well with a heat pump?
a: It only needs lukewarm heating water
It needs very hot heating water
109165.e: The large area of the floor gives off enough heat at only about 30 to 35 °C. Heat pumps work especially efficiently at low temperatures.
109165.m: Underfloor heating manages with low water temperatures.

109166.q: What was the Roman underfloor heating called, the remains of which can be seen at Augusta Raurica, for example?
109166.e: In a hypocaust, hot flue gases from a furnace flowed under a floor resting on pillars and so warmed the rooms.
109166.m: The Romans heated with the hypocaust.

109167.q: What does a thermostatic valve on a radiator control?
a: The water pressure in the house
The electricity used by the lamps
109167.e: The valve opens or closes the flow of heating water depending on the room temperature. This keeps the room evenly warm.
109167.m: A thermostatic valve keeps the room temperature constant.

109169.q: Which household appliance works on the same principle as a heat pump?
109169.e: The fridge pumps heat from inside to the outside. The heat pump pumps heat from outside into the house.
109169.m: A heat pump is a fridge in reverse.

109170.q: A heat pump supplies 4 kilowatt-hours of heat for every kilowatt-hour of electricity. How much heat does it supply with 2500 kWh of electricity?
109170.e: You calculate 2500 times 4 and get 10,000 kWh. This number 4 is also called the seasonal performance factor.
109170.m: A good heat pump supplies several times the electricity used as heat.

109171.q: A heat pump supplies 3 kilowatt-hours of heat for every kilowatt-hour of electricity. How much electricity does it need for 9000 kWh of heat?
109171.e: You calculate 9000 divided by 3 and get 3000 kWh of electricity. The other 6000 kWh come from the surroundings.
109171.m: Heat divided by the performance factor gives the electricity needed.

109172.q: How deep are ground probes for heat pumps typically drilled in Switzerland?
109172.e: Ground probes usually go about 100 to 300 m deep. There, the ground is roughly the same temperature all year round.
109172.m: Ground probes reach far down into the ground.

109173.q: Which part of a heat pump raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant?
109173.e: The electrically driven compressor squeezes the gaseous refrigerant. This makes it hot.
109173.m: The compressor makes the refrigerant hot.

109174.q: What happens to the refrigerant in the heat pump’s evaporator?
a: It evaporates and takes in heat from the surroundings
It gives off heat to the house
109174.e: The refrigerant boils at very low temperatures. As it evaporates, it takes in heat from the air, the ground or water.
109174.m: When it evaporates, the refrigerant takes in heat.

109175.q: The heat pump in Zurich City Hall from 1938 is considered a pioneering system. Where did it get its heat from?
a: From the water of the Limmat
109175.e: A heat pump takes heat from the surroundings. At Zurich City Hall, this was the river water of the Limmat.
109175.m: Zurich was a pioneer of the heat pump.

109176.q: Why does a ground-source heat pump usually work more efficiently in winter than an air-source heat pump?
a: The ground is warmer than the air in winter
There is more oxygen in the ground
109176.e: Deep down, the ground is about 10 °C or more all year round. The smaller the temperature difference the pump has to overcome, the less electricity it needs.
109176.m: Heat from the ground is easier to use in winter than heat from cold air.

109177.q: Which plants supply district heating in many Swiss towns?
109177.e: Burning waste produces a lot of heat. Instead of letting it go unused, it is used to heat water for the district heating network.
109177.m: Waste incineration plants heat whole neighbourhoods.

109178.q: What usually flows through the pipes of a district heating network?
109178.e: At the heating plant, water is heated strongly and pumped through insulated pipes to the houses. Once cooled, it flows back.
109178.m: District heating brings hot water into the houses.

109179.q: Why must district heating pipes be well insulated?
a: So that little heat is lost on the way
So that the pipes are lighter
So that the water flows faster
So that the pipes do not rust
109179.e: The hot water often travels several kilometres. Without good insulation, it would cool down a lot on the way.
109179.m: Insulated pipes keep the district heating water hot.

109180.q: What transfers the heat from the district heating network to the building’s heating circuit inside the house?
109180.e: In the heat exchanger, the hot pipes of the network give off their heat to the house’s heating water without the two water circuits mixing.
109180.m: A heat exchanger transfers heat without mixing.

109181.q: What is it called when a plant produces electricity and usable heat at the same time?
109181.e: In combined heat and power, the waste heat from producing electricity is used, for example for district heating.
109181.m: Combined heat and power uses fuels twice over.

109182.q: Which capital city is heated almost entirely by district heating from geothermal energy?
109182.e: Iceland lies on volcanic ground. In Reykjavík, hot water from deep underground is piped directly into the houses.

109183.q: What advantage does a district heating connection have for a single house?
a: It needs no boiler of its own
109183.e: The heat is produced at the heating plant. In the house, a small transfer station is enough, and there is no need for a boiler or fuel store.
109183.m: With district heating, you do not need your own boiler.

109184.q: Where does a raised bog get its water from?
109184.e: A raised bog has grown up above the groundwater. That is why it is fed only by rain and snow.
109184.m: A raised bog lives on rainwater alone.

109185.q: Why is a raised bog called a “raised bog”?
a: It bulges upwards like a watch glass
109185.e: The layer of peat grows most in the middle and bulges above its surroundings. The name has nothing to do with altitude.
109185.m: A raised bog bulges upwards in the middle.

109186.q: What is the water in a raised bog like?
109186.e: Peat mosses release acid, and rainwater contains hardly any nutrients. That is why only specialists can grow there.
109186.m: In a raised bog, the water is acidic and poor in nutrients.

109187.q: Why should you stay on the paths in a raised bog?
a: The wet moss ground is sensitive and you can sink in
Dangerous predators live in the bog
The ground there is red hot
Most berries grow on the paths
109187.e: A raised bog consists of wet peat and peat mosses. Footsteps destroy the plant cover, which grows back only very slowly, and you can sink in at wet spots.
109187.m: In a raised bog, you stay on the path.

109188.q: What forms over thousands of years from dead peat mosses?
109188.e: In the wet, acidic bog, dead mosses are hardly broken down. They build up layer by layer as peat, only about one millimetre a year.
109188.m: Peat forms from dead peat mosses.

109189.q: Why are raised bogs strictly protected in Switzerland?
a: They are rare and home to specialised species
They supply most of the drinking water
109189.e: Many bogs used to be drained or dug for peat. The remaining raised bogs are rare and home to specialists such as sundew. Since 1987, bogs of national importance have been protected.
109189.m: Raised bogs are rare and therefore strictly protected.

109190.q: What share of Switzerland's land area is covered by raised bogs of national importance?
109190.e: The roughly 1,600 hectares of raised bog are only about three hundredths of a per cent of the country's area.
109190.m: Raised bogs are a great rarity in Switzerland.

109191.q: Which group of plants mainly builds up a raised bog?
109191.e: Peat mosses keep growing at the top while they die off at the bottom. That is how layer after layer forms.
109191.m: Without peat mosses there would be no raised bogs.

109192.q: Which small carnivorous plant with sticky droplets on its leaves often grows in raised bogs?
109192.e: The sundew catches small insects with its sticky glandular hairs. That way it gets nutrients that are missing in the raised bog.
109192.m: The sundew adds insects to its diet.

109193.q: Where does a fen get its water from?
a: From groundwater or water running off slopes
109193.e: A fen is influenced by groundwater, spring water or water from slopes. This brings minerals with it.

109194.q: What other name is often used for a fen (flat bog)?
109194.e: Fen, flat bog and low bog all mean the same type of wetland. In Switzerland it is also often called “Ried”.
109194.m: A fen is also called a low bog.

109195.q: Why do more plant species grow in fens than in raised bogs?
a: The water brings more nutrients with it
The sun shines there for longer
109195.e: Groundwater contains minerals. So more species, such as orchids, sedges and gentians, find enough food.
109195.m: Fens are richer in nutrients and species than raised bogs.

109196.q: What are fen meadows called that are only mown in autumn and whose cuttings are used as bedding in the cowshed?
109196.e: The cuttings are not good feed, but they are suitable as litter for cowsheds. Late mowing spares flowering plants and animals.
109196.m: Litter meadows are mown late and provide bedding.

109197.q: What happens to a fen if it is no longer mown?
a: Scrub spreads and it slowly becomes overgrown
It automatically becomes a raised bog
It stays the same for ever
109197.e: Without mowing, shrubs and trees spring up. The typical light-loving bog plants then disappear.
109197.m: Many fens need care by mowing.

109198.q: Why are bogs and fens protected in Switzerland today?
a: Many were drained in the past and have become rare
Drinking water for all towns comes from them
They all belong to the army
109198.e: In the past, most bogs and fens were drained and turned into farmland. Since 1987, the Federal Constitution has protected the remaining ones of special beauty and national importance.
109198.m: Switzerland's last bogs and fens are protected.

109200.q: What part of Switzerland is still covered by fens today?
109200.e: Together, the fens of national importance cover only about half a per cent of the country's area. There used to be many more.
109200.m: Fens cover only a tiny part of Switzerland.

109201.q: Which tall grass with a brown, feathery flower head often grows in wet fens on lake shores?
109201.e: Reed forms dense stands on shores and in wet fens. It can grow several metres tall.
109201.m: Reed grows in wet fens and on shores.

109202.e: In a wet bog, there is no oxygen. That is why dead plants are not completely broken down and build up as peat.
109202.m: Peat is a store of half-decomposed plants.

109203.q: About how much does a layer of peat in a raised bog grow each year?
109203.e: Peat grows very slowly, on average about one millimetre a year.
109203.m: Peat grows only about one millimetre a year.

109204.q: Which plants mainly form the peat in a raised bog?
109204.e: Peat mosses keep growing at the top and die off at the bottom. The remains are hardly broken down in the wet, acidic bog and form peat.
109204.m: In a raised bog, peat forms mainly from peat mosses.

109205.q: Why do plant remains hardly break down in peat?
a: There is no oxygen and the water is acidic
There is too much light there
109205.e: Bacteria and fungi need oxygen to break down plants. In wet, acidic peat they can hardly work.
109205.m: Wetness and acid slow down decay in peat.

109206.q: What was dried peat mainly used for in the past?
109206.e: Dried blocks of peat burn in a similar way to wood. Peat was especially important at times when there was not enough coal.
109206.m: Dried peat was used for heating in the past.

109207.q: What is peat mainly used for today?
109207.e: Peat holds water well, so it is added to many potting composts. Because bogs need protecting, there are now peat-free composts.
109207.m: Many garden composts contain peat, but there are peat-free alternatives.

109208.q: What do people sometimes discover in peat, because it preserves things for thousands of years?
a: Liquid water from the Stone Age
109208.e: In peat, which has little oxygen, pollen, wood and even old tools are preserved. Researchers use them to read the history of the climate.
109208.m: Peat is an archive of the past.

109209.q: What is the science called that uses pollen from layers of peat to study the plant life of earlier times?
109209.e: Every layer of peat contains pollen from the plants of that time. This shows which trees used to grow there.
109209.m: Pollen in peat reveals what the landscape looked like in the past.

109210.q: Which fossil fuel can form from peat under pressure over millions of years?
109210.e: If peat is covered by rock and pressed for a long time, it first becomes lignite (brown coal) and later hard coal.
109210.m: Over millions of years, peat can turn into coal.

109211.q: What is it called when peat is cut out with a spade?
109211.e: In peat cutting, blocks of peat are cut from the wall of the bog and stacked up to dry.
109211.m: Peat used to be cut by hand.

109212.q: At what times was a particularly large amount of peat dug in Switzerland?
109212.e: During the World Wars there was no imported coal. That is why peat was cut in many bogs as a substitute fuel.
109212.m: During the World Wars, peat was dug as a substitute for coal.

109213.q: What had to happen to freshly cut blocks of peat before they could be burnt?
a: They had to dry in the air for a long time
They had to lie in water
They had to be baked in an oven
109213.e: Fresh peat is mostly water. It only burns well once it is dry.
109213.m: Peat has to dry before it will burn.

109214.q: Why is digging peat harmful to the climate?
a: The stored carbon gets into the air as CO2
It uses a lot of rainwater
109214.e: Peat that has been dug decays or is burnt. This releases the carbon stored in it as carbon dioxide.

109215.q: What can you do in the garden to protect bogs?
109215.e: Bogs are dug up for the peat in garden composts, mostly abroad. Switzerland wants to reduce the use of peat. Peat-free compost protects the bogs.

109216.q: Where does most of the peat sold in Switzerland today come from?
109216.e: Bogs are protected in Switzerland. That is why peat is mainly imported from places such as the Baltic states or Germany.
109216.m: The peat in Swiss garden composts is imported.

109217.q: What happens to the plants and animals of a bog when peat is dug there?
109217.e: When peat is dug, the living layer of the bog is removed and the bog is drained. Specialised bog dwellers then have nowhere left to live.
109217.m: Digging peat destroys the habitat of many bog dwellers.

109218.q: Roughly how long does it take for a thick layer of peat to form again in a bog that has been dug?
a: Many centuries to thousands of years
109218.e: Peat grows very slowly. For people, a bog that has been dug is therefore practically lost.
109218.m: A destroyed bog only grows back over thousands of years.

109219.q: What are the white cotton-wool tufts of cotton grass?
109219.e: After flowering, long white bristles grow on the fruits. These hairs form the eye-catching woolly tufts.
109219.m: The wool of cotton grass helps the fruits to fly.

109220.q: How are the fruits of cotton grass spread?
109220.e: The woolly hairs work like a parachute. This lets the wind carry the fruits far across the bog.
109220.m: The wind spreads the fruits of cotton grass.

109221.q: Which plant family does cotton grass belong to?
109221.e: Cotton grass is not a true grass. Like the sedges, it belongs to the sedge family.

109222.q: Why are bogs with cotton grass protected in Switzerland?
a: They are rare and home to rare species
109222.e: Many bogs were drained in the past. The remaining ones are valuable for rare plants and animals, so they are protected.

109223.q: Why should you stay on the path in a bog with cotton grass?
a: The ground is wet and fragile
It is too hot in the bog
109223.e: Bog ground is soft and full of water. If you walk on it, you trample rare plants and may sink in.
109223.m: In a bog, you stay on the path.

109224.q: What did people sometimes use the wool of cotton grass for in the past?
109224.e: The soft hairs were collected and used, for example, as a filling material.
109224.m: Cotton grass wool used to be used as a filling.

109225.q: What does a patch of cotton grass in a landscape usually show?
109225.e: Cotton grass grows almost only on wet and rather acidic soils. That is why it shows where bogs are.
109225.m: Where cotton grass grows, the soil is usually wet and acidic.

109226.q: In which season are the white woolly tufts easy to see in Swiss bogs?
109226.e: Cotton grass flowers early in the year. The woolly tufts then appear in early summer.
109226.m: In early summer, bogs shine white with cotton grass.

109227.q: Where does the bog cranberry grow?
a: On cushions of peat moss in raised bogs
109227.e: The bog cranberry creeps with thin stems over the peat mosses of raised bogs.
109227.m: The bog cranberry grows on peat moss.

109228.q: What colour are ripe bog cranberries?
109228.e: The round berries turn red in late summer and autumn. They taste very sour.

109229.q: Which well-known fruit from North America is closely related to the bog cranberry?
109229.e: The American cranberry is the large-fruited cranberry. It belongs to the same genus as our bog cranberry.
109229.m: The American cranberry is a relative of the bog cranberry.

109230.q: Which plant family does the bog cranberry belong to?
109230.e: The bog cranberry belongs to the heather family, like the bilberry, the lingonberry and common heather.
109230.m: The bog cranberry belongs to the heather family.

109231.q: What do the stems of the bog cranberry look like?
a: Very thin and creeping along the ground
Thick and woody like a tree
109231.e: The thread-like stems lie on the moss. The plant is a dwarf shrub.
109231.m: The bog cranberry is a tiny creeping shrub.

109232.q: What shape are the pink flowers of the bog cranberry?
a: They are closed like a tube
109232.e: The four petals are strongly turned back. This makes the flower look like a small bird's head.
109232.m: The flowers of the bog cranberry have petals that are turned back.

109233.q: Why should you not pick bog cranberries in Swiss raised bogs?
a: The raised bogs are strictly protected
109233.e: Raised bogs of national importance are strictly protected. Anyone who walks on the bog can destroy delicate mosses.
109233.m: In protected bogs you pick nothing and stay on the paths.

109234.q: Why can the bog cranberry survive in a raised bog that is poor in nutrients?
a: Fungi on its roots help it take up nutrients
It needs no nutrients at all
109234.e: The bog cranberry lives together with root fungi. These unlock nutrients from the acidic soil.
109234.m: Root fungi help the bog cranberry to survive.

109235.q: How are the leaves of bogbean made up?
109235.e: Bogbean has leaves with three leaflets. That is where its German name, ‘fever clover’, comes from, although it is not related to clover.
109235.m: Bogbean has leaves with three parts.

109236.q: Is bogbean, which is called ‘fever clover’ in German, related to meadow clover?
a: No, it belongs to a different family
Yes, it is a type of clover from Asia
Yes, it is the ancestor of clover
109236.e: Bogbean belongs to the bogbean family. Only the shape of its leaves is like clover.
109236.m: Despite its German name, bogbean is not a clover.

109237.q: What is special about the white flowers of bogbean?
a: They are covered with fringes inside
They are completely smooth and yellow
109237.e: The petals have lots of white hairs, which makes them look bearded. The buds are pink.

109238.q: Where does bogbean especially like to grow?
a: In shallow water and in wet bogs
109238.e: Bogbean grows on banks, in areas where water is silting up and in wet bogs, often with its feet in the water.

109239.q: What do the leaves of bogbean taste like?
109239.e: Bogbean contains bitter substances. That is why it was used as a bitter remedy.

109240.q: Why is bogbean called ‘fever clover’ in German?
a: It was used against fever in the past
It only grows in hot weather
109240.e: In the past, the bitter leaves were used as a folk remedy against fever.
109240.m: The German name ‘fever clover’ recalls old remedies.

109241.q: What is bogbean mainly used for in herbal medicine today?
109241.e: The bitter substances stimulate appetite and digestion.
109241.m: Bitter substances from bogbean help digestion.

109242.q: In which months does bogbean usually flower in Switzerland?
109242.e: Bogbean flowers in late spring and early summer. Then you can see its clusters of white flowers above the water.
109242.m: Bogbean flowers in May and June.

109243.q: Which building project was opposed by the resistance that led to the Rothenthurm Initiative?
109243.e: The federal government wanted to build an army training ground near Rothenthurm. A large bog would have been used for it.
109243.m: The dispute over a training ground saved Switzerland's bogs.

109244.q: In which canton is the raised bog of Rothenthurm?
109244.e: Rothenthurm is in the canton of Schwyz, between Biberbrugg and Sattel.
109244.m: The Rothenthurm bog is in the canton of Schwyz.

109245.q: What was written into the Federal Constitution through the Rothenthurm Initiative?
a: The protection of bogs and bog landscapes
A ban on all army training grounds
A right to peat for heating
109245.e: Since it was accepted, the Federal Constitution has protected bogs and bog landscapes of special beauty and national importance.
109245.m: Since Rothenthurm, bogs have been in the Federal Constitution.

109246.q: How did the people vote on the Rothenthurm Initiative in 1987?
a: They were not allowed to vote
109246.e: The people and the cantons accepted the initiative in 1987. The planned training ground could not be built in the bog, and bogs have been protected ever since.
109246.m: The Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted in 1987.

109247.q: What kind of people's right was the Rothenthurm Initiative?
109247.e: With a popular initiative, voters can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. This needs signatures and the approval of the people and the cantons.
109247.m: With a popular initiative, the people can change the constitution.

109248.q: Who had to agree to the Rothenthurm Initiative for it to be accepted?
109248.e: A change to the constitution needs a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons. Both were achieved.
109248.m: A popular initiative needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

109249.q: What effect did the Rothenthurm Initiative have on peat digging in Switzerland?
a: Digging peat in protected bogs is banned
Peat must be dug in winter
109249.e: No facilities may be built and no peat may be dug in protected bogs.
109249.m: Since Rothenthurm, digging peat in protected bogs has been banned.

109250.q: In which article of the Federal Constitution is bog protection found today?
a: In the article on the protection of nature and cultural heritage
In the article on the army
In the article on the railways
109250.e: Bog protection is part of Article 78 of the Federal Constitution on the protection of nature and cultural heritage.
109250.m: In the constitution, bog protection belongs to the protection of nature and cultural heritage.

109251.q: Where are most of Switzerland's bog landscapes?
a: In the Pre-Alps and the Alps
On the shore of Lake Geneva
109251.e: Most bog landscapes are in the Pre-Alps and the Alps, for example in the Entlebuch or near Rothenthurm. On the Central Plateau most bogs were drained.
109251.m: Most bog landscapes are in the Pre-Alps and the Alps.

109252.q: What is a bog landscape according to Swiss bog protection?
a: A landscape with bogs and the surroundings that shape it
A store of peat in a hall
109252.e: A bog landscape includes bogs, forests, streams, pastures and typical buildings. The whole landscape is protected.
109252.m: A bog landscape includes bogs and their surroundings.

109253.q: Roughly what share of the country's area do the bog landscapes of national importance cover?
109253.e: The 89 bog landscapes cover about 2 percent of the country's area. They also include forests, pastures and settlements.
109253.m: Bog landscapes cover about two percent of Switzerland.

109254.q: Which region in the canton of Lucerne with many bog landscapes is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve?
109254.e: The UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch is known for its many bogs and bog landscapes.
109254.m: The Entlebuch is a bog area of international rank.

109255.q: Which plants are typical of bog landscapes?
109255.e: Peat mosses and cotton grass grow on wet, acidic soils. In summer the white tufts of cotton grass can be seen from far away.
109255.m: Peat moss and cotton grass are typical bog plants.

109256.q: What is allowed in a protected bog landscape if it does not harm the bog?
109256.e: Farming that helps to preserve the landscape is allowed. Farmers look after many bog landscapes.
109256.m: Farming can help to preserve bog landscapes.

109257.q: Why are bog landscapes important for the water balance?
a: They store water and release it slowly
They evaporate all the water at once
They send rain straight to the sea
109257.e: Bogs work like a sponge. They can reduce floods and release water in dry periods.
109257.m: Bogs work like a giant sponge.

109258.q: What does it mean that a bog landscape is of “national importance”?
a: The federal government protects it as important for all of Switzerland
It is only open to tourists
109258.e: Sites of national importance are listed in a federal inventory. The cantons must protect them.
109258.m: National importance means that an area matters to the whole of Switzerland.

109259.q: Why were bogs drained with ditches in the past?
a: To gain land for fields and meadows
109259.e: Drained bogs can be used as fields or meadows. This gave more land for farming.
109259.m: Bogs were drained to gain farmland.

109260.q: Roughly how much has Switzerland's bog area shrunk since the 19th century?
109260.e: Since the 19th century, Switzerland's bog area has shrunk by around 90 percent. Many bogs were drained or had their peat removed.

109261.q: In which campaign during the Second World War were many bogs drained in Switzerland?
109261.e: With the Anbauschlacht, Switzerland was meant to produce more of its own food. Many wetlands were drained for this.
109261.m: During the Anbauschlacht, many bogs became fields.

109262.q: What happens to the peat when a bog is drained?
a: It decays and the ground sinks
109262.e: Once air gets in, microorganisms start to break down the peat. The ground shrinks and sinks over time.

109263.q: Which great construction project of the 19th century lowered the lake levels in the Seeland and helped to drain the bogs on the plains there?
109263.e: During the first Jura water correction from 1868, the Aare and the lakes were regulated. After that, the wet plains could be drained.
109263.m: The Jura water correction made the Seeland drier.

109264.q: What is the name of the large former bog plain in the Seeland that is now known for growing vegetables?
109264.e: The Grosses Moos (‘Great Bog’) between the lakes of Murten, Neuchâtel and Biel was drained. Today a lot of vegetables are grown there.
109264.m: The Grosses Moos is a drained bog in the Seeland.

109265.q: What problem can be seen in the Grosses Moos today because of drainage?
a: The ground is sinking and losing peat
The ground is getting wetter and wetter
109265.e: The drained peat is breaking down. The soil layer is getting thinner and the ground is lower than it used to be.

109266.q: Which structures in the ground carry water away underground during drainage?
109266.e: Drainage pipes collect the water in the soil and carry it into ditches or streams.

109267.q: Why did draining bogs lead to a decline in many animals such as the tree frog and the snipe?
a: They were poisoned by the peat
It became too cold for them
109267.e: Many species depend on wet meadows and ponds. When the bogs went, they lost their habitat.
109267.m: When bogs disappear, so do the creatures that live in them.

109268.q: What is the most important aim of restoring a bog?
a: To raise the water level again
109268.e: Bogs need a lot of water. When the water level rises, peat mosses can grow again.
109268.m: A bog is saved by making it wet again.

109269.q: How is water kept in a bog when it is being restored?
a: Pipes are laid in the bog
109269.e: Old ditches are blocked with dams made of wood, peat or sheet piling. This makes the water level rise.
109269.m: Blocked ditches keep the water in the bog.

109270.q: What is it called when a dried-out bog is made wet again?
109270.e: Rewetting means raising the water level again to just below the surface.
109270.m: Rewetting is at the heart of every bog restoration.

109271.q: Why are trees and bushes often removed from a bog when it is restored?
a: They take water from the bog and shade it
109271.e: Trees evaporate a lot of water and take the light away from bog plants that need it.
109271.m: Bushes spreading over a bog harm many bogs.
