110111.e: The more people one sick person infects, the more people must be immune to stop it spreading.
110111.m: The more contagious a disease, the higher the vaccination rate must be.

110112.q: What does the basic reproduction number of a disease tell you?
a: How many people one sick person infects on average
How many days the disease lasts
How many vaccine doses there are
How old the sick people are
110112.e: The basic reproduction number applies to a population without protection. If it is 3, for example, one sick person infects three others on average.
110112.m: The basic reproduction number shows how contagious a disease is.

110113.q: A disease has a basic reproduction number of 4. Using the formula 1 minus 1 divided by 4, what percentage must be immune?
110113.e: 1 divided by 4 gives 0.25. 1 minus 0.25 gives 0.75, which is 75 per cent.
110113.m: You can work out the vaccination rate needed from the basic reproduction number.

110114.q: Why is there no herd immunity for tetanus?
a: Because tetanus is not passed from person to person
Because there is no tetanus vaccine
110114.e: Tetanus germs live in the soil and enter the body through wounds. Because people do not infect each other, only your own vaccination protects you.
110114.m: Only your own vaccination protects you against tetanus.

110115.q: Which other term is also used for herd immunity?
110115.e: Because the community is protected together by many vaccinated people, it is also called community protection or herd protection.
110115.m: Herd immunity is also called community protection.

110116.q: What can happen if the vaccination rate falls below the level needed?
110116.e: If there are too many unprotected people, a germ can spread again. Measles outbreaks in areas with a low vaccination rate show this.
110116.m: If the vaccination rate falls, diseases come back.

110117.q: What does an mRNA vaccine contain?
a: Building instructions for a protein of the germ
110117.e: The body's cells read the instructions and briefly build a harmless protein of the germ. The immune system learns to recognise this protein.
110117.m: An mRNA vaccine gives the cells building instructions.

110118.q: What does the “m” in mRNA stand for?
110118.e: Messenger RNA carries information in the cell to the places where proteins are built.

110119.q: Against which disease were mRNA vaccines first widely approved from the end of 2020?
110119.e: During the coronavirus pandemic, the first mRNA vaccines were approved at the end of 2020, in Switzerland too.
110119.m: The first mRNA vaccines were used against Covid-19.

110120.q: Does an mRNA vaccine change the genetic material in the cell nucleus?
a: No, the mRNA does not get into the cell nucleus
Yes, but only in older people
110120.e: The mRNA stays outside the cell nucleus, where the genetic material is. The cell breaks it down again after a short time.
110120.m: mRNA vaccines do not change genetic material.

110121.q: Where is an mRNA vaccine normally injected?
a: Into the muscle of the upper arm
Into a vein in the foot
110121.e: mRNA vaccines are injected into the upper arm muscle. There, cells take up the mRNA and build the protein.
110121.m: The mRNA vaccine is injected into the upper arm muscle.

110122.q: For which protein of the coronavirus did the first mRNA vaccines contain the building instructions?
110122.e: The spike protein sits on the surface of the virus like little spikes. It helps the virus get into cells.
110122.m: The coronavirus vaccine teaches the body the spike protein.

110123.q: Why did the first mRNA vaccines have to be stored very cold?
a: Because mRNA breaks down very easily
Because the cold kills the viruses in them
Because warmth makes the vaccine poisonous
110123.e: mRNA is a delicate molecule that breaks down quickly when warm. Low temperatures make it last longer.
110123.m: mRNA is delicate and must be kept well chilled.

110124.q: What protects the mRNA in the vaccine and carries it into the cells?
110124.e: The mRNA is packed in tiny balls of fat called lipid nanoparticles. These merge with the cell's outer layer and bring the mRNA inside.
110124.m: Fat coatings bring the mRNA safely into the cells.

110125.q: What is a clinical trial for?
a: To test how well and how safely a treatment works in people
110125.e: In clinical trials, strict rules are used to test whether a new medicine or vaccine works and is well tolerated.
110125.m: Clinical trials test new treatments in people.

110126.q: What is mainly tested in phase I of a clinical trial?
a: How well it is tolerated by a few volunteers
How well it works in tens of thousands of patients
110126.e: In phase I, usually a few healthy volunteers receive the medicine. The main things studied are safety and dosage.
110126.m: Phase I mainly tests safety in a few people.

110127.q: What is typical of phase III of a clinical trial?
a: Very many participants and testing of how well it works
110127.e: In phase III, often thousands of people take part. Only after this can approval be applied for.
110127.m: Phase III tests how well it works in very many people.

110128.q: What happens in phase IV of a clinical trial?
a: The medicine continues to be watched after approval
The medicine is tested on mice for the first time
110128.e: After approval, very many people receive the medicine. In phase IV, people also look for rare side effects.
110128.m: A medicine is still monitored even after approval.

110129.q: What does “randomised” mean in a clinical trial?
a: The participants are placed in groups by chance
The doctors pick the healthiest people
The trial lasts a random length of time
110129.e: Random allocation makes the groups as similar as possible. Differences in the results can then be put down to the treatment.
110129.m: Random allocation to groups makes trials fairer.

110130.q: What does “double-blind” mean in a clinical trial?
a: Neither the participants nor the doctors know who gets which medicine
The trial takes place in the dark
110130.e: This way, the expectations of participants and trial staff cannot influence the result.
110130.m: In a double-blind trial, neither side knows who gets what.

110131.q: What is the group called that receives no new treatment in a trial, for comparison?
110131.e: The control group receives a dummy medicine or the existing treatment. Only by comparing with it can you see what the new medicine does.
110131.m: Without a control group you cannot know whether a medicine really works.

110132.q: In Switzerland, who must approve a clinical trial before it may begin?
110132.e: Cantonal ethics committees check whether the trial protects the rights and safety of the participants. For medicines, approval from Swissmedic is also needed.
110132.m: Clinical trials need the approval of an ethics committee.

110133.q: What must a person do before taking part in a clinical trial?
110133.e: All participants must be told clearly about the aims and risks and then agree of their own free will. They may drop out at any time.
110133.m: Taking part in a trial is always voluntary.

a: A dummy medicine without an active ingredient
A device for taking someone's temperature
110134.e: A placebo looks like a real medicine but contains no active drug.
110134.m: A placebo is a medicine without an active ingredient.

a: Feeling better just because you expect an effect
110135.e: Someone who expects a medicine to help can really feel better, even though it contains no active ingredient.
110135.m: Just expecting it can make you feel better.

110136.q: What does the Latin word “placebo” literally mean?
110136.e: Placebo comes from the Latin verb “placere”, to please. So placebo means “I will please”.
110136.m: In Latin, placebo means “I will please”.

110137.q: What is it called when a dummy medicine causes symptoms because of negative expectations?
110137.e: Someone who expects side effects can sometimes feel them, even though the medicine has no active ingredient. This is the opposite of the placebo effect.
110137.m: The nocebo effect is the negative counterpart of the placebo effect.

110138.q: Why are placebos used in clinical trials?
a: For comparison with the real medicine
110138.e: Only if a medicine works better than a placebo is its effect more than a result of expectation.
110138.m: A new medicine must work better than a placebo.

110139.q: What are placebo tablets often made of?
110139.e: Placebo tablets usually contain harmless substances such as milk sugar or starch, so that they look like real tablets.
110139.m: Placebos usually contain only sugar or starch.

110140.q: When is using a placebo in a trial ethically difficult?
a: When sick people are denied an effective treatment because of it
When the trial takes place in summer
110140.e: If there is already an effective treatment, a new medicine is usually compared with it rather than with a placebo.
110140.m: No one may lose a treatment they need because of a placebo.

110141.q: With which complaints is the placebo effect felt especially often?
110141.e: How strongly we feel pain also depends on the brain and on expectations. But a placebo does not heal a broken bone.
110141.m: Placebos can affect how pain feels, but they cannot heal bones.

110142.e: Penicillin comes from moulds of the genus Penicillium, hence the name.
110142.m: Penicillin is made by a mould.

110143.q: Which part of the bacterial cell does penicillin attack?
110143.e: Penicillin disrupts the building of the cell wall of bacteria. Without a stable wall, the bacteria burst. Human cells have no such cell wall.
110143.m: Penicillin weakens the cell wall of bacteria.

110144.q: What did Fleming notice around the mould on his dish of bacteria?
110144.e: Around the mould, the bacterial colonies dissolved. The fungus produced a substance that kills bacteria: penicillin.
110144.m: Fleming saw how mould killed bacteria.

110145.q: Even before penicillin, where did Fleming find a substance that harms bacteria?
110145.e: In the early 1920s, Fleming discovered the enzyme lysozyme. It is found in tears, saliva and nasal mucus and can harm bacteria.
110145.m: Even our tears contain a substance against bacteria.

110146.q: What can develop if antibiotics are taken too often or in the wrong way?
110146.e: Bacteria that survive a treatment can multiply. The medicines then no longer work against these resistant bacteria.

110147.q: During which event was penicillin first made in large amounts?
110147.e: In the Second World War, production was greatly increased to protect wounded soldiers from infections.
110147.m: In the Second World War, penicillin became a mass medicine.

a: The Swiss authority for approving and supervising medicines
110148.e: Swissmedic tests and monitors medicines and medical devices in Switzerland.
110148.m: Swissmedic decides which medicines are approved in Switzerland.

110149.q: In which city is Swissmedic based?
110149.e: The Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products, Swissmedic, is based in Bern.

110150.q: What must happen before a new medicine may be sold in Switzerland?
a: The people must vote on it
110150.e: Since 2002, Swissmedic has checked whether a medicine is safe, effective and of good quality. Only then may it be sold.
110150.m: New medicines need approval from Swissmedic.

110151.q: Which law forms the basis for Swissmedic's work?
110151.e: The Therapeutic Products Act sets out how medicines and medical devices are tested, approved and monitored.
110151.m: The Therapeutic Products Act governs Swissmedic's work.

110152.q: Which three things does Swissmedic check before a medicine is approved?
110152.e: A medicine is only approved if it is of good quality, safe and effective.
110152.m: Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness.

110153.q: What does Swissmedic do with reports of side effects after approval?
a: It assesses them and can take action
It passes them on to the police
110153.e: Doctors, pharmacists and companies report suspected side effects. Swissmedic checks them and can, for example, publish warnings.
110153.m: Swissmedic also monitors medicines after approval.

110154.q: Before Swissmedic, which body was responsible for checking medicines?
a: The Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines
110154.e: Swissmedic was created in 2002 from the Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines and a department of the Federal Office of Public Health.
110154.m: Before Swissmedic, an intercantonal office checked medicines.

110155.q: Besides medicines, which products does Swissmedic also monitor?
110155.e: Medical devices include, for example, syringes, plasters, pacemakers or contact lenses.
110155.m: Swissmedic also monitors medical devices such as syringes and plasters.

110156.q: Which federal department does Swissmedic belong to?
a: The Federal Department of Home Affairs
110156.e: Swissmedic is a public institution of the Confederation and is attached to the Federal Department of Home Affairs, which the FOPH also belongs to.
110156.m: Swissmedic comes under the Federal Department of Home Affairs.

110157.q: In which year did the World Health Organization declare smallpox wiped out?
110157.e: On 8 May 1980, the World Health Assembly of the WHO officially declared the world free of smallpox.
110157.m: Smallpox has been considered wiped out since 1980.

110158.q: On which continent did the last natural case of smallpox occur in 1977?
110158.e: The last person to catch it naturally was a cook in Somalia in East Africa. He survived the disease.
110158.m: The last natural case of smallpox occurred in Africa in 1977.

110159.q: Which organisation led the worldwide programme to wipe out smallpox?
110159.e: The WHO, based in Geneva, coordinated the programme, in which experts from many countries took part.
110159.m: The WHO led the worldwide fight against smallpox.

110160.q: Why was it possible to wipe out smallpox?
a: Because the virus only infects humans and there was a good vaccine
Because the virus survived in animals
110160.e: The smallpox virus had no animals to hide in. Sick people were easy to spot because of the rash, and the vaccine gave reliable protection.
110160.m: With no animal host and a good vaccine, smallpox could be defeated.

110161.q: Which strategy stopped the last smallpox outbreaks?
a: Finding cases and vaccinating all their contacts
110161.e: In what is called ring vaccination, sick people were found quickly and everyone around them was vaccinated. So the virus found no new victims.
110161.m: Targeted ring vaccination closed in on smallpox.

110162.q: Where are smallpox viruses still officially kept today?
a: In two laboratories, in the USA and in Russia
In every hospital in the world
In the Federal Palace in Bern
Nowhere in the world any more
110162.e: After the disease was wiped out, only two high-security laboratories were allowed to keep samples of the virus, one in the USA and one in Russia.
110162.m: Smallpox viruses are now kept only in two high-security laboratories.

110163.q: Roughly how long did the WHO's stepped-up programme take to defeat smallpox worldwide?
110163.e: The WHO stepped up its programme in 1967. About ten years later, in 1977, the last natural case of smallpox occurred.
110163.m: Smallpox was defeated in about ten years.

110164.q: Which animal disease was wiped out worldwide in 2011, as only the second disease ever?
110164.e: After smallpox in humans, rinderpest in animals was declared wiped out in 2011.
110164.m: After smallpox, rinderpest is the second disease to be wiped out.

110165.e: Polio, in full poliomyelitis, is caused by the poliovirus.

110166.q: What serious effect can polio have?
110166.e: The virus can damage nerve cells in the spinal cord. Muscles then become paralysed, often permanently.

110167.q: Why is polio very rare in Switzerland today?
a: Because almost all children are vaccinated against it
Because the virus dies in the cold
Because there are no viruses in Switzerland
Because the disease only affects adults
110167.e: There have been vaccines against polio since the 1950s. Because so many people are vaccinated, the virus can no longer spread in Switzerland.
110167.m: Vaccination has made polio almost disappear in Switzerland.

110168.q: How did many children get the polio vaccine in the past?
a: As drops on a sugar lump
As a plaster on the arm
As a cream on the skin
110168.e: The oral vaccine was dripped onto a lump of sugar and eaten. Today in Switzerland it is injected instead.
110168.m: In the past, the polio vaccine was given on a sugar lump.

110169.q: Which type of polio vaccine is used in Switzerland today?
a: A nasal spray with live viruses
110169.e: In Switzerland today, a vaccine with inactivated polioviruses is injected. It cannot cause the disease.
110169.m: In Switzerland, vaccination today uses inactivated polioviruses.

110170.q: What has Europe achieved in the fight against polio?
a: The wild poliovirus no longer occurs there
Nobody needs to be vaccinated any more
The disease has become more common there
There is a cure in tablet form there
110170.e: Thanks to vaccination, the WHO declared the European region free of polio in 2002. Vaccination is still important so that the virus does not come back.
110170.m: Thanks to vaccination, Europe is free of wild polio.

110171.q: According to the WHO, in which two countries did wild polio still occur most recently (as of 2026)?
110171.e: Wild polioviruses are now only passed on in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The WHO's goal is to wipe them out worldwide.
110171.m: Wild polio now exists only in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

110172.q: How is the poliovirus usually passed on?
a: Through dirty water and dirty hands
110172.e: The virus leaves the body in faeces and gets into other people's mouths through contaminated water, food or hands.
110172.m: Good hygiene and clean water slow the spread of polio.

110173.q: What was the “iron lung” used for in people with polio?
a: To help them breathe when their breathing muscles were paralysed
To cool them when they had a fever
110173.e: When polio paralysed the breathing muscles, patients could no longer breathe on their own. The iron lung created low pressure and helped them breathe.
110173.m: The iron lung helped paralysed polio patients breathe.

110174.q: Where does the outer ear canal of a human end?
110174.e: The outer ear canal leads inwards from the outer ear to the eardrum. Behind it the middle ear begins.
110174.m: The outer ear canal ends at the eardrum.

110175.q: Roughly how long is the outer ear canal in adults?
110175.e: In adults the outer ear canal is around 2.5 to 3.5 centimetres long. It is slightly curved in an S shape.
110175.m: The outer ear canal is only a few centimetres long.

110176.q: What does earwax do in the ear canal?
a: It protects against dirt and germs
110176.e: Earwax (cerumen) traps dust, keeps the skin supple and slows down bacteria. Over time it moves outwards by itself.
110176.m: Earwax is a natural protection for the ear canal.

110177.q: Why do doctors advise against cleaning the ear canal with cotton buds?
a: The earwax gets pushed further in
110177.e: Cotton buds often push earwax inwards, where it can form a plug. You can also injure the eardrum.
110177.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear canal.

110178.q: What is the wall of the outer third of the ear canal made of?
110178.e: The outer third of the ear canal has a wall of cartilage; the inner part lies in the temporal bone and is made of bone.
110178.m: The ear canal is cartilage on the outside and bone on the inside.

110179.q: Why should you let your ears dry well after swimming?
a: Damp skin in the ear canal gets inflamed more easily
Otherwise you only hear low notes
110179.e: If water stays in the ear canal, the skin softens. Germs then get in more easily and an ear canal infection can develop.
110179.m: After swimming you should let your ears dry well.

110180.q: What job does the outer ear canal do?
a: It carries sound to the eardrum
110180.e: The ear canal is a short tube leading inwards from the outer ear. Sound travels through it to the eardrum.
110180.m: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum.

110181.q: Why does the doctor gently pull an adult's outer ear backwards and upwards before looking into the ear?
a: So that the curved ear canal becomes straighter
So that the earwax becomes runny
So that the semicircular canals rest
110181.e: The ear canal is curved. Pulling the outer ear backwards and upwards straightens it, so the eardrum can be seen better.
110181.m: A straightened ear canal gives a view of the eardrum.

110182.q: How many ear bones does each human ear have?
110182.e: In each middle ear lie the hammer, anvil and stirrup. Together they form the chain of ear bones.
110182.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110183.q: In which part of the ear are the ear bones?
110183.e: The ear bones lie in the air-filled cavity of the middle ear. They connect the eardrum to the inner ear.
110183.m: The ear bones sit in the middle ear.

110184.q: What job do the ear bones do?
a: They pass vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear
110184.e: The eardrum vibrates when sound hits it. The hammer, anvil and stirrup pass this vibration on to the inner ear.
110184.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110185.q: In what order do the ear bones pass sound on from the eardrum?
110185.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil lies in the middle, and the stirrup presses on the oval window of the inner ear.
110185.m: Sound goes from hammer to anvil to stirrup.

110186.q: Which ear bone passes the vibrations directly to the inner ear?
110186.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil in the middle. The stirrup is the last little bone and pushes the vibrations into the inner ear.
110186.m: The stirrup is the last ear bone before the inner ear.

110188.q: Where is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body?
110188.e: The stapedius muscle in the middle ear is only a few millimetres long. With very loud noises it tightens and dampens the vibrations a little.
110188.m: The smallest skeletal muscle is in the middle ear.

110189.q: What happens if the stirrup in the ear becomes fixed and can no longer vibrate?
a: You can no longer smell anything
110189.e: The stirrup must vibrate freely to carry sound into the inner ear. If it becomes fixed, less sound arrives. An operation can often help.
110189.m: A fixed stirrup makes hearing worse.

110191.q: Which part of the ear is the hammer firmly attached to?
110191.e: The handle of the hammer is attached to the eardrum. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves with it.
110191.m: The hammer hangs on the eardrum.

110192.q: In which part of the ear is the hammer?
110192.e: The hammer is one of the three ear bones. Together with the anvil and stirrup, it lies in the middle ear, just behind the eardrum.
110192.m: The hammer lies in the middle ear behind the eardrum.

110193.q: What is the rounded upper part of the hammer called?
110193.e: The hammer consists of a head, neck and handle. The head of the hammer lies at the top of the middle ear cavity.
110193.m: The upper part of the hammer is its head.

110194.q: Which ear bone is the hammer connected to by a small joint?
110194.e: There is a tiny joint between the hammer and the anvil. The vibration is passed on through it.
110194.m: The hammer and anvil are connected by a joint.

110195.q: What is the tiny muscle attached to the hammer in the ear for?
a: It dampens the vibration a little with loud noises
110195.e: The tensor tympani pulls on the hammer and tightens the eardrum. It then vibrates less strongly, which protects the inner ear a little from loud sounds.
110195.m: A tiny muscle on the hammer dampens loud noises a little.

110196.q: What can a doctor often see through the eardrum when looking with an otoscope?
110196.e: The eardrum is thin and slightly see-through. The attached handle of the hammer shows on it as a light stripe.
110196.m: You can see the handle of the hammer through the eardrum.

110197.q: Which of the three ear bones is the longest?
a: They are all the same length
110197.e: The hammer is around 8 to 9 millimetres long, the anvil only about 5 to 7 millimetres. The stirrup is the shortest.
110197.m: The hammer is the longest ear bone.

110198.q: Where does the hammer in the ear get its name from?
a: From its shape, which looks like a hammer
110198.e: The little bone looks like a small hammer. The anvil and stirrup are also named after their shapes.
110198.m: The hammer is named after its shape.

110199.q: How big is a newborn baby's anvil compared with an adult's?
a: About a tenth of the size
110199.e: The ear bones are already fully grown and fully turned to bone at birth. They do not grow any more after that.
110199.m: The ear bones are already fully grown at birth.

110200.q: In which part of the ear is the anvil?
110200.e: The hammer, anvil and stirrup lie in the middle ear behind the eardrum. They pass sound on to the inner ear.
110200.m: The anvil lies in the middle ear.

110201.q: Which tool is the anvil in the ear named after?
110201.e: The blacksmith puts the hot iron on an anvil and strikes it with a hammer. The ear bone has a similar shape.
110201.m: The hammer and anvil are named after blacksmith's tools.

110202.q: Which little bone is the long process of the anvil connected to?
110202.e: The long process of the anvil reaches to the head of the stirrup. There is a small joint there.
110202.m: The anvil passes the vibration on to the stirrup.

110203.q: How many ear bones does one ear have?
110203.e: In each middle ear there are three ear bones: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the body.
110203.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110204.q: What job do the hammer, anvil and stirrup do?
a: They pass on the vibrations of the eardrum
They protect the ear from water
110204.e: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The three ear bones pass these vibrations on, amplified, to the inner ear.
110204.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110205.q: What happens if the connection between the anvil and stirrup is broken after an accident?
a: You hear much worse in that ear
You lose your sense of smell
110205.e: If the chain is broken, the vibration no longer reaches the inner ear properly. This causes conductive hearing loss, which can often be treated with an operation.
110205.m: A broken chain of ear bones makes hearing worse.

110206.q: How many joints does the anvil have with neighbouring ear bones?
110206.e: The anvil is connected by a joint to the hammer and by another to the stirrup. That makes two joints in total.
110206.m: The anvil is joined to two neighbours.

110207.q: In which part of the ear is the cochlea?
110207.e: The cochlea lies in the inner ear, well protected in the petrous bone. There sound is turned into nerve signals.
110207.m: The cochlea lies in the inner ear.

110208.q: What is the cochlea filled with?
110208.e: The passages of the cochlea contain fluids, the perilymph and the endolymph. The stirrup sets them in motion.

110209.q: Which cells in the cochlea turn vibrations into nerve signals?
110209.e: The hair cells carry tiny hairs. When these are bent, the cells send signals to the brain through the hearing nerve.
110209.m: Hair cells turn sound into nerve signals.

110210.q: Roughly how many turns does the human cochlea have?
110210.e: The human cochlea winds about two and a half times around a bony axis. That is why it looks like a snail shell.
110210.m: The cochlea has about two and a half turns.

110211.q: Which sounds do older people often hear worse first?
110211.e: The hair cells for high sounds sit at the start of the cochlea and wear out first. That is why older people often hear high sounds worse.
110211.m: In old age you often hear high sounds worse first.

110212.q: What is converted in the cochlea?
110212.e: In the cochlea, sound waves make a fluid vibrate. Hair cells turn this into nerve signals that go to the brain.
110212.m: The cochlea turns sound into nerve signals.

110213.q: Why is protection from noise so important for the hair cells?
a: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans
Hair cells need noise to grow
Otherwise hair cells move out of the ear
Otherwise hair cells turn into bone
110213.e: Very loud noise can permanently damage the delicate hair cells. In humans they do not form again, so the hearing loss stays.
110213.m: Destroyed hair cells do not come back.

110214.q: Which device can directly stimulate the hearing nerve in the cochlea with electricity in cases of very severe hearing loss?
110214.e: A cochlear implant has an electrode that is inserted into the cochlea. It stimulates the hearing nerve with electrical signals.
110214.m: A cochlear implant does the work of the hair cells.

110215.q: How is the cochlea protected from injury?
a: It lies deep in the hard skull bone
It lies in the soft outer ear
It is surrounded by thick hair
110215.e: The cochlea lies in the petrous bone, part of the skull. It is one of the hardest bones in the body.
110215.m: The cochlea is protected in the hard skull bone.

110216.q: How many semicircular canals does each inner ear have?
110216.e: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals. Together with two little sacs they form the organ of balance.
110216.m: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals.

110217.q: Which movements do the semicircular canals detect?
110217.e: The semicircular canals react to rotation, for example when nodding, shaking or tilting your head. That way the brain knows how the head is turning.
110217.m: The semicircular canals sense turns of the head.

110218.q: How are the three semicircular canals arranged in relation to each other?
a: Roughly at right angles in three planes
One behind the other in a row
In circles one inside the other
110218.e: The three semicircular canals are roughly at right angles to each other. That way every turn in space can be detected.
110218.m: The three semicircular canals cover all three directions in space.

110219.q: What is inside the semicircular canals of the inner ear?
110219.e: The semicircular canals are filled with fluid. When you turn, it lags behind a little and bends tiny sensory hairs.
110219.m: Fluid moves in the semicircular canals.

110220.q: Where in the body are the semicircular canals?
110220.e: The semicircular canals are well protected in the skull bone in the inner ear. The cochlea lies right next to them.
110220.m: The semicircular canals lie in the inner ear.

110221.q: After spinning fast in the playground, why does everything still seem to turn even though you are standing still?
a: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving
Your eyes grow for a moment
The ear canal fills with air
110221.e: Because of its inertia, the endolymph keeps flowing for a moment after you stop. So the brain reports a turn that is no longer happening.
110221.m: After spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving for a moment.

110222.q: Which organ tells the brain whether we are standing upright or lying down?
a: The organ of balance in the inner ear
110222.e: The organ of balance contains tiny chalk crystals that gravity pulls downwards. That way the brain senses how the head is tilted.
110222.m: The organ of balance senses gravity.

110223.q: Through which nerve do the signals from the semicircular canals reach the brain?
110223.e: The vestibular nerve (nervus vestibularis) forms the eighth cranial nerve together with the hearing nerve. It carries the signals from the semicircular canals.
110223.m: The vestibular nerve reports turns to the brain.

110224.q: Besides the semicircular canals, which senses help the brain to keep its balance?
a: The eyes and the position sense in muscles and joints
110224.e: The brain compares the messages from the organ of balance with what the eyes see and what muscles and joints report. That is why you wobble more with your eyes closed.
110224.m: Balance comes from several senses working together.

110225.q: Which two spaces does the Eustachian tube connect?
a: The middle ear and the upper throat
The outer ear and the mouth
The inner ear and the brain
The ear canal and the nose
110225.e: The Eustachian tube, also called the auditory tube, leads from the middle ear cavity to the upper throat behind the nose.
110225.m: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear and the throat.

110226.q: What is the Eustachian tube mainly for?
a: Balancing the pressure in the middle ear
110226.e: When it opens, air can flow into or out of the middle ear. That way the pressure is the same on both sides of the eardrum.

110227.q: What is another name for the Eustachian tube?
110227.e: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube. It connects the middle ear with the upper throat.
110227.m: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube.

110228.q: What helps when your ears start to feel blocked as a plane comes in to land?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
110228.e: When you swallow or yawn, the Eustachian tube opens briefly. This balances the pressure in the middle ear.

110229.q: How do divers balance the pressure in their ears?
a: Pinch their nose and gently push air in
Hold their breath for a long time
110229.e: With your nose pinched, you gently push air through the Eustachian tube into the middle ear. This balances the pressure.
110229.m: You can balance ear pressure by pinching your nose.

110230.q: Why do young children get middle ear infections more often than adults?
a: Their Eustachian tube is shorter and flatter
They do not have an eardrum yet
Their ear canal is full of water
110230.e: In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and lies flatter. Germs from the throat can get into the middle ear more easily.
110230.m: A short, flat Eustachian tube makes middle ear infections more likely.

110231.q: Why does your ear often feel dull and blocked when you have a bad cold?
110231.e: With a cold, the lining swells and closes the Eustachian tube. Then the pressure can no longer balance out.
110231.m: A blocked Eustachian tube makes the ear feel dull.

110232.q: Roughly how long is the Eustachian tube in adults?
110232.e: In adults the Eustachian tube is around 3.5 centimetres long. Part of it is bone, the larger part is cartilage.
110232.m: The Eustachian tube is only a few centimetres long.

a: A noise in the ear with no outside source
An inflammation of the outer ear
A loud echo in the mountains
110233.e: With tinnitus you hear whistling, rushing or humming, even though no matching sound is coming from outside.
110233.m: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear that only you can hear.

110234.q: Which language does the word “tinnitus” come from?
110234.e: The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, which means “to ring”.

110235.q: What is a common cause of tinnitus in teenagers?
110235.e: Very loud music in headphones or at concerts can damage the hair cells. Whistling afterwards is a warning sign.
110235.m: Loud music can cause noises in the ears.

110236.q: According to experts, after how long is tinnitus called chronic?
110236.e: Tinnitus that lasts longer than around three months is considered chronic. Before that it is called acute tinnitus.
110236.m: Tinnitus lasting over three months is considered chronic.

110237.q: How can you best protect yourself from tinnitus at a loud concert?
a: With ear protection and distance from the speakers
By standing as close to the speakers as possible
110237.e: Ear protection lowers the sound level in the ear. The further you are from the loudspeakers, the quieter it also gets.
110237.m: Ear protection and distance protect your ears.

110238.q: Is tinnitus a disease in itself or a symptom?
110238.e: Tinnitus is a sign of illness. It can occur, for example, after noise, with sudden hearing loss or with stress.
110238.m: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a disease in itself.

110239.q: What helps many people with long-lasting tinnitus to live better with the noise?
a: Learning to pay less attention to the noise
Blocking their ears with cotton wool for ever
110239.e: With chronic tinnitus, people learn in therapy to pay less attention to the noise. The brain often gets used to it this way.
110239.m: You can learn to pay less attention to tinnitus.

110240.q: What is tinnitus called that only the person affected can hear and nobody else can measure?
110240.e: Almost all ear noises are subjective and arise in the hearing pathway. Objective tinnitus is rare, for example a rushing of blood that others can hear.

110241.q: When do many people affected notice their tinnitus most strongly?
a: In quiet surroundings, for example when falling asleep
110241.e: In silence there are no other sounds to cover the tinnitus. That is why it is often most bothersome in bed at night.
110241.m: In silence, an ear noise is especially noticeable.

a: The length of the ear canal
110242.e: Decibels show how loud a sound is. Pitch, on the other hand, is measured in hertz.

110243.q: Which sound level roughly matches the hearing threshold of a healthy young person?
110243.e: 0 decibels does not mean silence; it is roughly the quietest sound that a healthy young ear can just hear at 1,000 hertz.
110243.m: 0 decibels is at the hearing threshold.

110244.q: Roughly how loud is a normal conversation?
110244.e: A normal conversation at a distance of one metre is around 60 decibels. A vacuum cleaner, at around 70 to 80 decibels, is much louder.

110245.q: Roughly from what sound level does sound start to hurt your ears?
110245.e: The pain threshold is around 120 to 130 decibels, about as loud as a jet plane close up.

110246.q: Why is there an upper volume limit at concerts in Switzerland?
a: So that the musicians use less electricity
So that the loudspeakers last longer
So that the drinks stay cool
110246.e: Very loud music over a long time can permanently damage hearing. That is why a regulation limits the sound level at events.
110246.m: Concerts have a volume limit to protect people's ears.

110247.q: What is the best way to protect your hearing at a loud concert?
a: With a hat over your eyes
110247.e: Earplugs reduce the sound by many decibels. Keeping your distance from the loudspeakers and taking breaks somewhere quiet also help.
110247.m: Ear protection lowers the volume in your ear.

110248.q: Why can listening to music through headphones for a long time at high volume damage your hearing?
a: The louder and longer the sound, the more hair cells are damaged
Headphones cool down the inner ear
110248.e: For hearing damage, what counts is the sound dose made up of level and time. Even from about 85 decibels over a long time, the hair cells can suffer.
110248.m: Loud music does more harm the longer it lasts.

110249.e: Quiet whispering is around 30 decibels, so it is much quieter than a normal conversation.

a: A sudden loss of hearing, usually in one ear
Slow hearing loss in old age
110250.e: With sudden hearing loss, you suddenly hear worse or hardly at all in one ear, usually for no obvious reason.
110250.m: Sudden hearing loss is hearing that goes suddenly.

110251.q: Which part of the ear does sudden hearing loss affect?
110251.e: Sudden hearing loss is a disorder in the inner ear, that is, in the cochlea with its hair cells.
110251.m: Sudden hearing loss happens in the inner ear.

110252.q: What feeling do people often describe with sudden hearing loss?
a: As if there were cotton wool in the ear
As if the ear were itching
As if the ear were ice-cold
As if they could hear better
110252.e: Many feel a dull pressure, as if there were cotton wool in the ear. Often there is also a noise in the ear.
110252.m: Sudden hearing loss often feels like cotton wool in the ear.

110253.q: What should you do if you suddenly can hardly hear anything in one ear?
a: Rinse the ear with cotton buds
110253.e: Sudden hearing loss should be checked by a doctor soon. That way other causes can be ruled out and treatment can be started.
110253.m: With sudden hearing loss, you go to the doctor soon.

110254.q: Which medicine is often used for sudden hearing loss?
110254.e: Cortisone is meant to reduce inflammation and swelling in the inner ear. It is the most common treatment for sudden hearing loss.
110254.m: Sudden hearing loss is often treated with cortisone.

110255.q: Which ear symptom often also occurs with sudden hearing loss?
a: Hair growing in the ear canal
110255.e: Many people with sudden hearing loss also hear whistling or rushing, that is, tinnitus.
110255.m: Sudden hearing loss often comes with a noise in the ear.

110256.q: How is sudden hearing loss different from acoustic trauma caused by a bang?
a: With sudden hearing loss, usually no cause can be found
With sudden hearing loss you hear better
Acoustic trauma only affects the nose
110256.e: Acoustic trauma has a clear cause, for example a firework close to the ear. With sudden hearing loss, the reason is usually not found.
110256.m: With sudden hearing loss, the cause usually stays unknown.

110257.q: How does mild sudden hearing loss turn out in many cases?
a: The ear always stops working completely
110257.e: In mild cases, hearing often improves within days or weeks, even without treatment. It should still be checked by a doctor.
110257.m: Mild sudden hearing loss often heals by itself.

110258.q: Why do you easily feel sick when reading in the car?
a: Your eyes and sense of balance report different things
There is too little light in the car
110258.e: Your eyes see a still book, but the organ of balance in your ear feels movement. This contradiction can make you feel sick.
110258.m: Travel sickness happens when the senses report different things.

110259.q: At what age does sudden hearing loss happen most often?
110259.e: Sudden hearing loss can happen at any age. It most often affects adults around 50; in children it is rare.
110259.m: Sudden hearing loss mostly affects middle-aged adults.

110260.q: Which is a typical sign of travel sickness?
110260.e: Typical signs are feeling sick, looking pale, cold sweat and being sick. When the movement stops, the symptoms usually go away soon.
110260.m: Travel sickness makes you feel sick.

110261.q: What helps against travel sickness in the car?
a: Looking out of the window into the distance
110261.e: If you look forwards into the distance, you see the movement that the organ of balance feels. Then the senses match better.
110261.m: Looking into the distance helps against travel sickness.

110262.q: Where is the best place to sit on a ship if you tend to get seasick?
a: In the middle of the ship
Right at the front in the bow
Right at the top of the mast
Right at the back in the stern
110262.e: In the middle of the ship it rocks the least. At the front and back the up and down movements are stronger.
110262.m: In the middle of a ship it rocks the least.

110263.q: What is the travel sickness called that astronauts can get when weightless?
110263.e: When weightless, the organ of balance is missing the usual signals from gravity. Many space travellers feel sick in the first few days.
110263.m: You can get travel sick in space too.

110264.q: Which age group is especially often affected by travel sickness?
110264.e: Children between about 2 and 12 are especially prone to it. Babies, on the other hand, are rarely affected.
110264.m: Schoolchildren get travel sick especially often.

110265.q: Which plant is often used as a natural remedy for travel sickness?
110265.e: Ginger has been used against nausea for a long time. Studies show a slight effect in some people.
110265.m: Ginger can help with travel sickness.

110266.q: What does spinning dizziness feel like?
a: As if everything were turning in a circle
As if you were very tired
As if your legs had gone to sleep
110266.e: With spinning dizziness, your surroundings or your own body seem to turn, like after a ride on a merry-go-round.
110266.m: With spinning dizziness, everything seems to turn.

110267.q: Why do you still feel dizzy for a moment after a merry-go-round ride?
a: The fluid in the organ of balance keeps turning
Blood only flows into your feet
Your eyes go blind for a moment
110267.e: In the inner ear there are semicircular canals with fluid. After stopping, the fluid keeps moving for a moment, and the brain reports a turn.
110267.m: After spinning, the fluid in the inner ear keeps moving.

110268.q: What helps if you feel dizzy after spinning?
a: Sitting down and looking at a fixed point
Running quickly in the other direction
110268.e: Sitting prevents falls. A fixed point to look at helps the brain find its bearings again.
110268.m: When dizzy, you sit down and look at a fixed point.

110269.q: Why should you not ride a bike if you suddenly feel spinning dizziness?
a: You can lose your balance and fall
110269.e: With spinning dizziness, your sense of balance is no longer right. Anyone who rides a bike then can easily fall.
110269.m: You do not ride a bike when you have spinning dizziness.

110270.q: Which complaint often also occurs with strong spinning dizziness?
110270.e: When the organ of balance and the eyes do not match, many people feel sick. Some even have to be sick.
110270.m: Strong spinning dizziness often makes you feel sick.

110271.q: How do ballet dancers stop themselves getting dizzy during pirouettes?
a: They fix their gaze on a point
110271.e: With “spotting”, the gaze stays on one point for as long as possible and then the head turns quickly. This reduces the dizziness.
110271.m: A fixed point to look at helps against spinning dizziness.

110272.q: Which nerve carries the signals from the organ of balance to the brain?
110272.e: The vestibular nerve connects the organ of balance in the inner ear with the brain. If it is inflamed, strong spinning dizziness can occur.
110272.m: The vestibular nerve tells the brain the position of the head.

110273.q: Where does spinning dizziness often come from?
a: From the organ of balance in the inner ear
110273.e: Very often the cause of spinning dizziness lies in the organ of balance or the vestibular nerve. Less often it comes from the brain.
110273.m: Spinning dizziness often comes from the organ of balance.

110274.q: What kind of wave is sound in air?
110274.e: In air the particles vibrate back and forth in the direction the wave travels. Such waves are called longitudinal waves.
110274.m: In air, sound travels as a longitudinal wave.

110276.q: What forms alternately in the air as a sound wave travels?
110276.e: The sound source squeezes the air particles together and lets them spread apart again. So areas of higher and lower pressure travel through the air.
110276.m: A sound wave consists of compressions and rarefactions.

110277.q: What does a sound wave carry from the source to the ear?
110277.e: The air particles only vibrate back and forth around their place. What is passed on is the energy of the vibration, not the air itself.
110277.m: A sound wave carries energy, but not air.

110278.q: What is the distance between two neighbouring compressions of a sound wave called?
110278.e: The wavelength is the distance between two identical points of a wave, for example between two compressions. It is measured in metres.
110278.m: The wavelength is the distance between two compressions.

110279.q: What do you call the sound that comes back to you in the mountains when you shout loudly?
110279.e: When sound hits a rock face it is reflected. If it comes back noticeably later, you hear it as an echo.

110280.q: Why can you hear music round the corner of a house even though you can't see the speakers?
a: Sound passes through all walls unhindered
Sound flies upwards in an arc
110280.e: Sound waves have wavelengths from centimetres to metres. So they bend strongly at edges and also reach places behind obstacles.

110281.q: What is the wavelength of a 680 Hz tone in air if sound travels at 340 m/s?
110281.e: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency: 340 m/s divided by 680 Hz gives 0.5 m.
110281.m: The wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency.

110282.q: In which kind of material can sound also travel as a transverse wave?
110282.e: In gases and liquids there are only longitudinal waves. Solids can also transmit shearing forces, so they have transverse waves too.
110282.m: In solids there are longitudinal and transverse waves.

110283.q: Roughly how many km/h is 343 m/s, the speed of sound in air at 20 °C?
110283.e: To convert m/s into km/h, you multiply by 3.6. 343 times 3.6 gives around 1235 km/h.
110283.m: In air, sound travels at over 1200 km/h.

110284.q: In which material is sound fastest?
110284.e: In air it is about 340 m/s, in water about 1480 m/s and in steel about 5000 m/s or more. Solids carry sound especially fast.
110284.m: Sound is usually fastest in solids.

110285.q: Roughly how fast is sound in water?
110285.e: In water, sound travels at about 1480 metres per second, more than four times as fast as in air.
110285.m: In water, sound travels at about 1500 m/s.

110286.q: The sound of a hammer blow travels 1000 m through a steel rail in 0.2 seconds. How fast is the sound in the rail?
110286.e: Speed equals distance divided by time: 1000 m divided by 0.2 s gives 5000 m/s.
110286.m: Speed is distance divided by time.

110287.q: How does the speed of sound in air change when the air gets warmer?
110287.e: In warm air the particles move faster and pass the vibration on more quickly. For each degree Celsius, the speed of sound rises by about 0.6 m/s.
110287.m: Sound is faster in warm air.

110288.q: What is it called when a plane flies exactly as fast as sound?
110288.e: The Mach number says how many times faster than sound something is. Mach 1 means the speed of sound.
110288.m: Mach 1 is the speed of sound.

110289.q: What do you hear on the ground when a plane flies past faster than sound?
a: A quiet whistle in front of the plane
110289.e: In supersonic flight the sound waves form a cone-shaped pressure wave. When it hits the ground, you hear a loud bang.
110289.m: A supersonic plane makes a bang.

110290.q: What is the imaginary barrier called that a plane breaks when it reaches the speed of sound?
110290.e: When a plane flies as fast as sound, the sound waves pile up in front of it. It is said to break the sound barrier. This causes a loud bang.
110290.m: Flying faster than sound means breaking the sound barrier.

110291.q: A cyclist sees a woodcutter's axe strike and hears it 2 seconds later. How far away is the woodcutter, at 340 m/s?
110291.e: Distance equals speed times time: 340 m/s times 2 s gives 680 m.
110291.m: The distance is the speed of sound times the travel time.

110292.q: What does the frequency of a vibration tell you?
a: The number of vibrations per second
The length of a guitar string
110292.e: The frequency counts how often a vibration happens in one second. It is given in hertz.
110292.m: Frequency counts the vibrations per second.

110293.q: How does the pitch change when the frequency gets higher?
110293.e: The more vibrations per second, the higher the note sounds. A piccolo makes high frequencies, a tuba low ones.
110293.m: High frequency means a high note.

110294.q: What frequency is concert A, which many orchestras tune to?
110294.e: Concert A is set internationally at 440 hertz. Some orchestras tune slightly higher, for example to 442 hertz.

110295.q: A note has 300 Hz. What frequency does the note one octave higher have?
110295.e: One octave higher means double the frequency. 300 Hz times 2 gives 600 Hz.
110295.m: One octave higher doubles the frequency.

110296.q: One vibration lasts 0.002 seconds. What is its frequency?
110296.e: The frequency is 1 divided by the period. 1 divided by 0.002 s gives 500 Hz.
110296.m: Frequency and period are reciprocals of each other.

110297.q: At what frequency does the current from a Swiss socket change direction?
110297.e: Like the rest of Europe, the Swiss power grid uses 50 hertz alternating current at 230 volts. In North America it is 60 hertz.

110298.q: How does the frequency of a guitar string change when you tighten it?
a: It rises, the note gets higher
It falls, the note gets lower
110298.e: A tighter string vibrates back and forth faster. That is why you turn the tuning peg to adjust the pitch.

110299.q: A string vibrates 1000 times in 4 seconds. What is its frequency?
110299.e: Frequency equals the number of vibrations divided by the time: 1000 divided by 4 s gives 250 Hz.
110299.m: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second.

110300.q: Who is the unit hertz named after?
110300.e: The unit hertz was named in honour of the physicist Heinrich Hertz, who lived in the 19th century.
110300.m: The unit hertz honours Heinrich Hertz.

110301.q: How else can you write 1 hertz?
110301.e: 1 Hz means that one vibration happens per second. You can also write it as 1/s.
110301.m: One hertz is one vibration per second.

110302.e: Kilo means thousand. 3 kHz times 1000 gives 3000 Hz.
110302.m: One kilohertz is a thousand hertz.

110303.q: What did Heinrich Hertz prove for the first time with his experiments?
110303.e: Between 1886 and 1888 Heinrich Hertz was able to produce and detect electromagnetic waves. This confirmed James Clerk Maxwell's theory.
110303.m: Heinrich Hertz proved that electromagnetic waves exist.

110304.q: At rest, a heart beats 60 times per minute. What frequency is that?
110304.e: 60 beats per minute are 60 beats in 60 seconds, so 1 beat per second. That is 1 Hz.
110304.m: Once per second is one hertz.

110305.q: What does the abbreviation MHz, often seen with radio stations, stand for?
a: Millihertz, a thousandth of a hertz
Microhertz, a millionth of a hertz
110305.e: Mega means a million. FM radio stations broadcast between about 87.5 and 108 megahertz.
110305.m: One megahertz is a million hertz.

110306.q: Which country did the physicist Heinrich Hertz come from?
110306.e: Heinrich Hertz was born in Hamburg in 1857 and did research in Karlsruhe and Bonn, among other places.
110306.m: Heinrich Hertz was a German physicist.

110307.e: You divide by 1000: 20,000 Hz divided by 1000 gives 20 kHz.
110307.m: A thousand hertz make one kilohertz.

110308.q: What is the amplitude of a vibration?
a: The greatest displacement from the rest position
The number of vibrations per second
The distance between two wave crests
110308.e: The amplitude tells you how far a vibrating object moves at most from its rest position.
110308.m: The amplitude is the greatest displacement.

110309.q: What happens to a sound when the amplitude of the vibration gets bigger?
110309.e: A bigger amplitude means stronger pressure changes in the air. The ear then hears the sound as louder.
110309.m: Bigger amplitude means a louder sound.

110310.q: Does the pitch change if you pluck a guitar string harder?
a: Yes, the note gets much higher
Yes, the note gets much lower
110310.e: Plucking harder increases the amplitude, not the frequency. The note gets louder but stays at the same pitch.
110310.m: The amplitude decides the loudness, not the pitch.

110311.q: What do you call a vibration whose amplitude keeps getting smaller over time?
110311.e: Because of friction, a vibrating object loses energy. Its amplitude decreases until it comes to rest.
110311.m: In a damped vibration the amplitude decreases.

110312.q: How can you see the amplitude of a sound on an oscilloscope?
a: From the height of the curve
From the colour of the curve
From the width of the screen
110312.e: An oscilloscope shows the vibration as a curve. The higher the peaks up and down, the bigger the amplitude.
110312.m: High peaks show a large amplitude.

110313.q: Why does a sound get quieter the further you are from the source?
a: The amplitude of the sound wave decreases
110313.e: The sound energy spreads over a bigger and bigger area. The pressure changes, and so the amplitude, get smaller.
110313.m: With growing distance the amplitude decreases.

110314.q: A pendulum swings 10 cm to the left and 10 cm to the right of its rest position. What is the amplitude?
110314.e: The amplitude is measured from the rest position. The greatest displacement is 10 cm; the whole way from left to right would be 20 cm.
110314.m: The amplitude is measured from the rest position.

110315.q: What is the resting position called from which the amplitude is measured?
110315.e: Without a push, a pendulum or a string stays in the rest position. The amplitude is the greatest distance from it.
110315.m: The amplitude is measured from the rest position.

110318.q: What does the prefix “deci” in decibel mean?
110318.e: Deci means one tenth, as in decilitre. So a decibel is one tenth of a bel.
110318.m: A decibel is one tenth of a bel.

110319.q: Who is the unit bel, from which the decibel comes, named after?
110319.e: The bel honours Alexander Graham Bell, a pioneer of the telephone.
110319.m: The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell.

110320.q: Which device measures the sound level in decibels?
110320.e: A sound level meter picks up sound with a microphone and shows the level in decibels. It is used, for example, to check the noise at concerts.
110320.m: Sound level is measured with a sound level meter.

110321.q: Roughly how does an increase of 10 dB affect how loud something sounds to humans?
a: About a hundred times as loud
110321.e: The ear does not hear loudness in the same proportion as the sound energy grows. A sound with 10 dB more only seems about twice as loud.
110321.m: Ten decibels more sounds about twice as loud.

110323.q: From what sound level can listening for a long time damage your hearing?
110323.e: If you listen to noise above 85 dB for a long time, such as loud music through headphones, you can damage your hearing permanently. Ear protection helps.
110323.m: Loud noise over a long time damages hearing.

110324.q: Roughly what frequency range can young people hear?
110324.e: The human hearing range goes from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz. In older people the upper limit is often lower.
110324.m: People hear from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz.

110325.q: What happens to the upper limit of hearing as people get older?
110325.e: As you get older, you hear high sounds less well. Many adults only hear up to about 15 kilohertz or less.
110325.m: With age, high sounds are harder to hear.

110326.q: In which frequency range is the human ear most sensitive?
110326.e: In the range of about 2 to 5 kilohertz, even a very quiet sound is enough for us to hear it. Important speech sounds are also in this range.
110326.m: The ear is most sensitive to middle and high sounds.

110327.q: Which animal can hear much higher sounds than humans?
110327.e: Dogs hear very high sounds that we humans cannot hear at all. That is why there are dog whistles that are silent to us.
110327.m: Dogs hear higher sounds than people.

110328.q: Why are there alarm tones of around 17 kHz that mostly young people hear?
a: Older people often can't hear such high sounds any more
Adults only hear low sounds above 20 kHz
110328.e: The upper limit of hearing starts to drop in young adulthood. So a very high tone of around 17 kHz is usually only heard by young people.
110328.m: Very high sounds are mainly heard by young people.

110329.q: How many octaves does the human hearing range from 20 Hz to 20,480 Hz cover?
110329.e: Each octave doubles the frequency. 20 times 2 to the power of 10 gives 20,480, so it is 10 octaves.
110329.m: The human hearing range covers about ten octaves.

110330.q: What is the curve called that shows how quiet a sound can be at each frequency and still be heard?
110330.e: The threshold of hearing is lowest at middle frequencies. For very low and very high sounds, much more sound is needed to hear them.
110330.m: The threshold of hearing shows the quietest sound you can hear.

110331.q: Where are the lowest notes on a piano keyboard?
110331.e: From left to right the notes get higher and higher. The lowest note on the far left is close to the lower limit of human hearing.
110331.m: On a piano the low notes are on the left.

110332.q: Which test does an ear doctor use to check which sounds you hear and how well?
110332.e: In an audiogram you hear tones of different frequencies through headphones. It records how quiet they can be for you still to hear them.
110332.m: An audiogram shows how well a person hears.

110333.q: How does an ultrasonic humidifier make the air moist?
a: It turns water into a fine mist
It draws in rain from outside
110333.e: A fast-vibrating plate creates ultrasound in the water. This releases tiny droplets from the surface, which form a cool mist.
110333.m: Ultrasound can turn water into mist.

110334.q: What is ultrasound often used for in medicine?
a: To make organs inside the body visible
110334.e: In sonography, a probe sends ultrasound into the body. The echoes create an image, for example of the heart or liver.
110334.m: Ultrasound lets you look inside the body.

110335.q: What is the device on ships called that uses sound to locate objects underwater?
110335.e: Sonar sends sound pulses into the water and measures the echoes that come back. This finds shoals of fish, submarines or obstacles.
110335.m: Sonar locates things underwater with sound.

110336.q: How does an ultrasonic bath clean glasses or jewellery?
a: The water is brought to the boil
It blows air onto the jewellery
110336.e: The ultrasound creates tiny bubbles in the water that suddenly collapse. This loosens dirt even from fine cracks.
110336.m: Ultrasound loosens dirt with tiny bubbles.

110337.q: Why can a dog hear a dog whistle but a person can't?
a: It produces no sound at all
110337.e: A dog whistle produces sounds above 20 kilohertz. These are outside the human hearing range but within that of dogs.
110337.m: Dog whistles whistle in the ultrasound range.

110338.q: What does industry use ultrasound for when testing materials?
a: To find hidden cracks in components
110338.e: Ultrasound is reflected by cracks or hollow spaces inside. This is how rails or aircraft parts are checked without destroying them.
110338.m: Ultrasound finds hidden faults in components.

110339.q: Which device in a car uses ultrasound to measure the distance to obstacles?
110339.e: Sensors on the bumper send out ultrasound and measure the time until the echo returns. From this the distance is calculated and shown with beeps.
110339.m: Parking sensors measure distances with ultrasound.

110340.q: Why is gel spread on the skin during an ultrasound scan?
a: So there is no air between the probe and the skin
So the device doesn't get hot
110340.e: Air would reflect almost all the ultrasound. The gel makes sure the sound gets into the body well.
110340.m: The gel lets the ultrasound into the body.

110341.q: Below which frequency is sound called infrasound?
110341.e: Infrasound is too low for human hearing. It is below about 20 hertz.
110341.m: Infrasound is too low for people to hear.

110342.q: Which land animal also communicates over several kilometres using infrasound?
110342.e: Elephants make deep rumbling sounds, some of which are below 20 hertz. These carry over great distances.

110343.q: Why does infrasound travel especially far?
a: The air hardly absorbs low sounds
Infrasound is boosted by the wind
110343.e: Air strongly damps high frequencies but hardly damps low ones. So infrasound can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometres.
110343.m: Low sounds travel further than high ones.

110344.q: Which natural event produces strong infrasound?
110344.e: Volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and avalanches move huge masses. This creates infrasound that measuring stations far away record.

110345.q: Which sea animal makes very deep sounds, some of them in the infrasound range?
110345.e: Blue whales make very deep and loud calls. These are around 20 hertz and below and can be measured over long distances in the sea.
110345.m: Blue whales call with very deep sounds.

110346.q: Can people sense infrasound even though they can't hear it?
a: Yes, very strong infrasound as pressure or vibration
Yes, as a taste on the tongue
110346.e: Very strong infrasound can be felt as a sense of pressure or vibration in the body, even if you hear no sound.

110347.q: Why does the organisation monitoring the nuclear test ban treaty run infrasound stations around the world?
a: To detect nuclear weapons tests in the air
110347.e: Explosions create strong infrasound that spreads far. A worldwide network of stations can thus detect nuclear tests.

110348.q: An infrasound tone has 10 Hz. How long is its wavelength in air at 340 m/s?
110348.e: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency: 340 m/s divided by 10 Hz gives 34 m.

110349.q: Which mammal uses echolocation to find its prey in flight at night?
110349.e: Bats give out ultrasonic calls and hear the echoes from insects. This lets them hunt even in total darkness.

110350.q: Which sea animal uses clicking sounds for echolocation?
110350.e: Dolphins make clicking sounds and interpret the echoes that return. This lets them detect fish and obstacles.

110351.q: An echo sounder receives the echo from the seabed after 2 seconds. How deep is the sea at 1500 m/s?
110351.e: The sound travels there and back: 1500 m/s times 2 s gives 3000 m. The depth is half of that, so 1500 m.
110351.m: With an echo, only half the distance counts.

110352.q: Someone shouts at a rock face and hears the echo after 3 seconds. How far away is the wall at 340 m/s?
110352.e: The sound travels 340 m/s times 3 s, which is 1020 m, there and back. The wall is half as far, so 510 m away.
110352.m: For the distance, halve the path of the echo.

110353.q: Why do bats use very high sounds for echolocation?
a: Short waves also reveal small insects
Low sounds don't exist at night
110353.e: Ultrasound has very short wavelengths of a few millimetres. This means even small insects can still be detected as an echo.
110353.m: Short waves make small things detectable.

110354.q: How does a bat tell how far away an insect is?
a: From the time it takes for the echo to return
From the colour of the insect
From the smell of the echo
110354.e: The further away the insect, the longer the call takes to go there and back. From this time the bat estimates the distance.
110354.m: The travel time of the echo gives away the distance.

110355.q: How can some blind people explore their surroundings with echolocation?
a: With tongue clicks and listening to the echoes
110355.e: Some blind people click their tongues and listen to how the sound comes back from walls or cars. This lets them detect obstacles.

110356.q: How does a dolphin use its clicks to find out where a fish is swimming?
a: From the echoes that come back
From the smell in the water
From the colour of the water
From the warmth of the fish
110356.e: Dolphins send out clicks. When they hit a fish, an echo comes back, and the dolphin knows where the fish is. It focuses the sounds with a fatty organ on its forehead.
110356.m: Dolphins find prey using the echoes of their clicks.

a: Strong vibration at the natural frequency
110357.e: During resonance, an object that can vibrate takes in a particularly large amount of energy. Its amplitude can then become very large.
110357.m: Resonance is strong vibration at the right rhythm.

110358.q: How must you push a swing to make it go higher and higher?
a: In time with its own swinging
110358.e: If you push the swing exactly in the rhythm of its natural swing, energy is added with each push. That is resonance.
110358.m: At the right rhythm, a vibration builds up.

110359.q: What is the hollow wooden body of a guitar for?
a: It vibrates too and makes the sound louder
It makes the guitar easier to tune
110359.e: The strings make the sound box vibrate. It moves much more air than a string alone, so the sound gets louder.
110359.m: The sound box amplifies the sound.

110360.q: Why shouldn't soldiers march in step across a bridge?
a: The bridge could start vibrating dangerously
The echo would be too loud
The wind would blow them away
110360.e: If the rhythm of the steps matches the bridge's natural frequency, resonance can make it sway more and more. That is why soldiers break step on bridges.
110360.m: Marching in step can make a bridge sway.

110361.q: Which bridge in London had to be closed in 2000, shortly after it opened, because it swayed a lot under pedestrians?
110361.e: The steps of many people set the Millennium Bridge swaying sideways. After alterations it reopened in 2002.
110361.m: Even pedestrians can set a bridge swaying.

110362.q: Why does a tuning fork sound louder when you stand it on a suitable wooden box?
a: The box vibrates along in resonance
The wood makes a new note
The box makes the fork heavier
110362.e: The resonance box is built so that its column of air is tuned to the frequency of the tuning fork. It vibrates strongly too and amplifies the note.
110362.m: A resonance box amplifies a tuning fork.

110363.q: What can happen if a very loud sound exactly matches the natural frequency of a wine glass?
110363.e: With resonance the glass vibrates more and more. If the vibration gets too big, it can break.
110363.m: Resonance can make a glass shatter.

110364.q: How do we stop resonant vibrations in buildings and bridges from becoming too strong?
110364.e: Dampers take energy from the vibration. This stops the amplitude from building up dangerously.

110365.q: What mainly explains why a flute and a violin sound different when playing the same note?
110365.e: Both play the same fundamental note, but with overtones of different strengths. This mix gives the tone colour.

110366.q: In acoustics, what do you call a sound made of a fundamental and several overtones?
110366.e: A pure tone has only one frequency. When overtones are added, it is called a complex tone, like those made by almost all musical instruments.
110366.m: A fundamental and overtones together make a complex tone.

110367.q: What frequencies do the overtones of an instrument's note have?
110367.e: In string and wind instruments the overtones fit in fixed ratios to the fundamental. This series of notes is called the harmonic series.
110367.m: Overtones are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

110368.q: Which Swiss instrument without keys or valves can only play the notes of the harmonic series?
110368.e: The alphorn is a long wooden tube without finger holes. The player uses their lips to choose notes only from the harmonic series.
110368.m: The alphorn only plays natural notes.

110369.q: Which sound source produces almost a pure tone without overtones?
110369.e: A struck tuning fork vibrates almost like a sine wave. Its note contains hardly any overtones, so it sounds very pure.
110369.m: A tuning fork produces an almost pure tone.

110370.q: A fundamental has 110 Hz. What frequency does the first overtone have?
110370.e: The first overtone has double the frequency of the fundamental. 110 Hz times 2 gives 220 Hz.
110370.m: The first overtone has double the frequency of the fundamental.

110371.q: What is the singing called in which a person makes a low note and a high, whistling melody at the same time?
110371.e: In overtone singing you shape your mouth and throat so that single overtones sound especially strong. This technique is common in Tuva and Mongolia, for example.
110371.m: In overtone singing, one person seems to sing in two voices.

110372.q: What happens if you lightly touch a guitar string exactly in the middle and pluck it?
110372.e: The light touch in the middle suppresses the fundamental. Only an overtone sounds, one octave higher.
110372.m: A harmonic in the middle of the string sounds an octave higher.

110373.q: Why do some notes of the alphorn sound slightly “off” to our ears?
a: It plays natural notes that don't fit exactly into our scale
The players play wrongly on purpose
The alphorn is always built out of tune
110373.e: The alphorn can only play notes of the harmonic series. Some of them, such as the well-known alphorn fa, lie between the notes of our usual scale.
110373.m: The alphorn fa is a typical natural note of the alphorn.

110374.q: Which living things break down dead plants and animals in an ecosystem?
a: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria
Predators such as birds of prey
110374.e: Decomposers break down dead living things. This returns the nutrients to the soil, where plants can use them again.
110374.m: Decomposers are the bin collectors of the ecosystem.

110375.q: What role do green plants have in an ecosystem?
110375.e: Through photosynthesis, green plants make nutrients from light, water and carbon dioxide. This produces the food on which all other living things depend.
110375.m: Green plants are the producers in an ecosystem.

110376.q: What is the whole of all the habitats and living things on Earth called?
110376.e: The biosphere includes all the parts of the Earth where there is life, from the sea floor to the lower layer of the air. It is, in a way, the largest ecosystem.
110376.m: The biosphere is the living part of the Earth.

110377.q: From which source does the energy for almost all of Earth's ecosystems come?
110377.e: Plants capture sunlight and store its energy in nutrients. Through food, this energy reaches all other living things.
110377.m: The sun is the energy engine of almost all ecosystems.

a: A meat eater that eats predators
110378.e: Primary consumers feed directly on producers, that is, on plants. An example is the caterpillar that eats leaves.

110379.q: Which of these ecosystems was created by humans?
110379.e: A field of grain is laid out, sown and looked after by people. Without this care, it would turn into a meadow over time and later into a forest.
110379.m: Fields are ecosystems created by humans.

110380.q: Why is a mixed forest usually more stable than a plantation of only spruce?
a: Many species make it more resistant to pests and storms
Spruces do not grow at all in mixed forests
A mixed forest needs no water
No insects live in a mixed forest
110380.e: In a pure spruce plantation, the bark beetle, for example, can spread quickly. In a mixed forest, only some of the trees are lost when there is damage.

110381.q: What is usually at the start of a food chain on land?
110381.e: Every food chain begins with a producer, on land usually a green plant. Then come plant eaters and then meat eaters.
110381.m: Food chains begin with a producer, on land usually a plant.

a: The habitat of a community of living things
All the animals of an area together
A cycle of substances in the soil
110382.e: A biotope is a habitat that can be marked off, with certain conditions such as soil, water, light and temperature. A certain community of living things lives in it.
110382.m: A biotope is a habitat with typical conditions.

110383.q: What does the Greek word “topos” in the term biotope mean?
110383.e: Biotope is made up of the Greek words “bios” for life and “topos” for place. So a biotope is a “place of life”.
110383.m: Biotope literally means place of life.

110384.q: Which of the following examples is a biotope?
110384.e: A pond is a habitat with certain conditions, such as still water and a muddy bottom. The brown hare is a living thing, not a habitat.
110384.m: A pond is a typical biotope.

110385.q: What is meant by a stepping-stone habitat?
a: A small habitat that links larger habitats
A paved path through the forest
A biotope made only of stones
110385.e: Stepping-stone habitats such as small ponds or bushes lie between larger habitats. Animals can use them as stopovers to get from one habitat to the next.
110385.m: Stepping-stone habitats help animals to move between habitats.

110386.q: What is the habitat along a river that is regularly flooded called?
110386.e: Floodplains are flooded during high water and then dry out again. This change creates gravel banks, ponds and softwood forests with many species.
110386.m: Floodplains are shaped by the change between floods and dry periods.

110387.q: Which habitats does the federal government list in an inventory as “biotopes of national importance”?
110387.e: The federal government keeps inventories of biotopes of national importance, for example raised bogs, fens, floodplains, amphibian spawning sites and dry meadows and pastures.
110387.m: Raised bogs are among the biotopes of national importance.

110388.q: At a pond, what is part of the biotope and not of the community of living things?
110388.e: The biotope includes the non-living conditions such as temperature, light and the ground. Frogs, water lilies and dragonfly larvae are living things and belong to the community.
110388.m: Non-living conditions belong to the biotope.

110389.q: Why are no fish put into a pond meant for amphibians?
a: Fish make the water dirty at once
Fish make the pond dry out
110389.e: Many fish eat frogspawn and tadpoles. In ponds without fish, frogs, toads and newts therefore have a much better chance.
110389.m: A pond for amphibians is best left without fish.

110390.q: Why is dead wood left in the forest on purpose?
a: It is a home for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers
It protects the forest from thunderstorms
It makes the soil acidic and infertile
It keeps deer away from the forest
110390.e: Countless insects, fungi and mosses live in dead wood. Woodpeckers look for food there and make holes that other animals use later.
110390.m: Dead wood is a valuable habitat in the forest.

110391.q: What is meant by a biocoenosis?
a: All the living things in a particular habitat
The non-living part of a habitat
110391.e: The biocoenosis is the community of all the plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms that live together in a biotope.
110391.m: The biocoenosis is the community of living things in a biotope.

a: All the plants, animals and fungi in a pond
The water and the mud of a pond
110392.e: The biocoenosis includes all the living things that live together in a habitat. Water, mud and temperature are non-living and belong to the biotope.
110392.m: The biocoenosis includes all the living things in a habitat.

110393.q: What belongs to the biocoenosis of a forest floor?
110393.e: The biocoenosis includes all living things, even tiny bacteria. Minerals, water and oxygen are non-living.
110393.m: Bacteria are part of the community of living things too.

110394.q: Which living things in a community break down dead plants and animals?
110394.e: Decomposers such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down dead living things. This releases minerals that plants can take up again.
110394.m: Decomposers close the cycle of substances in the community.

110395.q: What belongs to the plant part of a forest's community of living things?
110395.e: Mosses and ferns are plants. Roe deer, foxes, beetles and ants are animals, and stones and water are non-living.
110395.m: The community of living things includes plants and animals.

110396.q: What often happens when all the predators of a prey species disappear from a community?
a: The prey species multiplies a lot
The prey species dies out at once
110396.e: Without predators, an important brake is missing. The prey animals become more numerous and can, for example, eat far too many plants.
110396.m: Predators keep the numbers of their prey in check.

110397.q: Why is the beaver considered a keystone species in its community?
a: It dams streams and creates habitat for many species
It is the largest animal by the water
It lives in only one single valley
110397.e: With its dams, the beaver creates ponds, wetlands and dead wood. Amphibians, dragonflies, fish and birds benefit from this.
110397.m: The beaver shapes habitats for many other species.

110398.q: What kind of relationship is there between the fox and the field vole?
110398.e: The fox hunts and eats voles. It is the predator, and the vole is the prey.
